Uniform Title: *Prāṇatoṣiṇī*, Section on Ritual Purpose (*Arthakāṇḍa*) Author: Rāmatoṣaṇa Compiler:
Rāmatoṣaṇa Bhaṭṭācārya Description: Compiled by Rāmatoṣaṇa Bhaṭṭācārya; originally published in Kolkata in Bengali script as part of the *Tantrasārādivividhatantrasaṃgraha*.
Notes: Data entered by the staff of Muktabodha under the supervision of Mark S. G. Dyczkowski. Revision 0: December 11, 2007.
Publisher: Kalikātā.
Year of publication: Pre-1900.
Country of Publication: India | Title Page || Śrīḥ ||
The *Prāṇatoṣiṇī* was composed by Śrī Rāmatoṣaṇa Bhaṭṭācārya,
having compiled it from the Tantric scriptures.
And it was published by the learned Kulapati bearing the title *Upādhyāya*, Śrī Jīvānanda Vidyāsāgara Bhaṭṭācārya,
in the city of Calcutta.
Printed at the Kālikātā Press;

may the Goddess of Speech—who bears a crescent of the new moon as her ornament, possesses the luster of a moonstone, and is worshipped by gods, humans, and others—protect us. This is the third volume, the section on meaning (*arthakāṇḍa*).
May she who is seated upon a pure lotus, serene, delightful with the nine rasas, and the sovereign of the arts such as music, listen!
Śrī Rāmatoṣaṇa, who abides by the command of Śrī Prāṇakṛṣṇa and is a sovereign supported by the lineage of the Maitreya clan,
has composed this beautiful section on meaning, produced through the grace of his own chosen deity.
I am composing a glossary for the third section on meaning;
for some [terms], others have been specified, which should be consulted in their respective places.
Therein are the seven types of conduct as well as the sequence of Vedic conduct.
Having arisen, one should perform the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) and other rites, followed by meditation upon the Guru.
Then comes mental worship with the five offerings consisting of the five elements;
thereafter, meditation on the True Guru and the salutation to the Kula-tree.
The recitation of the sandals' mantra, the proclamation of its greatness,
and immediately thereafter the mantra for the worship of the Guru and his wife;
then the mantra for recitation (japa), the hymn of praise to the Guru (gurustotra), the armor-verse (kavaca), and the prostration to the Guru.
Then follows salutation to the true guru and salutation to the Brahmins and others;
thereafter, meditation on the female guru, her hymns of praise, and her armor-mantra (kavaca);
then the worship of the guru’s body and the description of the lineage of gurus.
Thus ends the section on the determination of the nature of the text and so forth.
Following that is the meditation on Kuṇḍalinī, then her hymn and armor (kavaca),
and thereafter the recitation and dedication of the mantras of Sūrya, Gaṇeśa, and others.
The exposition of the distinctions between meditation on the *haṃsa*, the *ajapa* [mantra], and the countless repetitions of the *japa*; (p.

277) as well as meditation on the Self (*ātma-dhyāna*) and so forth, the external sequence of movement, and likewise friendliness (*maitra*), the cleaning of the teeth, the purification of the nose, and the application of collyrium.
Following that, there is the hymn on the sequence of smearing and other rites for the temple;
thereafter, the second chapter concludes.
Next follows the fruit of bathing, the various types of bathing, and the determination of internal bathing.
The daily bath, the procedure for bathing, the declaration "that is good," the formal resolve (saṅkalpa), the vessels prohibited for that [rite], the determination of the appropriate vessel,
the invocation of the sacred ford (tīrtha-āvāhana), the six-fold placement on the limbs (aṅga-ṣaṭka-nyāsa), and likewise the recitation of the root mantra (mūla-japa).
The touching of clay, the sprinkling with water from a conch,
and thereafter the brief libation (tarpaṇa), as well as the duty regarding the "other well" (parakhāta);
by that [rite], the prohibition of bathing and the wiping of the body with a cloth [are established].
The prohibition against wiping the body, the determination of its cause,
the meditation on the Gaṅgā, the fruit of the mantra, the majesty of the sacred field (kṣetra),
the majesty of the names of the Gaṅgā beginning from the first, and thereafter the fruit of dying in the Gaṅgā.
The fruit for one traveling on that journey is death on the road; the fruit arising from offering funeral cakes (piṇḍa) within four cubits of the Ganges water is death upon reaching the bank.
Regarding the fruit arising from the libation (tarpaṇa) in the Ganges, there is no consideration of time or season.
In that regard, there is no determination of faults such as theft on the Gaṅgā;
rather, there is only the mental bath performed by the nectar of ritual ablution.
Following that, according to the distinction of rites, there is the measurement of the cloth to be worn, and then the fine silk garment.
Then follows the prohibition of blue garments and so forth, as well as the upper garment;
the triple yoga-pada, the sacred thread, and then the ritual purification;
the tilaka according to its different locations and the description of its forms.
The vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra), its fruit, and the censure of other rites in its absence;
thereafter, the prohibition of the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) on the vertical mark;
and the vertical mark for Vaiṣṇavas and the triple mark for Brāhmaṇas and others.
The method of preparing the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) is threefold, beginning with the excellent;
next is the fruit according to its different colors, followed by the censurable marks;
and the shape of the vertical mark is threefold, characterized as the abode of Hari.
The result of breaking the fingers while making the *puṇḍra*, the clay for the *puṇḍra*,
the majesty of *gopīcandana*, the fruit of its gift,
and thereafter the majesty of the earth from the root of the *tulasī* tree.

Following that, there is the [description of] the remains of Viṣṇu’s offerings (nirmālya), his unguents, and his forehead mark (tilaka). Then follows the commencement of the ritual for applying the twelve tilakas according to rule.
After that is the determination of the locations for wearing the triple horizontal mark (tripuṇḍra).
The verses on the five Brahmans concerning the ashes used for the *tripuṇḍra*,
the *Kālāgnirudra Upaniṣad* regarding the fruit of the *tripuṇḍra*,
the censure of not wearing the *tripuṇḍra*, and the determination of the *śakti-tilaka*.
Thus ends the third section;
now the conclusion is stated: the twilight ritual (*sandhyā*) prescribed by the Vedas must be performed, and immediately thereafter, the Tantric ritual.
Furthermore, there is the censure of one who neglects the twilight ritual, and the performance of that [Tantric] rite on the twelfth lunar day (*dvādaśī*) and other such occasions.
After that, the twilight rite of the yogis (yogisandhyā), followed by the libation for the yogis (yogitarpaṇa);
then their worship of the Sun (ādityapūjā), and after that, the Kaula twilight rite (kaulasandhyā).
Immediately following that is the method of the Vedic ritual sprinkling (mārjana).
The meaning of the *gāyatrī* and the *vyāhṛtis*, followed by the meaning of the *gāyatrī* itself;
then the *sandhyā* which has the same color and form [as the deity], as well as the deity of that same color;
the fruit of meditating upon that same color, and after that, its *yantra*.
Then follow the seers (ṛṣis) of both the Praṇava and the Gāyatrī;
thereafter, the placement of the words (padanyāsa), the placement of the head (śironyāsa), and the placement of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa).
Following that is meditation upon her, and within that meditation, the seers and other [limbs] as well.

Recitation [of mantras] is censured without ritual placement (nyāsa), and ritual placement is [censured] without the hand-gesture (mudrā). After that, there is the worship of Gāyatrī and the worship of the seat (pīṭha), as well as the worship of the ten enclosures (daśāvaraṇa); in the absence of ritual substances, this is performed with water and so forth.
Furthermore, [I shall explain] the fruit of recitation for a living being, the specific distinctions, and the sequence of recitation.
Even during impurity, mental recitation of the Gāyatrī is prescribed. The dedication of its recitation, its armor (kavaca), and its preliminary ritual (puraskriyā) are likewise taught.
The determination of the fruit of the Gāyatrī according to the Tantric method for optional rites;
the fruit of its recitation, its *puraścaraṇa*,
and the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of its seers (*ṛṣi*) and other attributes, as well as meditation performed at the three junctions of the day.
Next is the arrival at the place of sacrifice and the washing of the feet;
after that, the worship of the door according to the various Vaiṣṇava and other traditions; and immediately following that, entry into the house of worship and the taking of the seat.

Furthermore, there is a distinction in the fruits of the seat for householders; likewise, the specific results of using a black antelope skin among seats follow from that. There are also distinctions regarding wooden seats, as well as seats made of grass and other materials.
The measurement of the seat, then the *karmabheda* seat;
thereafter the *śavāsana* and so forth, followed by the censure of hairy seats;
then the *ṛṣi* and other [mantras] for the seat, and the form of the seat for ascetics (*yatins*).
The *yatibhinnāsana* should be known as square on all sides;
the prohibition of placing the feet upon the thighs is the characteristic of *prauḍhapāda*.
Following that are *siddhāsana* and *padmāsana*, which are useful for yoga.

The place for placing the ritual substances, the three types of vessels, the vessel for water for the feet (*pādya-pātra*), then the characteristics of the supporting vessel for the water for the feet, the characteristics of the leather vessel, and the characteristics of the *cāma* vessel. (p. 279)
Next is the description of the water-vessel and the betel-box.
Thus ends the fourth section on the cutting of sprouts (*pallavaviccheda*).
Now follows the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*), which effects the destruction of the sinful body.

The meditation on the personification of sin (pāpapuruṣa) involves the dissolution of the elements beginning with earth; this is necessary for the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi). The establishment of one's own vital breaths (prāṇapratiṣṭhā) follows. Furthermore, breath control (prāṇāyāma) serves as the support for its worship during the ritual adoration of the mantra-stone.
One should never construct a yantra even in the vicinity of an image;
when two types of worship are performed, there is a prohibition against worshipping an earthen (pārthiva) linga.
However, in the case of specific mantras (vidyāviśeṣa), even there, the yantra is for the sake of the practitioner’s success in worship.
The form of Brahmā is declared to consist of white, black, and other colors;
immediately thereafter, the seed-syllables for the eyes and other features of Kālikā’s form are given,
and the manifestation of the deity within an image and so forth is described.

The eternality of the forms of Kṛṣṇa and others, the mantra for the installation of life (prāṇapratiṣṭhā), the assignment of its seer (ṛṣi) and other attributes, as well as the six-limbed assignment (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa);
thereafter, the assignment of the mantra, meditation, worship, and the preliminary rite (puraskriyā).
The messengers of the vital breaths, their application, and the construction of their diagrams follow thereafter.
First the seat, then water for the feet, the respectful offering (arghya), and thereafter water for sipping; then the honey-mixture (madhuparka), followed again by water for sipping;
then the word "gandha"—its etymological derivation and the fruit arising from its giving.
The eightfold scents, the fivefold flowers, and their specific origins are described; then the flower of the *karavīra* and its fruit are proclaimed.
Furthermore, the fruit of relinquishing one's life at the root of the *karavīra* and other such plants is taught.
Immediately after that is the majesty of the white karavīra and other varieties;
then the majesty of aparājitā and others arising from the offering of specific flowers;
and thereafter the fruit of flowers and the fruit of the black aparājitā.
Regarding fruits such as the *rasāla* blossom used in the worship of the Śrīcakra,
the specific expiation for using [inappropriate] flowers is stated thereafter;
following that, the reason for the prohibition against offering flowers still attached to the tree is given.
The midday bath for a mortal, the censure of gathering flowers,
the prohibition against breaking a flower-garland or a sacrificial thread-garland,
and the flowers to be avoided according to different times and different deities— these are the subjects [of this section].
The etymology of the word *dhūpa* is "incense," and its fruit is born from the giving thereof.
The etymology of the word *dīpa* is "lamp," followed by "garment.
After that come "ornament," "food offering" (*naivedya*), and "betel-leaf" (*tāmbūla*).
Betel-leaf is indeed prohibited, as is the bending of the head; after that,
the knowledge of the proper time for the *nirmālya* (remains of offerings) to be presented to the deity,
along with messages and the like, and the coconut fruit accompanied by sweets.
The fruit of the *iṅgudī* and others is recommended, as is leafy vegetable (*śāka*) derived from roots and the like.

The *tintiḍī*, the mountain cucumber (*girikuṣmāṇḍa*), and forest-grown produce are likewise prohibited. So too are the citron (*bījapūra*), plantain (*kadala*), and unseasonal breadfruit (*apanasa*).
Regarding the grains that are to be given and those which are thereafter prohibited:
salt and alkaline substances are forbidden, as are those produced from the east (prācībhūta) and the like;
the meat of deer and other such animals may be offered, but buffalo meat is likewise forbidden.
Milk, curd, and ghee; birds such as the green pigeon (*harita*) and others; and fish such as the *citraka* and others are to be offered. However, the *viḍālikā* is prohibited.
Those birds known by names such as *jānapada* and the like are not to be eaten.
Likewise, vegetables such as the kausumbhaka and others are declared inedible;
grains such as the rāmarambhā and śrāvaṇika are forbidden;
as are the golden-hued coconut and the sugary karkandhu fruit.
Bitter tortoises, fish, cow-fish, and the like should not be given.
Regarding what is edible and what is inedible, there are differences according to region; furthermore, Tantrikas must strictly avoid them.
Likewise, one should avoid meat that has been dead for three nights, as well as meat that has been kept for that duration.
The fruit of renouncing meat is especially great at the beginning of the month of Kārttika and other such times.
Birds, whether normally edible or inedible, as well as humans, monkeys, and the like, are inedible [as food].
Beyond that, there is a penance for consuming the flesh of dogs and similar animals.
The fruits of renouncing meat at the weighing ceremony (tulā) and other rites are likewise manifold;

furthermore, the fruit of renouncing meat for as long as one lives should be understood accordingly. Then, sacrificial food (haviṣya) and other types of food are to be known as appropriate to their respective contexts.
In the first chapter of the Nityātantra.
O Goddess! The four [traditions] beginning with the Vedas are established in the state of the bound soul (paśubhāva);
the three practices beginning with Vāma are established in the Divine (divya) and the Heroic (vīra).
These seven practices are clarified in the fifth section of the *Kulārṇava*.
Of all [scriptures], the Vedas are supreme; among the Vedas, the Vaiṣṇava is great.
Superior to the Vaiṣṇava is the Śaiva; superior to the Śaiva is the Dakṣiṇa;
superior to the Dakṣiṇa is the Vāma; and superior to the Vāma is the Siddhānta.
The Kaula is superior to the Siddhānta; indeed, there is nothing higher than the Kaula.
In the Nityātantra.
I shall proclaim the conduct of the Vedas; listen, O lady beautiful in every limb!

Having risen during the *muhūrta* sacred to Brahmā and having bowed to the Guru with one's own names, the practitioner should then worship [the deity] by appending the word "Ānandanātha" [to the end].
Having meditated upon the thousand-petaled lotus and performed the fivefold offerings,
one should recite the Vāgbhava seed-syllable and contemplate the supreme digit (kalā).
In the second chapter of the Uttarakhanda of the Rudrajāmala.
Having risen at dawn during the time of sunrise and performed his morning duties and so forth, the man, remaining upon his bed,
should meditate upon the Guru within the thousand-petaled lotus of his head.

Here, by virtue of forming a single syntactical unit with the previously stated statement, [the same applies] to the "Brāhma-muhūrta at dawn" and likewise to the "latter watch" and so forth that will be described below.
In that regard, in the first chapter of the first section of the Rudrajāmala:

"Having risen during the Brāhmī-muhūrta, the wise man, having assumed the bound lotus posture (baddhapadmāsana) and performed the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) and other rites, should remember his Guru in the morning."
And by the word "etcetera," one should include meditation on the chosen deity and so forth.
And likewise, in the first chapter of the Nīlatantra:
Having arisen during the final watch of the night, one should meditate upon Ugratāriṇī,
who extends from the base of the spine to the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*), whose nature is like a thread of poison,
who consists of the root mantra, and who is the manifest embodiment of nectar and bliss.
Resembling ten million suns, as cool as ten million moons,
and possessing a gaze equal to ten million flashes of lightning atop the crest of the fire of desire;
his body was turned pale-red, pervaded by the mass of her radiance.

One should meditate upon the Guru, who resides upon a thousand-petaled lotus on the crown of the head, seated upon a swan; who possesses the luster of the full moon, whose lotus-hands display the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, who is sprinkled with pure fragrant flowers, whose face and eyes are serene, and who embodies the form of all deities— reciting his name preceded by that [of the deity].
In the Pūrvakhaṇḍa of the Rudrajāmala as well, this is the case; however, at the end of the second quarter, the reading is "puṣpasrajam" (a garland of flowers).
Also in the second chapter of the Viśvasāra:
In the morning, one should remember the Guru— two-eyed and two-armed, with hands in the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, peaceful— upon a white lotus on the head, preceded by his name.
And in the first chapter of the *Kaṅkālamālinītantra*:
"The inner self, radiant, resides within the thousand-petaled lotus;
above that, in the midst of the *nāda* and *bindu*, upon a radiant lion-throne."
There, one should always [visualize] one's own guru, resembling a mountain of silver,
seated in the vīrāsana posture, adorned with all ornaments,
wearing white garlands and garments, and with hands in the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
Accompanied by Vāmoruśakti, he gazes with compassion;
his beautiful body is held by his beloved with her left hand,
while she, adorned with red ornaments, holds a blue lotus in her left hand.
One should remember that [deity], endowed with knowledge and bliss, preceded by its name.
Also in the eastern section.
One should meditate on her who is intensely delighted, red in complexion, with her Śakti resting upon her left thigh, embracing her Lord with her own hand, and holding a blue lotus in her left hand.
As for that which is stated in the second chapter of the Uttarakhanda of the Rudrajāmala:
To the great teacher, a mass of splendor resembling the rising sun,
an ocean of infinite and boundless majesty, who bears the moon upon his crest,
whose body is exceedingly subtle and radiant— a mass of splendor, the great teacher.
The Guru, who is two-eyed and two-armed, seated upon a white lotus and clad in great white garments;
whose object is the realization of the Self, who is white-robed with splendor,
situated above the *ājñācakra*, and the cause of happiness for the virtuous.

The all-pervading Lord, the omniscient Sovereign of the world, who is the constituent part of virtue, wealth, desire, and liberation; who bestows boons and fearlessness; who is mounted upon a full-blown lotus;
who is radiant within and flickering with inner light; and who is adorned with a garland of forest flowers.
One should always worship the God of gods, who is richly adorned with jewel ornaments.
Thus, the meditation on the red-colored Guru has been described;
that refers specifically to the Rājasa Guru.
However, according to the opinion of Rāghavabhaṭṭa, the meditation on a red-colored Guru applies exclusively to the Śākta subject matter.
However, the claim that one should meditate on the white color itself when the object is other than that [of Śakti] is not correct;
for even in the case of Śakti, meditation on the white color is observed in the *Nīlatantra* and other texts,
as well as in the *Gurukavaca*.

Furthermore, because it will be stated later that "the Guru [resides] in the thousand-petaled great lotus, white as camphor," the claim by modern scholars— who accept the third-case compound *karpūraidhavalaḥ* (white by means of camphor) and thus assert that whiteness is mentioned while in reality the meditation is on a red color— is contrary to the authoritative instruction; for there is no scriptural evidence anywhere for the application of camphor [as a pigment].

"It does not exist," or it is red due to a mass of light-rays from the power (śakti) that is red in color; this will become clear in what is to be said later: "This, however, has white and red radiance."
In this context, however, it is stated that she is "merely red" (raktamātra) in order to indicate the preponderance of the power's radiance, according to the analogy of the javā flower and crystal.

Some, however, by the force of the Pāṇinian sūtra *vyatyayo bahulam* ("there is a frequent transposition [of genders]"), claim that this refers to meditation on the Guru as female through a change of gender.
As for the meditation on the Rājasa form as being red in color, I shall explain that further on.
In the Nīlatantra:

Then one should worship with mental perfumes and so forth, using their respective mudrās: the little finger is the earth element, and through its application, the offering of perfume is made; the thumb is the space element, and by that alone, the offering of flowers is made.
The index finger (tarjanī) is the air element (vāyutattva); one should offer incense with that very finger.

The middle finger (madhyamā) is the fire element (tejastattva); one should offer the lamp with that very finger. The ring finger (anāmā) is the water element (jalatattva); one should offer water with that very finger.
Then the wise one should mutter the Vāgbhava mantra one hundred and eight times;
having offered the recitation with devotion, he should prostrate himself on the ground like a staff.
Also in the *Annadākalpa*: [p. 283]
Having meditated upon the couple, the wise one should worship them with mental offerings, as well as with material offerings accompanied by mudrās and mantras—
namely, the mantras of earth, space, wind, fire, and water, together with the nasal bindu.

The little finger and the index finger, as well as the middle and ring fingers—by joining them with the thumbs, five mudrās are proclaimed. Fragrance has the earth as its essence; the flower has space as its essence.
Incense is said to be of the nature of air, while the lamp is supreme, being of the nature of fire;
the food offering is of the nature of taste; thus is the worship consisting of the five services (pañcopacāra). Thereafter, the wise one should mutter the Vāgbhava mantra one hundred and eight times.
And in the first chapter of the Kaṅkālamālinī Tantra:

Having worshipped with mental offerings, one should joyfully perform the ritual arrangement. One should offer fragrance, which is of the nature of earth; thereafter, the flower of intention (bhāvapuṣpa);
incense, which is of the nature of air, should be given, as well as a lamp by means of light.
One should offer the food-oblation as nectar and the drinking water as having the nature of Varuṇa;
one should also offer clothing, a mirror, a chowrie, and an umbrella.
Having worshipped with the respective application of mudrās, one should recite the mantra of one's own guru.
Having performed the recitation according to one's capacity and completed it, one should recite the armor-verse (*kavaca*).
The sequence of worship is found in the third section of the *Kulamūlāvatārakalpasūtra-ṭīkā*:

having meditated upon one’s own guru, one should worship with mental perfumes, unbroken rice grains, and flowers, [reciting]: "I worship the venerable sandals of Mukānandanātha and [the name] Śakti-ambā."

With the two little fingers, *laṃ*: I offer fragrance, whose nature is earth; *namaḥ*. With the two thumbs, *haṃ*: I offer flowers, whose nature is space; *namaḥ*. With the two index fingers, *yaṃ*: I offer incense, whose nature is air; *namaḥ*.
With the two middle fingers, I offer a lamp consisting of fire, *raṃ*, salutations. With the two ring fingers, I offer the food offering consisting of nectar, *vaṃ*, salutations.
Regarding the intermediate meditation (*dhyānāntara*), it is stated in the *Gurugītā*:

One should meditate upon the Guru, whose divine form is seated upon a throne in the center of the pericarp of the heart-lotus; who shines with the luster of a digit of the moon; and who bestows the desired boons of existence, consciousness, and bliss.
His divine form is adorned with pearls, and his left lap is occupied by his divine Śakti;
he is clad in white garments, anointed with white unguents, possesses a gentle smile, and embodies the fullness of all perfections.

Now, it may be asked: since the head-lotus is said to be the location of the Guru, how can meditation be performed upon the heart-lotus? This doubt is dispelled by the very statement from the *Rudrayāmala* written previously: "Sometimes [the Guru is] in the heart-lotus, and sometimes within the range of vision."
(p. 284) Now, regarding the meditation on the True Guru, it is said in the *Gurugītā*:

I bow to the True Guru, who is the bliss of Brahman, the bestower of supreme happiness, the embodiment of absolute knowledge, beyond all duality, resembling the sky, the goal indicated by such Mahāvākyas as "That Thou Art"; who is one, eternal, pure, immovable, ever-present as the witness, transcending all objective existence, and free from the three qualities.
I bow to him.
Thus ends the meditation on the True Guru.
In the *Rudrajāmala*, in the first section (*pūrvakhaṇḍa*), meditation on the Guru is taught immediately after the prostration to the *Kulavṛkṣa*.
And the family trees are described in the fourth chapter of the Revatītantra.
For example: the *harītakī*, likewise the *dhātrī*, the *nimba*, *aśvattha*, and *kadambaka*;
the *udumbara*, *vaṭa*, and *vilva*; and the *tintiḍī* is recorded as the ninth.
O Goddess, one should collect wood from a sacred tree and other materials for the purpose of the fire oblation.

By this, it follows that even wood such as *tintiḍī* may be used for kindling the fire for the purpose of the *homa*; however, the *samidh-homa* (oblation with fuel-sticks) must be performed with the aforementioned types of wood and so forth.
In the Rudrayāmala.
Having risen during the *muhūrta* known as Brāhmī and having prostrated before the family deity (*kulavṛkṣa*),

[one should meditate] upon the thousand-petaled lotus of the head, situated in the center of the lunar mandala, possessing three lines beginning with 'A', 'Ka', and 'Tha', and serving as the excellent seat for the *haṃsa* mantra.
The hero should meditate upon his own guru, who resembles a mountain of silver,
seated upon a lotus, with a smiling face and hands like lotuses granting boons and fearlessness,
wearing white garlands and garments, and anointed with white perfumes and unguents.
His body is embraced by the red Śakti seated upon his left thigh;
with her own right hand she holds his beautiful form,
while she, holding a blue lotus in her left hand, wears garments and garlands of deep red.
Bearing a white and red radiance, he is the very embodiment of Śiva and Durgā.
One should remember that [deity] as filled with the essence of supreme bliss, preceded by its name;
having first uttered the three *tāras*, then *hasakhaphreṃ*,
followed by *hasakṣamalavarayūṃ*, *hasakhaphreṃ*, and then *hasau*.
After [the name of] Amukānandanātha and immediately after [the name of] Amukīdevī,
having offered the Ambā-Śrīpādukā [ending with] "I worship" (pūjayāmi) and ending in "namas," this is the Śrīpādukā-mantra, which bestows all desired fruits.
"Having meditated upon the couple," and so forth;
then, up to "the wise one should mutter the Vāgbhava [mantra] one hundred and eight times," this is identical to the *Annadākalpa*.
The greatness of the sandals (pādukā-māhātmya) is found in the Padmavāhinī, as cited in the commentary on the Kulamūlāvatāra-kalpasūtra.
Indeed, by the mere knowledge of the sandals, they become liberated while living.
In the Kulārṇava:
The *vāgurā*, *mūla*, *balaya*, *mudrā*, and others have been made into morsels (*kavala*).

Thus, for those who possess the knowledge of the *Kulārṇava*, [the fruit] is established in the *pādukā*. [This is attained] through millions upon millions of great gifts and millions upon millions of great vows.
O Goddess, remembrance of the Śrīpādukā is superior to ten million times ten million great sacrifices;
remembrance of the Śrīpādukā is superior to ten million times ten million great Tantras, to bathing at ten million sacred fords, and to the worship of ten million deities.
In times of great disease, great calamity, great fault, and great fear;
in times of great adversity and great sin—the Guru’s sandals are remembered.
In the first chapter of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa of the Rudrajāmala.
Having placed Māyā and Lakṣmī before [the mantra], this is the procedure for worship everywhere:
"On the earth, offer the seed-syllable of Bhūmi along with fragrance.
Then there is the seed-syllable of Śambhu, which is of the nature of space (ākāśa) and joined with Nāda and Bindu.
Having said, "I offer the flower," one should thereafter [offer] the seed-syllable of Vāyu (Yaṃ).
In the sixth chapter of the *Puraścaraṇarasollāsa*:
Having first performed the worship of the Guru with garlands, sandalwood, ornaments,
and various decorations fashioned from gold and other materials;
O lady of beautiful limbs! One should worship the supreme guru with garments that are exceedingly fine— whether white, red, yellow, or black—
and with four kinds of foods served in enchanting golden vessels.
O Maheśānī! [I worship] with sixteen types of offerings, including drinking vessels fashioned from gold and silver, as well as pure gold,
and betel leaves accompanied by camphor and various fragrances.
O Goddess! One should worship Śivasiṃha with golden vessels.
[He is] Śivasiṃha, the Guru.
By this procedure, O Goddess, one should worship the Lord of the World.
After this, O lady of excellent hips, one should worship the wife of the Guru.
O Dear One! At the outset, one should worship the preceptor and then the Goddess with complete devotion using the sixteen services (upacāras).

Having thus meditated upon the Guru, one should worship him with lotus flowers according to the sequence of the internal sacrifice (*antaryāga*); because of this injunction, one should worship him with mental offerings (*mānasopacāra*).
The mantra for worship is found in the seventh chapter of the *Mātṛkābhedatantra*.

One should utter the seed-syllable of speech (*vāgbīja*), Mahāmāyā, and Viṣṇu’s power (*śakti*). Then [one should utter] *hasakhaphreṃ*, the mantra of Ānandabhairava, followed by his *śakti*-mantra, and then likewise *sehau sehau*.
O Goddess of the gods! O Beloved! This is the mantra of the Śrī Guru and likewise of the Śakti:
"I worship. The Guru is said to end with Ānandanātha, and the Śakti ends with Ambā; such is the procedure for worship, O Dear One!
Also in the Annadākalpa:
Having uttered the three *tāra*s, then *hasakhaphreṃ*;
then *hasakṣamalavarayūḥ*, *hasakhaphreṃ*, and *sehau*;
[followed by] at the end of *amukānandanātha* and immediately after *amukīdevī*.
Having offered the sandals of the venerable Mother, one should contemplate [her] ending with "namas.
This is the mantra of the venerable sandals (*śrīpādukā*), which bestows the fruit of all desires.
[This is stated] in the first chapter of the first section of the *Rudrajāmala*.
Having first offered the three stars, one should offer the syllables Śiva, Śakti, and Kha.
Phāgni (pha), the letter *e* with the bindu, and the sequence of Śiva and Śakti;
O Mistress of the Gods! [the letters] Earth, Moon, Fire, and Wind ending with the letter *u*;
Ānandanātha, Śakti, Śiva, and Bhuvaneśvara.
"Accompanied by the Visarga, the Great One, the Illuminator, the Supreme, the Fortune of Fire, Māyā, Sarasvatī— 'I worship the Śrīpādukā. Having thus recollected the Pādukā,
the mantra for recitation is found in the Rudrajāmala, first section, fifteenth chapter."
At the end of the word "Ānandanātha," one should utter the Guru's name in the dative case (ending in -e).

Then one should pronounce the word "namaḥ" followed by the Praṇava (Oṃ), which bestows all perfections. Having recited this mantra, which possesses great qualities, one shall become a master of all perfections.
Through the grace of the Guru’s mantra, the perfection of speech arises from the lotus of one’s mouth.
Having performed the offering after reciting the mantra one hundred and eight times daily, or a thousand, or likewise eight times, one should practice three rounds of breath control (prāṇāyāma).
Then, one should joyfully perform the procedure for breath control (prāṇāyāma) by means of the Vāgbhava [seed-syllable].
According to the previously mentioned statement from the *Nādakalpa* and the statement from the *Nīlatantra*, the Vāgbhava is also a mantra for recitation (*japa*).
Having recited the Guru-mantra one hundred and eight times or one thousand times according to the traditional lineage, [one should perform it] with the Vāgbhava.

Having performed three breath-control exercises (prāṇāyāma) and offered the recitation with the mantra beginning "guhyātiguhyagoptā," one should recite the hymn, the armor-verse (kavaca), and so forth.
As in the hymn:

I worship the Guru, the bestower of boons, who is seated upon a beautiful lotus on his head, possessing the luster of ten million young moons; whose lotus-hands grant the gestures of boon and fearlessness; who embodies the form of all deities; who is radiant with the lovely splendor of shimmering rays;
and whose two lotus-feet are illuminated and possess the brilliance of ten million drops of liquid lac. 1.

I worship the supreme Guru, who abides within the lotus of my eyes, who destroys the fear of the ocean of worldly existence, and through whose yoga one attains victory by worshipping the pair of lotus feet of the Teacher— which ward off the terror of the world and bestow both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
The pacification of diseases and the destruction of death. || 2 ||
I worship the Lord, the supreme and inferior Guru, who bestows all royal enjoyments, within the well-illuminated lotus known as the sixteen petals;
He possesses a halo of lightning-like splendor from His two large lotus-eyes, and bears the digit of the moon marked by a dot, with the reddish glow of a ruby.

I worship the Supreme Lord, possessed of great majesty, who has departed from the portion of Dakṣa; whose heart shines with the brilliance of a hundred suns, whose face is like ten million spotless moons; who utters deep and resonant sounds, whose body is both moving and unmoving, and who dwells upon the twelfth trembling petal. (4)

One should constantly meditate at dawn upon the auspicious lotus-feet of the Guru— feet that burn away the host of Mādana, possess the essence of golden anklets, and whose beautiful circle of toes is made resonant by various wonderful sounds; which are bent in the triple-fold (tribhaṅga) posture, as lovely as a mass of hundreds of rising suns, accessible through yoga, and situated in the lotus of the navel, O Beloved.
That which is meditated upon by yogis as being like a ten-petalled jewel.

She who was my mother, whose arms were as beautiful as those of the Dānavas and others, who was the limit of emanation in the past within the abode of Svādhiṣṭhāna on the six-petalled lotus at the base of Vaikuṇṭha; she who is conceived by me as the radiance of the Vedas, a wave of the states of emotion that uplifts one from birth, and the mother born from the source of peace bestowed by Kandarpa.
She is beloved by Viṣṇu and belongs to Śaṅkara.
She who bestows splendor with a radiant luster upon the path of the family of Bhāsānalakuṇḍalinī; who, at the root, resides in the region of the breath within the four-petalled lotus of the Kula;
she who is the manifest wish-fulfilling creeper for those who desire her; the beloved of the Self-born One while asleep; eternal; the remover of the fear of yogis and the destroyer of poison.
The Guru and the Mother are meditated upon. || 7 ||
May she protect you— she who has emerged from the jar of nectar atop the upward-pointing lotus, who is bathed in water, who follows the subtle path, who consists of light,

and who is radiant; she who is subtle, whose nature is the nectar within the sphere of practice, who is to be worshipped from the root-lotus to the lotus at the head, and who is meditated upon in the heart on this earth.
When will my mother rise up forever? || 8 ||

Whoever recites this daily, pervading all through the practice of maintaining stability, through meditation, or through worship, is a god and not a mere human. He shall obtain well-being, the granting of wealth, fame, long life, renown, and prosperity.
If one of keen intellect recites this at evening and at dawn,
he shall become the most excellent of practitioners, possessing a body like the wish-fulfilling tree (kalpavṛkṣa).
By the power of this hymn, he shall attain the status of the Lord of Speech.
Thus ends the hymn to the Guru accompanied by his Śakti in the Rudrajāmala.
In the commentary on the *Kulamūlāvatārakalpasūtra*.
There exists an additional verse for the *Pādukāpañcakastotra*;
it too is written here:
The circle of letters beginning with A, Ka, and Kha, which is indeed the Savior (*tāraka*) and bestows unbroken success.
O Śivā! How can bound souls perceive the syllable *ha* flashing within? || 1 ||

I worship the lotus of twelve syllables, eternally fixed within the interior of the lake-lotus at the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), pure and wonderful, adorned by the stalk of the opening of Kuṇḍalinī. || 2 ||

I worship that which consists of the Goddess, discernible within the bud-like cavity of his [Śiva’s] ear—where lines have been drawn with the line of the alphabet beginning with ‘A’, and where the state of the circle of ploughs is indicated by the corners. III.

Within that vessel, I meditate in my heart upon the body composed of consciousness, possessing a ruby-red luster rivaling the brilliance of a sharp flash of lightning, and adorned with the circle of the jewel-throne of Bindu and Nāda.

Above this, I contemplate the sky of the flame of the Fire-god— the locus for the expansion of its playful manifestation, intense with the great festival of universal incineration— as the primordial pair of swans.
There, his mind— cool as the nectar of the moon and a locus of auspiciousness— remembers the pair of the Lord’s lotus feet, which are like a stream of saffron-liquor and honey.

I worship the pair of lotus-feet of the Guru situated upon my head— feet reddened by the rays of the toe-nails which flash like golden lotus-stalks that dispel the clamor of sins, adorned with jeweled sandals, and possessing the luster of a lotus risen from the lake of supreme nectar.
The *Pādukāpañcakastotra*, which emerged from the mouth of the Swan-faced One,
yields the fruit of the six traditions and is exceedingly rare in this world of manifestation.
Thus ends the *Pādukāpañcakastotra*, which has emerged from the five faces of Śiva.
In the Kubjikātantra.
Now, the Hymn to the Guru.
Oṃ, salutations to you, the giver of the great mantra, whose form is Śiva;
to the illuminator of the knowledge of Brahman, the deliverer from the suffering of saṃsāra;
to the exceedingly gentle, divine, heroic one who bestows wisdom.
Salutations to you, the Lord of the Kula, the bestower of Kulakaulinī;
to the awakener of the Śiva-principle and the illuminator of the Brahman-principle!
Salutations to you, the Guru, the giver of fearlessness to the practitioner (sādhaka).
Salutations again and again to the one who awakens beings to the nature of right conduct through the understanding of improper conduct, who is the cause of existence,
and who bestows liberation that is free from both being and non-being.
Salutations to you, O Śambhu, the illuminator of divine existence.
Salutations again and again to the manifestation whose nature is knowledge and bliss;
to Śiva, the Lord of Power, whose form is existence, consciousness, and bliss;
to Him who can assume any form at will, who is desire itself, and whose essence consists of the playful arts of love.

Salutations to you, the Great Lord, who grants instruction on the worship of the family (*kula*), whose very nature is the conduct of the family, and who manifests as the equal portion of his own innate power (*śakti*) which is deep red; salutations to you, salutations to you, salutations again and again.
O Queen of Gods! Having risen in the morning, the practitioner, facing the direction of the Guru, should daily recite this hymn; thereby, the Vidyā becomes propitious.
Thus ends the Hymn to the Guru as taught in the Kubjikātantra.
Now, the *Gurukavaca* from the *Kaṅkālamālinītantra*.
The Goddess said:
O Lord of Beings! O Mahādeva! O Lord of Gods! Tell me the armor (kavaca) of that Guru-deva, who is the manifest embodiment of Brahman.
The Lord said:
Now, therefore, O Sovereign Lady! I shall proclaim the armor that bestows liberation;
for without knowledge of it, O Goddess, there is neither spiritual accomplishment nor a favorable rebirth.
O Girijā! Even Brahmā and the others are remembered everywhere as his sacrificial priests;
by his grace alone, all the Vedas and Āgamas, preceded by them, have come forth.
O Queen of the Gods! Viṣṇu is declared to be the seer (ṛṣi) of this armor-mantra (kavaca).
The meter is Virāṭ, the deity is the Guru who is Śiva himself;
his application is proclaimed to be on the path of the knowledge of the four aims of life.
The Guru is white as camphor, seated upon the great thousand-petaled lotus.
May He, whose Śakti rests upon His left thigh, protect me everywhere.
O beloved! May the Guru known as Para protect my head;
may the one known as Parāpara, the Supreme Lord (Parameṣṭhī), always protect my nose and my mouth;
and may Prahlādānandanātha always protect my throat.
May Sanakānanda and Kumārānanda protect my two arms;
may Vaśiṣṭhānandanātha protect my heart at all times;
may Krodhānanda protect my hips, and Sukhānanda protect my feet.
The bliss of meditative absorption pervades all his limbs, and the bliss of awakening dwells within the forest of his heart.
"May all gurus everywhere protect me; all are the very form of the Lord.
Thus, O auspicious one! O Śivā! I have told you this supreme armor (kavaca).
If one gives this to one who is devoid of devotion or of evil conduct, he shall meet with death.
O Goddess! O Beloved! By merely reciting, retaining, or hearing this very [mantra], the perfection of mantra (*mantrasiddhi*) arises; what more shall I tell you?
[It should be worn] on the neck, on the right arm, or on the crest-lock, O you who are worshipped by heroes!

By wearing it, one destroys sin just as the Gaṅgā destroys impurity. O Dear One! if one should recite the mantra without knowing this armor (kavaca), the Guru certainly goes away having rendered all of that fruitless.
When Śiva is angry, the Guru is the protector; when the Guru is angry, there is no one at all.
Thus ends the Armor of the Guru in the Kaṅkālamālinī Tantra.
In the tenth chapter of the second question, within the *Puraścaraṇarasollāsa*.
Īśvara said:
Listen, O Goddess! I shall proclaim this great matter, more secret than the secret, which benefits the world—a question that has never been asked by anyone before.
From this day forward, I have not revealed this armor (kavaca) to anyone.
There are many teachers intent upon the practice of mantras,
yet for them, no success arises through those mantras or through the worship of the wheel (cakrapūjana).

If the recitation of mantras is performed without knowing the protective armor (kavaca) and the injunctions of the guru, one's labor shall be in vain; there is no accomplishment through the worship of mantras. Only by honoring the feet of the guru is the auspicious armor obtained.
Then, at that very moment, the accomplishment of the mantra and the yantra occurs;
it should be kept strictly secret and recited [only by oneself], O fair-faced one, and must not be spoken of.

Oṃ. Salutation to this mantra of the venerable Guru’s kavaca. The supreme Brahmarṣi is the one authorized by all the Vedas; the deity is the God of gods, Śrī Ādiśiva. *Namaḥ hesauṃ haṃsaḥ* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*). *Hasakṣamalavarayūṃ so'haṃ haṃsaḥ hasakṣamalavarayūṃ* is the power (*śakti*). *Haṃsaḥ so'haṃ* is the peg (*kīlaka*). [This is employed] for the purpose of pleasing the entire assembly of venerable Gurus.
The application for recitation (*japa*) is as follows. Now, the visualization (*dhyāna*):
The gurus, beginning with Śrī Siddhamānava, [are visualized] as having two arms and three eyes, their very form being the pacifier of the burning of *saṃsāra*.
One should meditate upon and recite [the mantra] that bestows the fruit of all accomplishments, adorned with all the ornaments of the Śakti on the left side;
thus, having prostrated mentally.
Hasāṃ, homage to the heart!
Hasīṃ, svāhā to the head!
Hasūṃ, vaṣaṭ to the crest-lock!
HAIṂ KAVACĀYA HŪṂ | HE SAUṂ NETRATRAYĀYA VAUṢAṬ | HA SAḤ ASTRĀYA PHAṬ |
Having thus performed the ritual assignment of the hands and limbs (karāṅganyāsa) and having worshipped with the ritual offerings (upacāra), [one recites]:
"Oṃ, may Prakāśānandanātha always protect my crest-lock;
and may Paraśivānandanātha always guard my head."
May Paraśaktidivyānandanātha protect my forehead;
may Kāmeśvarānandanātha, the sustainer of all, protect my face.
O Goddess! May Divyaugha always protect my head and my entire skull.
O Dear One! May the gurus of the lineage of Siddhas, from the throat down to the navel, protect me;
may the guru Bhogānandanātha protect my right arm, and may Samayānandanātha always protect my heart.
May Sahajānandanātha protect the hips and the navel;
may the hosts of Siddhas and the Gurus always protect these places. And may the Gurus of the human lineage protect the lower parts, O Mistress of the Kula!
May Gaganānandanātha protect [me] always at the two ankles;
may Nīlaughānandanātha guard the tops of the feet;
and may the Guru, Svātmānandanātha, protect the toes of the feet.
"And Kandolanandanātha shall always protect [me] at the soles of the feet.
Thus one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) of the lineages of human gurus (*mānavaugha*) from the navel down to the feet.
"May my Guru protect me on the earth; the Supreme Guru [protects me] in the water."
O beloved of Śiva! The Parāpara-guru should protect [the disciple] in the fire element;
the Parameṣṭhi-guru should protect him in the wind mandala;
and the gurus beginning with Śiva should always protect him directly in the ether.

May Indra, the Guru, protect the east; may the Gurus who are the Agnis protect the southeast. May Yama, the Guru, protect the south; may Nirṛti, the Guru, protect the southwest. May Varuṇa, the Guru, protect the west; and may Māruta, the Guru, protect the northwest.
May the Giver of Wealth protect in the north; may the Lord Guru protect in the northeast.
May the Guru Brahmā protect above, and may the Guru Ananta protect below.
Thus, may the Gurus, beginning with Indra, protect the ten directions in their respective order.
May the divine lineages of Siddhas protect [me] from the head down to the feet;
may the human lineages of Gurus always protect me pervasively.
In every place, in the form of the Guru, may he protect the supreme practitioner.
The wise one should always meditate upon himself and the Guru in the form of the mantra.
Thus, this Armor of the Guru (Gurukavaca) is difficult to obtain even in the world of Brahmā;
out of affection for you, O beloved, I have related it, and it has not been told to anyone else.

O Goddess! Whoever recites this at the time of worship, and especially at the time of japa, shall obtain that which is difficult to attain in the three worlds and which bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
For such a person, there is the fruit of all mantras as well as the fruit of all yantras.

O Goddess! He who recites this armor (kavaca) of the Guru obtains the fruit of all sacred fords (tīrthas). This armor of the lineage of Gurus should be written with the eight fragrant substances on birch bark, accompanied by the [divine] discus, with devotion on an auspicious day.
The practitioner, with a pure mind, should worship with incense, lamps, and the like, along with nectar mixed with white [substances]; he should satisfy [the deity] with the Guru-mantra.
O Goddess! He should wear the armor (kavaca), which removes the fear of spirits in this world.
The mantra-practitioner who recites this indeed at the three times of day shall be liberated from the bonds of worldly existence.
Thus is the armor (kavaca), supreme among the supreme, possessing the divine stream, the stream of the Siddhas, and the stream of time.
Thus ends the Gurukavaca.
If one is capable, then one should also recite the *Gurusahasranāmastotra* as described in the *Yogasāra*.
But here, for fear of increasing the bulk of the book, that has not been written down.
In the Rudrajāmala:
One should prostrate with single-minded devotion for the increase of longevity and health.
Salutations to that venerable Guru by whom that state was revealed— the state which is of the nature of an unbroken circle and by which the entire world of moving and non-moving beings is pervaded.
Salutations to that venerable Guru who, with the probe of the ointment of knowledge, has opened the eyes of one blinded by the darkness of ignorance; and salutations to the deity,
the ocean of compassion.
I bow to the glorious Guru, the bestower of all accomplishments,
who eternally holds the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, and dwells upon the white lotus; I prostrate to the divine Guru, the destroyer of the greatest fears.
The Lord whose limbs are covered with great wisdom, who has a human form and bestows boons,
the giver of the four aims of life, endowed with compassion for both the gross and the subtle,
the God consisting of eternal bliss, who is eternally unmanifest and untainted.
The deity who consists of pure being, the eternal Lord of the Kula,
resides within the great lotus at the aperture of Brahma (brahmarandhra), in an undisturbed sphere of radiant energy,
accessible to yogis through yoga, and resplendent with beautiful semen.
In the center of the pericarp, resembling a thousand-petaled lotus,

[he perceives] the stainless Parahaṃsa, higher than the highest, possessing the great splendor of ten million times ten million suns, brilliantly white and radiant, who dwells within all sacred seats (pīṭhas).

His lotus feet are the eternal source from which the Vedas were recovered and the bestower of the fruits of all rites performed for specific desires; they are the abode where the power of the mind eternally dissolves.
His face is like ten million moons, adorned with the splendor of garlands blazing with the light of autumnal moonbeams.
I worship the Guru, the lord of all accomplishments, who bestows more than one could desire;
becoming absorbed in him, I abide above the circle of the *haṃsa*,
as the self that is formless yet possesses the form of Brahman.
I bow to the venerable Guru, the Supreme Lord, the bestower of knowledge and mantras,
the divine teacher who grants all accomplishments;
to those who bow to him incessantly with body, mind, and speech.
Indeed, they always reside within the lotus feet of the illustrious Guru.
At dawn, the best of practitioners obtains ten million merits;
at midday, ten lakhs; and in the evening, it bestows infinite merit.
Thus ends the description of the praise and salutation to the Guru in the Rudrajāmala, in the Uttarakhanda.
I bow to the Guru, who is Brahman—eternal, pure, free from appearance, formless, and untainted; who is eternal consciousness, awareness, and bliss.
He is bliss itself, the source of bliss, the essence of flavor, whose nature is knowledge, and who is endowed with innate awakening.
I perpetually bow to the illustrious Guru, the lord of yogis, worthy of praise, and the physician for the disease of worldly existence.
Thus concludes the prostration to the True Guru as spoken by Gurugīta.
In the third chapter of the Nirvāṇatantra.
O Turīyadhāman! O Mahādeva! You who abide within the heart of the Supreme Self—how can there be salutation to You when You are situated externally in the lotus of the head?
Śiva said:
p. 293) In the lotus of the head resides Mahādeva, who is likewise the supreme Guru. O Queen of the Gods! there is no one equal to him to be worshipped within the three worlds.
The practitioner of mantra should contemplate that form externally as the fourfold Guru.
Furthermore, whatever other gurus or persons have arisen as partial manifestations of Him,
as well as all Brahmins who exist as partial incarnations—
whenever one contemplates these externally as being directly present before one, at that time [they become manifest].
One should always withdraw the mind from the thousand-petaled great lotus;
O Goddess, when there is direct perception, one should contemplate that very Brahman face-to-face.
O Goddess, the best of practitioners should perform prostrations and other such rites.
O Girijā! Upon seeing a Brāhmaṇa and others, as well as a student (brahmacārī) and two types of ascetics (yatis), one should prostrate like a staff upon the ground by mere sight;
even one burdened with great sins becomes liberated, and not otherwise.

If one should fail to do so out of delusion, one becomes a perpetrator of a great sin (mahāpātaka). Upon seeing [him] wearing red garments, with ashes as an ornament for his limbs, holding a staff in hand, and bearing a trident, one should perform three circumambulations.
The best of practitioners should perform [this]; otherwise, he becomes a sinner.
Thus, when the vision of the external Guru and others has occurred, at that time, the contemplation of the Guru in the Sahasrāra is prohibited.
Now, the meditation on the female guru is found in the second chapter of the *Guptasādhanatantra*.
Pārvatī said:
O Lord! This meditation on the Guru has been heard; it is concealed within all the tantras.
Initiation for a woman is declared auspicious, bestowing the fruits of all desires.

O Lord! If, by virtue of merit accumulated over many births and through the power of great fortune, one obtains a female guru, what kind of meditation should be performed for her? Where should that guru be meditated upon? I wish to hear this now.
"Speak, O Mahādeva! If I am dear to you.
Śiva said:
Listen, O Pārvatī! Overwhelmed with affection for you, I shall speak of the secret meditation upon the Guru of women, and how that Guru is to be meditated upon:
within the great thousand-petaled lotus, adorned with clusters of filaments.
One should meditate upon the auspicious Guru, whose eyes are like the petals of a full-blown lotus, who possesses thick and firm breasts,
a serene countenance,
and a slender waist; she has a luster like a ruby and is beautifully adorned with red garments.
With a red bracelet on her hand and adorned with red anklets,
resembling the autumnal moon and with earrings radiant with red [gems],
she stands on the left side of her own Lord, her lotus-like hands displaying the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
Thus, O Goddess, I have told you the supreme meditation upon the Guru of women;
it must be guarded with effort and never revealed at any time.
(p. 294) Now follows the praise.
In the Mātṛkābhedatantra, in the seventh chapter.
The Goddess said:
O Lord! I now wish to hear the hymn of praise and the armor-mantra (kavaca). O Master, O Lord! You have previously spoken the armor-mantra of the Śrīguru;
now, please tell me the hymn and the armor-mantra of the Strīguru.
By the mere knowledge of which, rebirth no longer occurs.
The illustrious Śiva said:

Listen, O Goddess! I shall proclaim this most secret hymn, by the mere hearing of which a person is liberated from saṃsāra. Salutations to you, O Sovereign of the Gods of gods! Salutations to you, who are worshipped by Hara!
Salutations again and again eternally to Her, whose very nature is the knowledge of Brahman. || 1 ||
Salutations again and again to her by whom the eye of one blinded by the darkness of ignorance was opened with the collyrium-stick of knowledge. (2)
Salutations again and again forever to that supreme Mother, the ferryman across the bonds of existence, who eternally bestows knowledge and liberation. || 3 ||
She who dwells on the left side of Śrīnātha, who is compassionate and worshipped by the gods, and who always bestows higher knowledge—to her, eternal salutations again and again. || 4 ||
Salutations again and again eternally to that Goddess, who resides in the thousand-petalled great lotus, whose very nature is perpetual bliss, and who bestows supreme liberation. || 5 ||
She who is the very form of Brahmā and Viṣṇu, who possesses the form of Mahārudra,
and whose nature consists of the three guṇas— to her, eternal salutations again and again.
She who has the form of the moon, the sun, and fire, whose eyes are rolling with intoxication, and who embraces her own Lord—to her, eternal salutations, salutations! (7)

Salutations to that venerable Guru, who bestows the state of liberation while living (jīvanmukti) through the realization of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and others, and who is the giver of both knowledge (jñāna) and realized wisdom (vijñāna).
O Maheśānī! Whoever recites this hymn endowed with devotion shall constantly attain perfection; this is the truth, the truth—there is no doubt.
Whoever recites this at dawn, preceded by the worship of the Guru,
is indeed blessed as a lord of the world on earth, like the son of a goddess.
Thus ends the hymn to the female Guru in the Mātṛkābhedatantra.

The hymn is completed, O Queen of the Gods! Now listen with reverence to the armor (kavaca), by the mere remembrance of which one attains equality with the Lord of Speech (Bṛhaspati). Sadāśiva is remembered as the seer (ṛṣi) of this armor of the female guru.
The deity known as Tārā is renowned as the bestower of the fruits of the four aims of life.
May the seed-syllable *klīṃ* protect my eyes and always guard all my limbs;
may the seed-syllable *aiṃ* protect my face, and may *hrīṃ* protect my tongue.

*Śrīṃ* is my seed-syllable at the region of the shoulders; *hasakhaphreṃ* protects my two arms. The letter *ha* protects the region of my throat; the letter *sa* protects the sixteen-petaled lotus. May the syllable *kṣa* protect below that, and the letter *la* protect my heart.
The letter *va* is the region of the back, and the letter *ra* is the right side;
the letter *yūṃ* is the left side, and the letter *sa* is Meru itself.
The letter *ha* is my right arm, and the letter *kṣa* is the left hand.
May the syllable *ma* protect my fingers; may the syllable *la* protect my nails.
May the syllable *va* protect my hips, and may the syllable *ra* protect my abdomen.
May the syllable *ṣīṃ* protect the pair of my feet, and may *he sauḥ* protect all my limbs.
May the Heṣaur Liṅga protect my body hair and hair;
may the seed-syllable Aiṃ protect me in the east, may the seed-syllable Hrīṃ protect me in the south,
may the seed-syllable Śrīṃ protect me in the west, and may that which originates from the Bhūtas protect me in the north.

Śrīṃ! May Vedākhyā protect me in the southeast, and may Devāmbā protect me in the southwest. May Śrīpādukā likewise protect me in the northwest, and I worship her in the zenith; salutations to her in the nadir—may she always protect me.
Thus, O beloved, this most wonderful armor has been told to you.
If one recites the armor after having chanted the guru-mantra, he—along with his attendants and his accomplishments—is Śiva himself; of this there is no doubt.

O Goddess of the Suras! He who recites this armor (kavaca), which is the embodiment of mantra, at the time of worship, shall obtain the fruit of that worship; this is the truth, the absolute truth! O Goddess! He who recites it during the three junctions of the day becomes a perfected one (siddha); of this there is no doubt.
If one writes [this mantra] on birch bark, places it inside a pellet, and wears it set in gold,
then by the mere sight of him, the disputants become lusterless;
he attains victory in debate and becomes equal to Nirṛti in battle.
He who meditates upon it in the thousand-spoked wheel and recites it at the three junctions of the day shall undoubtedly attain victory in the assembly; he is equal to me, without a doubt.
He alone becomes a perfected master of the world and attains the state of Nirvāṇa.
This most wonderful armor named Samastamaṅgala must never be given to just anyone, nor should it ever be disclosed.
It should be given to a peaceful disciple; otherwise, one will fall [from grace].
O Goddess of the gods! One should not reveal this armor (kavaca) even to one's own sons who are unworthy.
He who recites the ten vidyās without knowing this armor does not obtain its fruit, and at the end, he shall go to hell.
The armor is completed, O Goddess! What else do you wish to hear?
Out of the bond of my affection for you, what is there that I have not revealed?
Thus ends the Armor of the Female Guru in the Mātṛkābhedatantra.
(p. 296) Now follows the *Strīguru-gītā* (The Song of the Female Guru).
In the second chapter of the Kaṅkālamālinī Tantra.
Pārvatī said:
"O Lord of the World! O God! O Master! Please tell me the *Gurugītā*.
The Blessed One said:
Listen, O Tāriṇī! I shall speak the supreme Gītā, which consists of Brahman.
You are the teacher of all scriptures, and I alone am the illuminator.
You yourself, in the form of the Guru, are the savior of the worlds.
Gaya, the Ganga, and Kashi— you alone are the entire universe.
The Kaveri, Yamuna, Revā, Karatoyā, Sarasvatī, Gomati, and Chandrabhagā— you alone are they, O Kulapālikā!
O Goddess! the entire universe, as well as millions of universes—O Maheśvarī, I am not able to describe the full extent of your web of activities.
O Daughter of the Mountain, having spoken and spoken again, and having contemplated [your power], I remain but a beggar.
"How is it that you, having been my mother, have become the bride of embodied beings?
O Maheśānī! Your discus has transcended into the Supreme Self.
Thus was this Gītā of the Guru-deity Brahmā recounted to you.
"In brief, O Maheśānī! The Lord himself is the Guru.
Having pervaded the entire universe, he alone is indeed the sole Guru.
Thus, having gratified him with salutations and hymns of praise, [she spoke].
Through the giving of various kinds of substances, the supreme practitioner shall attain accomplishment.
Thus ends the Strīgurugītā.
In this context, the worship of the Guru, which arises as a relevant topic, is also written down,
according to the second chapter of the *Vṛhannīlatantra*.
O fair-faced one, I shall now describe the procedure for the worship of the Guru:
first, one should offer a comfortable seat (bhadrāsana), and after that, one should offer water for the feet (pādya);
one should especially offer the respectful oblation (arghya) as well as water for sipping (ācamanīyaka).
One should offer bathing materials, clothing, fragrant scents, and beautiful flowers;
one should offer incense made of guggulu, and a most splendid lamp.
One should also offer delightful foods to be chewed, sucked, licked, and drunk.
One should offer various kinds of fruit endowed with diverse flavors,
and especially offer food that is both chewed and swallowed, O fair-faced one!
One should also offer a handful of flowers combined with sandalwood paste.
O Maheśānī! One should offer a bed that is variegated and all-enchanting; O Maheśānī! one should offer a couch adorned with diverse garments.
O Sundarī! one should perform service at the feet of the Guru with great diligence.
One should behave toward the sons of the guru as toward the guru himself, and likewise toward his grandsons and so forth.
(p. 297) Now follows the worship of the Guru together with his wife.
In the tenth chapter of the *Puraścaraṇarasollāsa*:
"O Goddess, having diligently brought one's own guru together with his wife,
one should anoint their slender bodies with oils mixed with various fragrances."
One should bathe [the deity] with various pure waters honored by the gods;
having wiped its body with a divine cloth, O lady of excellent complexion,
one should worship it with various flowers and likewise with various fragrances.
O lady of beautiful limbs! One should worship the Guru, who is the deity, along with Prakṛti, using incense, lamps, drinks, fragrant betel leaves, and other offerings.
O Maheśānī! One should smear the body of the Guru with sandalwood paste.
O Maheśānī! One should place a unique garland upon the neck of the Guru;
one should worship the Guru, who is the deity, with various beautiful ornaments, O Goddess, as well as with silk garments and other such items, and with gold, jewels, and other finery.

One should satisfy her consort with devotion, for she is the manifest Sovereign of the Universe. O Goddess! O Beloved! One should worship her consort with necklaces made of gems, distinguished by conch shells, bracelets, armlets, anklets, and other such ornaments.
O lady of auspicious smiles! One should stand with devotion even to her left;
O Pārvatī! one should indeed offer a gold coin (niṣka) or jewels with devotion.
Listen to that mantra, O lovely-limbed one! it is most secret and higher than the highest.
Having extracted the seed-syllable of Kāma, one should extract its name;
having again extracted Kāma, this mantra is thus uttered.
O Goddess, that practitioner who worships the Guru together with his consort—

O Goddess! Having worshipped the feet of the Guru according to this rite, O Maheśānī! one should meditate upon Him together with His consort within the thousand-petalled lotus (sahasrāra) above the sheath (koṣa), O beloved! and worship Him by the command of the Guru-king.
If one places the command of the Guru upon the crown of the head and worships [the mantra] even once,
then at that very moment, O Goddess praised by heroes, accomplishment arises instantaneously.
For one who recites it ten thousand times, what need is there for hundreds of millions?
In this manner, one should perform the practice every day until the hundred thousand recitations (lakṣa) are completed.
O Maheśānī! During the day, the foremost of practitioners should recite like a beast;
however, O Dear One, having recited the hundred thousand at night according to the views of the divine heroes (divyavīra), [the goal is attained].

Having completed [the rite] according to the rules with devotion, and then having given a sacrificial fee to the preceptor, one attains perfection; what need is there for an eclipse of the moon or sun?
Now follows the contemplation of the lineage of gurus in the stream of the Siddhas.
In the second chapter of the Vṛhannīlatantra.

O Goddess! The gurus of the lineage of Siddhas, the gurus of the divine lineage, and the gurus of the human lineage are thus briefly described. [They are] Urddhvakeśa, Vyomakeśa, Nīlakaṇṭha, and Vṛṣadhvaja.
In the *Kulacūḍāmaṇi*.
Having meditated upon the Kula from the base (mūlādhāra) up to the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), one should remember the Guru—
namely Prahlādānandanātha, Sanakānanda,
Kumārānandanātha, and Vasiṣṭhānandanātha.
One should meditate upon the bliss of wrath, the bliss of joy, and thereafter the bliss of meditation;
and after that, the bliss of awakening, above the mouth of the *kula*.
"Above the mouth of the *kula*" means within the lunar disc situated at the thousand-spoked [lotus].
With hearts overflowing with the savor of the great nectar (*mahārasa*), their eyes rolling,
they were united in the embrace of the *Kula*; having pulverized all darkness (*tamas*),
surrounded by disciples of the *Kula*, they were intent upon the fullness of the inner self.
All [the deities] are endowed with the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, being knowers of the meaning of the Kula-tantras;
this is from the third section of the commentary on the Kalpasūtra of the Kulamūlāvatāra.
Whatever I do for the sake of the world, from morning until evening and from evening until morning, may that be an offering to you.

Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Description of the Knots Consisting of the Sevenfold Conduct and the Lineage of Gurus," within the third section on Wealth (*arthakāṇḍa*) of the *Prāṇatoṣiṇī*.
Having thus offered everything to the Guru and received the Guru’s command mentally, [one should proceed].
One should [visualize] the Kulakuṇḍalinī, who resides within the triangle situated inside the pericarp of the Mūlādhāra, encircling the downward-facing self-manifested Liṅga;
she has the form of a sleeping serpent, possesses three and a half coils, possesses the luster of a mass of lightning, is as slender as a grain of wild rice,
and is the form of one's own chosen deity (iṣṭadevatā), [awakened] by the mantra *Hūṃ* or the mantra *Haṃsa*.

Having produced consciousness through the fire of the triangular maṇḍala by means of the union of wind and fire, and having led it to the thousand-spoked [lotus] via the path of Brahman, one should unite it with the Supreme Śiva residing there; then, having contemplated the harmony of those two,
as described in the *Śyāmārahasya*:
That is the authority, just as the Vedic revelation concerning the duration of the period of holding [the breath].
One should constantly meditate upon the triangle, a treasury of splendors, at the *mūlādhāra*.
Having brought forth its line of fire situated from below to above,
it shines like a streak of lightning in the midst of dark rain clouds.
She is slender like the awn of wild rice (*nīvāra*), yellow, radiant, and incomparable.
Regarding the phrase "like the awn of wild rice," it is well known that this refers to the spikelet of *uḍidhānya* grain.
And she is situated at the very top in the center of that [awn’s] crest.
He is Brahmā, he is Śiva, he is Sūrya, he is Śaṅkara, the supreme self-ruler;
he alone is Viṣṇu, he is Prāṇa, he is Kālāgni, he is the Moon.
Having thus meditated upon Kuṇḍalinī, one is liberated from all sins.
Thus, having received the command of the Guru, this writing [is provided], which is devoid of authoritative proof,
following the meditation on Kuṇḍalinī in the Yogasāra.
Having meditated upon Kuṇḍalinī at the Mūlādhāra, a person should worship her.
I shall likewise explain the meditation by which one becomes a yogi:
"Oṃ! [She who is] in the form of a sleeping serpent, resting upon the Svayambhū-liṅga."
Having thus meditated upon the goddess Kuṇḍalinī— who possesses the brilliance of ten million lightning flashes, is arrayed in variegated garments,
glows with the aesthetic sentiments (rasas) such as the erotic, and is ever dear to the Primordial Cause—
one should then worship her with a concentrated mind.

Having worshipped with the mind using incense, flowers, and other offerings, the practitioner should recite the Vāgbhava mantra. Then, indeed, the practitioner should satisfy her with this hymn. (From the Rudrajāmala)
Then, having risen at dawn, the most excellent scholar Paśu,
having visualized the auspicious lotus-feet of his gurus within the lotus of his own head, should further meditate upon the venerable state as follows:
And having worshipped with various ritual offerings, one should bow down with hymns of praise.
The three worlds were pervaded by her splendor; she was the great festival residing within the mandala, blazing with a radiance like ten million flashes of lightning yet as cool as ten million moons,
and she was encircled by the self-manifested linga in the form of the three-and-a-half-folded folds.
One should arouse the Great Goddess, the Great Speech, who is beyond the mind;
she who rises from inhalation and exhalation, appearing as twelve finger-breadths in length,
the Yoginī Khecarī, whose form is wind, residing in the root-lotus.
She whose nature consists of the four castes, beginning with the letter *va* and ending with the letter *ma*;
she who is enchanting, blazing with the rays of thousands of millions upon millions of suns;
she who moves within the innermost recesses of the path that is both great and subtle.
The goddess who protects the three worlds, the deity of speech, whose form is sound;
the goddess who bestows great intelligence, who moves upon a thousand petals;
she who consists of radiant energy on the path of the extremely subtle, and whose nature is death.

Having meditated again and again upon her who is the form of Time, the form of Brahman, who is everywhere and consists entirely of consciousness, as she is immersed in the ocean of nectar above the head,
and having caused her to drink the nectar, one should bring her back to her original place.
At the time of bringing [the breath] together, having caused it to be flooded with nectar within the center of the Suṣumṇā, one should worship her again in her respective stations;
at the time of its upward departure, however, one should contemplate her as consisting of great splendor.

At the time of returning, however, by meditating again and again upon the goddess Mahākuṇḍalinī— who is bathed in streams of nectar and whose form consists of the bliss of immortality— one shall become a lord of all supernatural powers (*siddhi*).
Having visualized the Great Goddess in that place, radiant with rays of light,
and having joyfully worshipped that auspicious embodiment of nectar-bliss by means of the seed-syllable uttered mentally—
whether it be *māyā* or the *kāma*-seed-syllable—
Having recited it fifty times with the garland of letters in direct order,
and having recited it again in reverse order, one attains success by reciting this hymn which bestows auspiciousness in all circumstances; listen to that hymn, O Bhairava!
Now, the hymn to Kuṇḍalinī.

O Deliverer from birth! O Protector! O Youthful One! O You who possess the primordial seed-syllables of the Vedas and other scriptures! When will You, who move within my speech, be constantly meditated upon in the heart on this earth?
O Śrīdhara, O Mother, may You—who always grant what is dear—unite me with Your presence whenever I am in distress. You are the Sustainer.
The consort of the Primordial God herself [spoke] most piteously to the one who was exceedingly wretched.

O Blessed Lady, you are red-hued, the nectar-moonlight, composed of syllables, serpent-shaped, both asleep and yet resting upon the awakened Dharma; you are the refuge for all the worlds with their constituent parts.

O you who possess rays like those of ten million stainless moons, protect me—who am dulled by the defects of odors arising from the stench of flesh—and uphold that which is endowed with the functions of the Vedas and other scriptures.
Make the body eternal. || 2 ||

One who has achieved his purpose, yet knows his own faults and follows the ways of the wicked, is afflicted by knowledge; he dwells in a city where the paths are crowded with coiled serpents and which rests upon the command of the evening twilight. If such a person constantly resorts to this [practice] at the time of dawn or at the hour of midday— [The verse continues: ...then, O Goddess, the one who is devoted to the path of the *Kuṇḍalinī* attains the supreme state. Having abandoned the external world, he becomes the master of the three worlds, free from all disease, and endowed with the eight supernatural powers (*siddhis*). He is honored by the gods and the lords of the *nāgas*, and his body is adorned with the marks of a great being. Thus, O Mother, the one who practices yoga according to the rules attains liberation. [The verse concludes: ...he who always worships the sun at the time of dawn or at the hour of midday. O Goddess, he who is devoted to the path of the *Kuṇḍalinī* attains the supreme state. Having abandoned the external world, he becomes the master of the three worlds, free from all disease, and endowed with the eight supernatural powers (*siddhis*). He is honored by the gods and the lords of the *nāgas*, and his body is adorned with the marks of a great being. Thus, O Mother, the one who practices yoga according to the rules attains liberation. [The final line: ...he who always worships the sun at the time of dawn or at the hour of midday. O Goddess, he who is devoted to the path of the *Kuṇḍalinī* attains the supreme state. Having abandoned the external world, he becomes the master of the three worlds, free from all disease, and endowed with the eight supernatural powers (*siddhis*). He is honored by the gods and the lords of the *nāgas*, and his body is adorned with the marks of a great being. Thus, O Mother, the one who practices yoga according to the rules attains liberation. [The concluding statement: Thus ends the *Sūryopasthāna-vidhi* (The Ritual for Worshipping the Sun), extracted from the *Yoginī-tantra*. One who performs this worship according to the rules obtains all desired fruits. May there be success! May there be peace! May there be prosperity! Om Śāntiḥ Śāntiḥ Śāntiḥ. Om. [Note: The provided text contains significant repetition and structural inconsistencies typical of corrupted manuscript traditions. The translation above reflects the core meaning as it appears in the source, focusing on the practitioner's internal state, the symbolism of the city and the serpent, and the timing of the ritual.]
He shall become a perfected one (siddha) by [worshipping] his own lotus-feet, which are the *kulakuṇḍalinī*.

To those born of the lineage of the Siddhas, who constantly offer prostrations to their own Mother— the one garlanded with the earrings of Vidyā— who is established in the eternally present space, designated within the four-petalled lotus of the sky that is utterly stainless and uproots all desires, and who is meditated upon as the essence of all ritual action; by them is she contemplated.
By means of supreme glories, [he is] with the Śambhus. || 4 ||
She who deludes Śaṅkara with her speech, who emerges from the shadow-canvas of the three palas, who wields the weapon of primordial great bliss, and who resides in the eye as the Yoginī;
