she who pierces all knots, who possesses beautiful serpents, who is subtler than the subtlest, the supreme one who delights in the knowledge of Brahman.
It is cultivated as the one that strikes the axe-blow at the family tree. || 5 ||
I bow to the venerable Kulakuṇḍalī, who is dear to Svayambhū, who is accompanied by the three folds [of her waist],

who is the restless mind of the essence of the Asuras, the youthful and powerful one who is partless; that goddess who shines with four faces, who is the source of all things, the creative contemplation— I honor her, the beloved, upon my head.
I honor the ritual action consecrated by the Self-Existent One.

May that Mother protect you, O traveler on the subtle path! She who intoxicates with the sound of ten million lutes and drums; whose voice is like the resonance of ten million stairways; whose face is ever full with the blossoming of the lotus at the base of the left breast of the Lord of Life; and who dwells within the darkness of a mass of clouds arisen in the month of Āṣāḍha.
Consecrate me as a yogin. || 7 ||
Relying upon you, men go swiftly to Vaikuṇṭha and Kailāsa—the sole abode of bliss, whose moon-like face radiates joy, and who is the primordial cause.
O Mother! O beloved form of Śrī Kulakuṇḍalinī! O illuminator of the lineage of Kālī! O Consort of Rudra! I bow to you again and again.
Lift me up on this path.
This eightfold hymn, which abides on the path of the Kuṇḍalinī power and yields great fruit—
whosoever recites it upon rising in the morning certainly becomes a yogi; indeed,
by its recitation, one becomes a lord of poets in this very world in an instant.
"Through union with Kuṇḍalinī in the next world, one becomes the Great One absorbed in Brahman.
Thus, O Lord, I have told you this tender hymn of praise to Kuṇḍalinī.
By the grace of this hymn, among the gods, Bṛhaspati became the preceptor."
By the grace of her hymn of praise, all the gods have attained perfection;
Brahmā, the lord of all the gods, has become long-lived for half a Dvāpara age,
and you too, O Lord of the Goddess, remain here in my presence.
Know me to be the supreme power, whose nature is both gross and subtle,
the illuminator of all things, dwelling on the Vindhya mountains,
the daughter of Himālaya, the perfected one, whose very form is the perfected mantra.

She who resides in the Vedānta, Śakti-tantras, and Kulatantras; she who follows the meaning of the Kula-tantras; she who is established in the Rudra-jāmala; she whose nature is the contemplation that stabilizes all states;
she who is the embodiment of the five mudrās; and she who is adorned with the garland of the Śakti-jāmala.
Richly adorned with garlands of jewels and rows of cranes, illuminating like the sun and moon,
bestowing great wisdom upon all beings, destroying the demons, the cause of maintenance,
creation, and dissolution, she dwells within the ocean of compassion.
[She is] richly endowed with the abode of great delusion, residing within the body of Dāmodara;
supreme, holding a great trident in her hand, adorned with parasols, chowries, and jewels;
the bestower of knowledge and the giver of success; the Vidyā who grants a multitude of garlands of gems.

O Śambhu! O leader of yoga! O wise one! Always contemplate me—whose nature is all splendor, who possess infinite millions of forms, who am Lakṣmī who bestows wealth upon the poor, and who am the delight of Nārāyaṇa.
Thus ends the *Kuṇḍalīstotra* in the *Uttarakhaṇḍa* of the *Rudrajāmalatantra*.
Another hymn to Kuṇḍalinī is found in the third chapter of the *Yogasāra*.

Oṃ! Salutations to you, O Goddess of the lords of gods! O beloved of the life-force of the masters of yoga! O bestower of perfection! O giver of boons! O Mother, who are encircled by the self-manifested liṅga! || 1 ||
Oṃ! O Goddess who have the form of a sleeping serpent! O you who are always dear to the Cause (Kāraṇa)!
O Goddess endowed with the arts of love (kāmakalā)! Grant me my desired object. || 2 ||
O Kuleśvarī! In this essence-less and terrible saṃsāra, protect me always from the disease of existence; O Goddess! protect me from the ocean of birth and worldly life. || 3 ||
The wise person who, having meditated upon this hymn to Kuṇḍalinī, recites it,
is liberated from all sins within the form of worldly existence.
Thus ends the *Kuṇḍalinīstotra*.
Now follows the *Kuṇḍalinīkavaca*.
In the Rudrajāmala, in the Uttarakhanda, in the thirty-fifth chapter.
The venerable Ānandabhairavī said:
Now, O Mahādeva, I shall proclaim the auspicious Kuṇḍalī-kavaca,
which bestows supreme bliss, is perfected, and is served by hosts of Siddhas;
wearing which, all yogis become revealers of dharma and adharma.
The wise, the proud, and the steadfast move about like ordinary men;
yet the supernatural powers, beginning with *aṇimā*, as well as all the deities, remain within the palm of their hands.
By the recitation of this armor (*kavaca*), even the Lord of the Gods becomes a sovereign of yogis.
All the sages and yogis, matted-haired and belonging to the Kula-Bhairava tradition,
should recite this armor-mantra (kavaca) three times in the morning, twice at midday,
and once in the evening.
By the mere recitation [of this], the great yogi shall obtain the vision of Kuṇḍalī.
For the armor of Kuṇḍalī, Brahmā is the seer (ṛṣi), Gāyatrī is the meter (chandas), and Kuṇḍalī is the deity; its application (viniyoga) is for the sake of attaining all desired goals.
May the Sovereign Lady, the Sustainer of the World, Lalitā, Sundarī, Parā, Kuṇḍalī,
and Kulacaṇḍikā in her Kula-form protect me.
May Goddess Lalitā protect my head, and she known as Ugrā protect my cheeks.
May she who is sealed by the aperture of Brahmā protect my brow-center;
may Mahākālī, the devourer of the fire of time, protect my three eyes;
may Viśālākṣī protect the row of my teeth; and may iṣṭānnavāsinī protect my lips.

May the Vidyā, whose essence is the seed-syllable of desire (*kāma-bīja*), protect my lower face always. May Bhuvaneśī, who resides in the eyes and cheeks, possesses the pair of *caṇḍa* syllables, and is fond of the *rasa* seed-syllable (*māyā-bīja*), protect my two ears. May Krodhakālikā protect my chin.

May Kapilā, who embodies the nature of all seeds and is encased within the letters of the Mātṛkā, protect my throat; may Kuṇḍalī likewise protect it for an eon. May Kālaputrī protect my heart, and Kaṅkālī protect my face.
May Caṇḍadurgā protect the pair of arms, she who shatters the fierce staff-like arms [of enemies]; may the Goddess protect the pair of shoulders; may Krodhakālikā protect the chin;
may Kulānandā protect the tips of the fingers; and may Śrīvidyā protect the circle of the nails.
May Kālikā Bhuvaneśānī always protect the region of my back; may Mahāvīrā, who holds the heroic posture and bestows fearlessness, protect both sides;
O Mother, may Kuladarbhasthā protect my navel and Udarallikā protect my belly.
Established in the region of the waist and the back, she is the slayer of the great buffalo;
residing in the seat of the *liṅga*, she is Mahāmudrā, adorned with a garland of vulvas, and beloved by Manu.
She is fond of Bhagīratha, she is Dhūmrā, and as Gaṇeśvarī, she dwells in the *mūlādhāra*.
May the four-petaled [lotus]— whose petals are Kāmavidyā, whose tip is Mevasundharā,
and which is known as Dhīdharaṇā— protect my face; may Bhedinī protect Kamalā, and Vāgdevī protect the full petal.
May Chedinī on the right side protect me, and may Caṇḍā Mahātapā protect me;
may Caṇḍaghaṇṭā always protect the western petal, and may Yoginī protect the northern petal, which is cherished by Indra and is the Earth.
May she who rides upon all vehicles always protect the four-cornered [mandala] of Kāmavidyā and the eight-cornered [mandala] of Brahmavidyā;
may the four-armed Ḍākinī, who moves through the *kula*, always protect [me].
May the Support of Madana, residing in the generative organ, protect my beautiful lotus;
may the fair-limbed Koṭarākṣī, whose seat is the self-manifested liṅga, protect me;
and may she who dwells in the Kadamba forest, the goddess Kadambavanagā, protect me.

May the supreme Vaiṣṇavī Māyā protect my Vaiṣṇava station. May Rākiṇī protect the six-petaled lotus; may Raṅginī, who dwells in desire, protect it. May Kāmeśvarī, whose form is desire, protect Kṛṣṇa, who is clothed in yellow garments.
May Vanadurgā protect my bow; may Śaṅkhinī, the auspicious one, protect my conch;
may Cakreśvarī protect my discus; may Kamalākṣī protect my mace; and may Padmagandhā, who is enchanting with her lotus garland, protect my lotus.
May Lākinī, the purifier of the world, protect the final syllable of the Vādi-sānta [mantra];
may she who dwells on Kailāsa protect the deities stationed upon the six petals;
and may the Supreme Goddess, whose color is like fire, ever protect my throat.
May she who is adorned with a garland of jewels always protect Maṇipūra; may Trivikramā, whose ten petals are of ten colors and whose syllables begin with *ka* and end with *pha*, protect it;
and may Nīlā Mahākālī, Bhadrā, Bhīmā, and Sarasvatī protect it.
May the Goddess residing in Ayodhyā, dwelling in the great seat (mahāpīṭha),
the Great Knowledge (mahāvidyā) beginning with Vāgbhava, Kuṇḍalinī whose form is Time,
protect my hundred petals and ten petals, which are Rudra and consist of the nature of Rudra.
May the subtle one, subtler than the subtle, who dwells in the subtle abode, protect [me].
May Lākinī, the mother of the world, endowed with the peak syllables, protect [me].
May Rajakī, honored by kings, constantly protect the radiant one.

May Vijayā, who abides in the seed-syllable of the Kula, who is the *tavarga*, and who dispels darkness, protect me always; she who is of the nature of the Moon, the knotted pearl, and the piercer. May Bhagamālā, the daughter of Bhrigu, who dwells in the navel, protect me.
May Nandinī protect everything; may Kuṇḍalī, fashioned by Kāla, protect [me].
May she called Kālā, smoke-colored and captivating, protect the heart-lotus.
And may Bhāskarī, the bestower of the attainment of all states, protect the twelve syllables of the petals.

May the Supreme Vidyā, who moves at will, protect the *ka*-group for me; may she of the beautiful tongue protect the *ca*-group, and she with the tiger’s face, holding a chisel, protect the *ṭa*-group. May she known as Kṛṣṇā protect the letter *ṭa*, and may Kālikā protect the letter *kā*.
May the syllable *ṭha*, the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of great prosperity belonging to the goddess Ṭhaṅkurāṅgī, protect me; may the pure one dwelling in my heart-lotus protect the Lord;
[and may she protect] Kālikā, who is the context of Time, the Yoginī, and the Mother of Yoga.
May Indrāṇī and Vāruṇī protect the lineage and the other lineages;
may Tāriṇī and Śaktimātā always protect the speech of the throat.
[May] Vipracittā, Mahogrā, Ugrā, Prabhādīptā, and Ghanāmalā [protect it as well].
Vākstambhinī, Vajradehā, Vaidehī, Vṛṣavāhinī, Unmattā, Nandacittā, Kuleśī, and Bhagāturā—
may she who stands as my Mother protect my sixteen petals.
May she who knows the Vedas protect the Suras, and may Kālikā, who speaks all languages, protect me.
May Sadāśivā, seated upon half the throne of Īśvara, always grant me protection. May Śākambharī, Mahāmāyā, and Śākinī protect me at all times.
May Bhavānī, the mother of Bhava, who dwells within the lotus amidst the clouds and trees,

who possesses two petals, who is known by the vow as Kāmākhyā, and who bestows the eightfold perfections— she who is the bliss of all, whose form is the mind, and who is fond of recitation— protect me.

May the Goddess, who is pervaded by the *lakṣaṇas*, who is the defining characteristic of all characteristics, and who wears a black antelope skin, protect the letter *la* at all times. May the fair-faced one, who resides within the two petals, always protect the letter *kṣa*, which contains all the gods.
May Hākinī, who possesses many forms and universal forms, protect Caṇḍikā;
may Harā protect Paraśiva, and may the Fifth protect the mind.
May she who dwells in the six cakras and resides in the family of the six cakras always protect me.
May the letters of the alphabet, from *a* to *kṣa*, accompanied by the *bindu* and the *sarga*,
and the *mātṛkā* syllables— may they always protect [me]. May Kuṇḍalī, Jñānakuṇḍalī, Pūrṇakālī, Gatipretā, and the auspicious Śivā of the banks of Pūrṇagiri protect [me].
May the goddess Uḍḍīyāneśvarī protect everything at all times;
may she who dwells on Mount Kailāsa protect Mount Kailāsa;
[may] Ḍākinī, Rākiṇī, Śakti, Lākinī, Kākinī, and Kalā [protect us].
May the goddess Sākinī and Hākinī protect my six cakras and the rest;
may she who was born from the body of the five-faced one (Śiva) always protect the place called Kailāsa;
may she who is golden-hued, the night, and the devourer of the moon, sun, and fire protect me.
May Kulākulā always protect my thousand-petaled lotus;
may Bhairavī, residing upon the thousand-petaled lotus, protect the deity.
May Kālī, Tārā, the one called Ṣoḍaśī, and Mātaṅgī, who dwells in the lotus, [protect me].
May she whose form flows like ten million moons protect my entire body—
in battle, in the midst of a terrible flood, in fault, in combat, in debate, or in the cremation ground;
may the Daughter of the Mountain always protect me everywhere, in every movement and in every act of knowledge.
May Kuṇḍalinī protect me in the mountain with its various dwellings during destruction;

may the Sovereign of the Gods, who is all-pervasive space from the soles of the feet to the aperture of Brahma, always protect me; may she, the embodiment of all learning, always grant me all-knowledge.
"May the Great Knowledge (Mahāvidyā) of nine lakhs [of syllables] protect me in the ten directions!
O Goddess, this armor (kavaca) of Kuṇḍalinī bestows success. Those established on the path of Yoga who recite this while engaged in the yoga of meditation [attain their goal]."
They proceed along the path to liberation in this very life; of this there is no doubt.
Having established the mind in union within the root-lotus and remaining in a firm posture, the practitioner of mantra should meditate upon Kuṇḍalinī, who illumines the subtle lotus.
She who is the source of phenomena (dharmodayā), mounted upon compassion, dwelling in the station of space;
she who delights in the essence of nectar-bliss, who is both partless and whole, white, yet black,
devoid of redness, dispassionate, yet possessing a body of blood-red hue.

Having meditated upon her at the root—red-eyed, cast out from the family, radiant with the waters of the agitated gnosis, acting with hostility, and having the form of the mind—one should worship her.
Whatever yogi performs this in such a manner becomes a Siddha; of this there is no doubt.
If one who is ill recites this, he shall be freed from disease; if one who is bound recites it, he shall be released from bondage;
if one who lacks wealth recites it, he shall obtain beloved riches;
if one who is childless recites it, he shall obtain a son; and if one who lacks yoga recites it, he shall become self-controlled.
Whoever wears this armor on the crest-lock, on the right arm,
or holding it in the left hand with the left [hand], shall obtain all desired objects.
Having placed it in gold, silver, or likewise copper, one should worship it.
Having recited it in every place and at every time, one shall attain accomplishment;
he shall become a son of Kuṇḍalin—of this there is no need for deliberation.
Thus ends the *Kandavāsinī-kavaca* in the *Uttarakhaṇḍa* of the *Rudrajāmala*.

Then, according to tradition, having bowed to Kuṇḍalinī with the mantra of salutation to one’s own chosen deity (iṣṭadevatā), one should install the mantra of Caureśvara at the ten gates like a door-bolt; this is stated in the Gaṇeśavimarṣiṇī:
The two eyes, the two ears, the two nostrils, the mouth, the navel, the base of the penis, the region of the anus,
and likewise the gateway of the mind between the eyebrows— these are designated as the ten gateways.
One should recite the first seed-syllable, *Aṅkuśa*, ten times at the heart. At the conclusion of the recitation, O Mother! one should then place the *Kavāṭa* [syllable] there.
Likewise, one should place the *Kūrca* on the two ears, and then *Kālī* in the nostrils.
One should then recite the seed-syllable *strīṃ* twice in the mouth, and the syllable *vāṇī* at the navel.
The seed-syllable *hesauḥ* is proclaimed for the base of the *liṅga*, and *blūṃ* for its root.
Furthermore, the syllable *oṃ* is placed between the eyebrows, and likewise in the seat of the mind.
This eleventh seed-syllable is like a door-panel at each gate.
One should not perform even a mere ritual action without having recited the mantra of Caṇḍamuṇḍa (Cauragaṇeśa);
if one should so act, then a fault is declared in the Varṇavilāsa Tantra.
Gaṇeśa said:
Now I shall proclaim the mantra of the thief; listen to it, O Goddess Brāhmaṇī! He who recites the Purāṇa without knowing the mantra of the thief is indeed Kali incarnate.

In his next birth, that most wicked man shall become a thief-dog. Gaṇeśa himself seizes the splendor from all forms of worship— whether it be the worship of Śiva, the worship of Viṣṇu, or likewise the worship of Śakti.
O best of sages, the luminaries of the fifty classes of gods,
having proceeded along each gateway path, expand within each lotus;
stationed within each lotus, they steal away the splendor of the recitation.
Whatever splendor resides in the recitation and worship, there the lord of the host of thieves abides;
therefore, for the purpose of awakening the thieves, one should recite the ten thief-mantras.
Then the wise man should worship whichever deities are his chosen ones.
From that, one obtains the fruit [of the merit] of the gods beginning with Brahmā;
[one obtains] the Caura-mantra, the great mantra that gratifies the fifty Gaṇas.
O auspicious lady, without the Caura-mantra, whence can there be peace or a rite for well-being?
Likewise, the two ears, the two eyes, the nose, and the mouth;
then at the site of the navel, at the base of the *liṅga*, and likewise at the site of the anus;
at the gateway of the mind, and between the eyebrows—these are declared to be the eleven gateways.
O Brāhmaṇī-Īśvarī! One should place the mantra known as Caurya at each door.
O Bhadrā! I shall tell you the Caurya-mantra, which acts like a bolt upon each door;
I shall declare this secret that gratifies the fifty Gaṇas.
One should recite the fifth seed-syllable, *Aṅkuśa*, ten times over the first [syllable]. Having thus recited, O Fortunate Mother! one should then place the door-bolt.
Otherwise, the Gaṇas would break open the door with the *Aṅkuśa* seed-syllables.
She who is eternally within the moonlight, Śaṅkara, the most beautiful one;
she whose splendor is the moonlight, Sītā, the bowstring, and the quality of *aṇimā*;
she who is eternal, consisting of the moon and the bindu, and worshipped by Gaṇeśa.
One should place the two seed-syllables *hrīṃ hrīṃ* upon the two eyes;
likewise, *hrīṃ hrīṃ* on the two ears, and *huṃ huṃ* on the two nostrils.
One should place the twofold seed-syllable *strīṃ* on the mouth, and *klīṃ*, O Subhageśvarī, on the navel.
The seed-syllable *heṣauṃ* is proclaimed for the base of the *liṅga*, and *vluṃ* for the anus;
likewise, the syllable *huṃ* is for the middle of the eyebrows and for the seat of the mind.
One should thus perform the placement (*nyāsa*) of these eleven thief-mantras upon the eleven gates.
One should place the mantra of the thief tenfold, or the seed-syllable even once;
by this very recitation, one secures the door-panel at every gate.
The time for recitation is also in that very place.

Listen also as I shall explain the determination regarding the recitation of the mantra: at the time of dawn, having awakened from sleep upon one's bed, one should perform the placement of the Mātṛkās (mātṛkā-nyāsa) upon the body in the same manner as previously described, in the locations designated for the Mātṛkās.
Likewise, one should place the thief-mantras at the eleven gates;
one should recite the thief-mantra ten times or even once.
Through the recitation of the thief-mantra, Gaṇeśa will then be satisfied.
O Dear One! Even Yama has no authority over one who recites the mantra of the thief;
for from the recitation of all mantras, splendor arises from everything, and Gaṇeśa indeed possesses no power to take away that splendor.
Thus [it is said].
Now, the ritual application.
One should mutter "krom" ten times at the heart, and "hrīṃ hrīṃ" at the right eye.
In the left eye, [one recites] "hrīṃ hrīṃ. || 10 ||
In the right ear, [one should recite] "hrīṃ hrīṃ. || 10 ||
In the left ear, [one should recite] "hrīṃ hrīṃ. || 10 ||
At the right nostril, "huṃ huṃ. || 10 ||
At the left nostril, "huṃ huṃ. || 10 ||
In the mouth: Hrīṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ. || 10 ||
At the navel, "aiṃ līṃ. || 10 ||
At the *liṅga*, "hauḥ" || 10 ||
In the secret place, VLUM. || 10 ||
The syllable *hūṃ* at the center of the eyebrows. || 10 ||
One should recite ten times in every instance.
Then, one should perform the offering of the ajapā-mantra at various locations.
In the third section of the *Kulamūlāvatārakalpasūtra-ṭīkā*, regarding this Ajapāgāyatrī mantra, [one should place] "Haṃsāya ṛṣaye namaḥ" upon its head.
Salutation to the unmanifest Gāyatrī metre in the mouth.
Salutation to the deity Paramahaṃsa in the heart;
salutation to the seed-syllable "Haṃ" in the liṅga.
On the support: "Obeisance to Śakti.
For the pleasure of the Supreme Self, by means of twenty-one thousand six hundred recitations performed with inhalations and exhalations, I offer this to the beings of the past.

In the pavilion of the *mūlādhāra*, upon a four-petalled lotus of golden hue endowed with the four letters beginning with *va* and ending with *sa*, I offer salutations and dedicate six hundred recitations day and night to Gaṇanātha together with Gāyatrī. In the pavilion of the *svādhiṣṭhāna*, upon a six-petalled lotus resembling many flashes of lightning and endowed with the six letters beginning with *va* and ending with *la*.
I offer salutations; I present six thousand recitations of the *ajapā* mantra to Brahmā, accompanied by Sāvitrī.

In the pavilion of Maṇipūra, which resembles a blue lotus cloud and is endowed with the ten syllables from *ḍa* to *pha*, I offer salutations and present six thousand recitations to Viṣṇu, accompanied by Lakṣmī, within the ten-petaled lotus.

In the Anāhata-maṇḍala, within a twelve-petalled lotus resembling the rising sun and endowed with twelve colors, I offer salutations by presenting six thousand repetitions of the Ajapā mantra to Śiva together with Gaurī.
In the Viśuddha-maṇḍala, in the center of the pericarp of a sixteen-petalled lotus, [I offer salutations] to the Jīvātman, beginning with the letter *a* and ending with the letter *aḥ*.
I offer this recitation of one thousand *ajāpa* repetitions; obeisance!

In the pavilion of command (*ājñāmaṇḍapa*), within the glorious moon-light (*śrīcandraprabha*) two-petaled lotus endowed with the syllables *ha* and *kṣa*, I offer this recitation of one thousand repetitions to the form of the Guru accompanied by *māyā*; obeisance!
In the pavilion of the *brahmarandhra*, which is radiant with various colors, the term "thousand" (*sahasra*) should be understood as meaning "innumerable.
As it is said: "The lotus is endowed with ten million [petals].

To the Self of Consciousness (*pramātman*) residing upon that thousand-petaled lotus, who is accompanied by the letters from *a* to *kṣa*, one should perform a recitation (*japa*) of one thousand times.
"I offer this; obeisance.
Having thus offered the recitation (*japa*), one should perform the *ajapājapa* one hundred and eight times.
The letters from *a* to *kṣa*, together with "haṃsa," [constitute] Śiva, Śakti, and Bindu; [and] "a" [is] Brahmā.
Through the two dots in the form of the *visarga*, there is non-duality between Hari and Hara.
By means of the contemplation of non-duality through the realization "I am He" (*so'ham*), one's own nature is contemplated as being of the essence of Brahman; thus it has been stated.
(p. 309) By reciting [the mantra] twenty-one thousand six hundred times, one becomes the Supreme Lord (*śrīparameśvara*), whose form is that of the Supreme Deity.
Having made the formal resolve (saṅkalpa) once, saying "May [the Lord] be pleased," one should perform the meditation on the Haṃsa as follows.
I worship my own *liṅga*, which resembles a jewel, seated within the lotus-heart of Māyāpurī;
I immerse it in the pure water of the mind, the river of faith, constantly with the flowers of meditative absorption (*samādhi*) for the sake of non-rebirth.
In this context, the secret of recitation (japa) is written down.

By forming a "box" (*sampuṭa*) with the fifty letters in both direct and reverse order, one should conceive the letter *kṣa* as Meru, the form of Brahman; by performing recitation together with that [Meru], one is not afflicted by even a trace of faults.
By this, the entire universe itself is said in the world to be the conscious self (*cidātman*), through the single form of the *haṃsa* and the *mātṛkā* as the essence of time.
Without the practice of the *ajapā*, one would be ineligible for any vidyā, such as the *Śrīvidyā*.
Thus it has been said:
"Even that which has been performed by one who is deluded regarding the knowledge of the *haṃsa* shall become as if unperformed.
Thus it is stated in the seventh chapter of the *Dakṣiṇāmūrtisaṃhitā*, as cited in another Tantra by Padmapādācārya (Rāghavabhaṭṭa).

O Goddess, O sinless one! I shall now describe to you the practice of Ajapā-dhāraṇā, by the mere knowledge of which the Supreme Brahman itself becomes the teacher. O Sovereign Lady! A person should recite the syllable *Haṃsa* every single day.

One who does not know the aperture of delusion (moharandhra) has no liberation. O Goddess! When it is known and recited through the grace of the venerable Guru, then, by means of inhalation and exhalation, the destruction of bondage occurs.
In inhalation and exhalation, there are these two syllables, "haṃsa.

Therefore, the vital breath (prāṇa) has the nature of the *haṃsa*, abiding in the form of the Self (*ātman*). From the inhalation and exhalation from the navel, there is the establishment of the fire of the heart.
The count of the ajapā-japa within a day and night is also given in that same source:
sixty breaths constitute one prāṇa; six prāṇas are considered one nāḍikā;
and sixty nāḍikās make up a day and night—this is the established sequence for the number of japa repetitions.

O Īśvarī! A living being recites twenty-one thousand six hundred [times] daily the supreme mantra consisting of intense bliss. Its origin is the commencement of the recitation, and its death is the reporting [of the count].
The reason for its name, "Ajapā," is also stated in that very same place:
"O Goddess of the gods! Even without recitation, the recitation of the mantra-practitioner occurs [spontaneously].
Therefore, this is called 'Ajapā' (the non-recited), which severs the bonds of worldly existence."

O Maheśānī! Having thus performed the recitation, one should offer it every day to Gaṇeśa, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Hara, O Parameśvarī! Likewise, one should offer it in due order to the individual soul (jīvātman) and similarly to the supreme soul (paramātman).

p. 310) Six hundred thousand, one thousand, and indeed another thousand—one should offer these to the Guru in due order. Thus, having described the dedication of that recitation to Gaṇeśa and the others situated in their respective places, [the text proceeds] regarding those various locations...
And he describes the form of the phonemes of the Mātṛkā situated in those respective positions in that very same [text].
Upon this golden-colored *ādhāra*, one should contemplate the letters from *va* to *sa*;
likewise, O Supreme Goddess, these letters should be visualized as molten gold.
In the *svādhiṣṭhāna*, which has the luster of coral, one should contemplate the letters from *va* to *la*.

In the deep blue Maṇipūraka, one should contemplate the letters from *ḍa* to *pha*, which possess the radiance of a mass of lightning and the luster of great sapphires; in the tawny-colored [Anāhata], one should contemplate those which have the brilliance of the flame of a great fire.
O Dear One! One should worship the forty-three consonants from *ka* to *ṭha* in the fourth center, Anāhata; and in Viśuddhi, which is smoke-colored, one should worship the vowels of red color.
In Ājñā, which has the luster of lightning, one should contemplate the two letters *ha* and *kṣa*, which are white.
O Supreme Goddess! Know that the Brahma-randhra, whose essence is Nāda, is a thousand-petaled lotus shining with the luster of camphor.
O Supreme Goddess! [Know this] regarding those situated within these seven cakras.
O Dear One! Having offered the recitation performed during the day and night, O Supreme Goddess! the wise practitioner should perform the innate (sahaja) ritual placement (nyāsa).
Haṃsa is the seer (ṛṣi) in manifest form, and Gāyatrī is said to be the meter (chandas).
The deity is the Supreme Beginning; "Haṃ" is said to be my seed-syllable (bīja), and "Saḥ" is my power (śakti). "So'ham" is the pin (kīlaka), for you indeed are the Praṇava.
O Supreme Goddess! The region of the eyes shall be white in color.
Then,
O Pārvatī, know that the application for the sake of liberation is proclaimed as being thus with the mind;
thereafter, one should perform the placement of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga-vinyāsa) upon the body for the sake of accomplishment.
O Maheśānī! One should sequentially assign Sūrya, Soma, Nirañjana, and beyond that Nirābhāsa— ending with the dative case and followed by "svāhā"—
and having assigned them ending with the "kavaca" mantra, one should then meditate upon the state of Ananta.
The two-fold nature of the ajapā has been explained, as it is also stated in the fourth chapter of the Niruttara Tantra.
"Hamsa" is to be known as the primordial nature (prakṛti), and the syllable "Oṃ" is a quality of that nature.
By the sound "haṃ," one goes out; by the sound "sa," one enters again. The individual soul (jīva) constantly recites this supreme mantra, "Hamsa."

Twenty-one thousand six hundred times, day and night, is the Gāyatrī known as Ajapā, which bestows liberation upon yogis. O Goddess, Ajapā is twofold: manifest and hidden, according to their sequence.

The manifest [form] is said to be twofold: that which has the nature of the light of sound (*śabdajyotis*) and that which is the form of light (*jyotīrūpā*). That Goddess is established in the location of the heart.
She is also proclaimed as the secret Śiva-Śakti in the form of the syllable *ṭha*.
The seed-syllable of the Moon is the letter *ṭha*, which is said to be repeated with a vowel;
it is the secret essence of the *ajapā* mantra, proclaimed as the "wife of fire" (*svāhā*).
Merely by the mental resolve (*saṅkalpa*) regarding this, it is called the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*).
Thus, with his mind and body purified by meditation upon his chosen deity, the Guru, and Kuṇḍalinī, he should contemplate as follows,
according to the citation held by Rāghavabhaṭṭa:
"I am the Divine, and not another; I am Brahman alone, not subject to sorrow.
I am of the nature of Existence-Consciousness-Bliss, possessing an eternally liberated essence.
Having thus contemplated the oneness of the Guru, the Deity, and the Self, one should pray.
The method of meditation has been shown in the *Dharmakāṇḍa*:

"O Supreme Deity consisting of the consciousness of the three worlds! O Śrīnātha! O Viṣṇu! By Your command alone, having risen at dawn, I shall follow the course of worldly life for the sake of Your pleasure."
I know what is dharma, yet I have no inclination toward it; I know what is adharma, yet I have no aversion to it. Whatever I am commanded by the deity residing in my heart to do, that I perform.
In this context, the modification "Śrīnātha Viṣṇu" should be made in the Śaiva and other traditions.
For this very reason, it is stated in the fifth chapter of the *Śāktānandatarangiṇī*:
"O Goddess of the lords, whose nature is the consciousness of the three worlds! O Śrī Pārvatī! By the command of Your feet alone..."
Thus, half [of the mantra] regarding Śakti has been spoken; this is the prayer-mantra.
Then, having risen and bowed to the ground, one should void urine and feces, beginning with the left foot; as it is said in that very same place:
"Having thus reflected in his mind, the practitioner, having gone out from the house, self-controlled and pure, should perform the cleansing of the teeth after sipping water."
By the word *prayata*, it is indicated that one is purified after the elimination of urine and feces;
and so it is stated in the fifth chapter (*ullāsa*) of the *Mahānirvāṇatantra*:
Having paid obeisance, one should go outside, leading with the left foot;
having discharged urine and feces, one should perform the cleansing of the teeth.
(From the Gandharva Tantra, Chapter Five)
Endowed with all auspiciousness, the practitioner, having gone outside and discarded urine and feces, should perform the cleansing of his teeth.
For he who worships the deity without having chewed a tooth-stick [commits a fault].
O Goddess! That worship is fruitless; indeed, when [the preceptor] has died, one goes to hell.
—From the Dakṣiṇāmūrtti [Tantra].
One should then write the god Kāmadeva, whose essence is *klīṃ*, followed by "to all people" (*sarvajanam*).

This mantra, ending with "to my beloved" (*priyāya*) and "to the heart" (*hṛdayāntaḥ*), is for the purification of the teeth. One should wash the mouth with these fourteen syllables for the sake of attaining success (*siddhi*).
In the *Mantratantraprakāśa*.
Having performed the necessary purification, sipping water, and cleaning the teeth, and having completed the rinsing of the mouth and other such acts, one should perform the ritual bath.
In the perception of the nature of things.
Having risen during the *brāhma-muhūrta*, one should cleanse one's hands and feet;
having washed the mouth, O Goddess of Gods, as well as both nostrils,
and having applied collyrium to the eyes, one should resort to a pure place.
"He who looks upon the solar disc without having applied collyrium to his eyes shall lose the merit acquired throughout his life; what more need be said of that evil-minded person?
This is a declamatory passage (arthavāda) intended as a censure, which establishes the necessity [of applying collyrium] in places such as Haridvāra.
Because of such statements as these, [this practice] is known to indicate that [the rite] is optional (*kāmya*) in other cases.

Having performed purification (*śauca*) and the cleansing of the body (*deha-śuddhi*) according to the procedure prescribed in the *Smṛtis*, having discarded the night-garment and put on another garment, and having performed the ritual bath with mantras (*mantra-snāna*), one should enter the temple and perform the sweeping, smearing, and other [preparatory rites].
Having removed the *nirmālya* (remnants) of the deity and having cleared away the leaves and other materials remaining from the previous day, one should perform worship and offer salutations;
otherwise, there is a fault. As they say:
An animal bound while suffering from thirst, a maiden who has reached her menses,
and a deity with its floral offerings still upon it— these destroy previously accumulated merit.
(From the *Mantratantraprakāśa*)
Having performed the ritual purification correctly according to the procedure prescribed in the Smṛtis,
having washed his feet, sipped water, and performed the ritual placement (nyāsa), the self-controlled practitioner,
having entered the abode of the deity and removed the remains of the previous offering (nirmālya), [should proceed].

The wise one should offer a handful of flowers, as well as water for the guest-offering (arghya) and for washing the feet (pādya). He should provide water for rinsing the mouth and indeed offer a tooth-stick. He should also offer water for sipping (ācamanīya) and a pure, auspicious garment.
The ritual sweeping is found in the Yoginītantra, in the third part, in the ninth chapter.

I shall now proclaim the rules for sweeping; listen to that, O fair-faced one! Hear, my dear, what destination men or women—whose fates are determined by their actions—attain based on the amount of dust removed during the sweeping of the ground.
For that many thousands of years, he is known as Maheśvara throughout the seven continents;
therein also reside the substances of injunctions and prohibitions.
One should never sweep with wood, nor with a leaf, nor with *kuśa* grass;
one should avoid sweeping with cloth, with a cluster of grass, with *vīraṇa*, or with *nala*.
One should avoid using a cluster of grass, and one should also avoid *kuśa* and *kāśa* grasses.
Thus concludes the sweeping of the temple;
the smearing [with cow dung] is also performed in that very same place.

O beloved! If the earth is smeared with clay and cow dung, by that single application of ointment one is not born again from a womb. O Goddess! He who bathes, applies ointment, and offers water [to the ancestors] likewise attains this merit.
O illustrious and beautiful one! Listen to his merit in its true essence:
for as many drops of water as there are in the plastered area, O beautiful one, for that many thousands of years he is honored in the heavenly world.
One should perform the sprinkling with earth and water and the anointing of the deity;
thus liberated from all sins, one attains the world of Varuṇa.
This concludes the section on smearing.
Then, by means of mere praise, one should offer salutation as it is stated in the third chapter of the Viśvasāra Tantra.
The Lord said:
Having risen early in the morning and purified one's hands and feet,
and having turned toward the north, one should perform a prostration to the Guru with devotion,
especially through mind, speech, and body.
One should always bow to Kṣetreśa, Vāsturāja, and thereafter to Vighnarāja;
to Durgā, Vināyaka, Śambhu, Bhairava accompanied by Vaṭuka,
Brahmā, Nairṛti, and Cakrapāṇi.
Salutations to the obstructors and the lords of obstructions, and likewise to the sages;
salutations indeed to the gods, to the Vedas and the scriptures, and to the meanings of the Vedas; and always, O beloved, salutations to the Rāmāyaṇas, the Bhāgavatapurāṇas, and the Purāṇas!
One should always bow to the Brahmins, to one's gurus, and especially to the Yoginīs; to the ascetics, to those of Manu’s lineage, and to all human beings;
as well as to the trees, the medicinal herbs, and even the creepers and shrubs.
Salutations again and again to the Kulācalas and to the guardians of the directions from all quarters;
salutations again and again to the Saṃhitās, to the auspicious Rudras,
and also to the Yogas, the Karaṇas, and those very lunar days.
One should bow at all times to the Yoginīs, from the days, the fortnights, and indeed from all seasons;
from the moments, the twinklings of an eye, the actions, and the causes.
One should first bow down to the sacred seats (pīṭhas), the oceans, and the holy fords (tīrthas);
one should prostrate before the rivers, the yogas of action, and the mantras;
and likewise before the trees, the medicinal herbs, and the creepers and shrubs.
One should always bow down to both artificial and natural ponds;
to all living beings and to all states of existence, and especially to the flavors;
then, having bowed to the flowers, one should thereafter pay homage to the Āgamas.
O Pārvatī, one should always bow to the commentaries, the treatises on worldly affairs, and the narrative legends;
to the weapons, all the sciences, and the Mātṛkā-s;
and likewise to men, the Śakti-s, and the treatises on Dharma.
O Pārvatī! Having bowed to the beings, to the five elements, and indeed to the great elements (mahābhūtas);
to the luminaries and to the celestial bodies;
to the teachers and to the Vedas; one should then always bow down to the seasons.
One should always bow to the phonemes (varṇas), to the powers of the phonemes (varṇa-śaktis), and to the Kalās;

one should always bow to [the deities] along with Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra, and to the Mudrās; one should bow to the locations (sthānas) and to the deities of the locations, and salutation to the Soul of all time (sarvakālātman).
To the Vighnas, to the Kālapīṭhas, to the protectors of the host of Yoginīs; to the Bhairavas and their consorts, to the circle of the assembly of Mothers;
to the Jewels and to the Vowels, and also to those who cause delight to the Goddess.
Having thus prostrated, O Queen of the Gods! the wise one should meditate upon the Goddess.
Whether in a wilderness, a cremation ground, an empty dwelling, or likewise in a house, he should cultivate the realization of non-duality, [visualizing] the body as being like the entire universe.
Having meditated upon the foundational power (Ādhāraśakti) as holding two lotuses,
one should then contemplate Janārdana in the form of a tortoise upon her head, O Goddess—
a deity resembling a dark cloud and endowed with all the principles (tattvas).
One should meditate with the intellect upon the god Ananta situated upon his back,
endowed with a thousand hoods and resembling pure crystal;
one should visualize a plow on his right shoulder and a mallet on his left side.
Adorned with the jewel-ornament of a single earring,
one should contemplate the earth above the Single Wheel (Ekacakra) with the intellect;
the wise person should contemplate this in such a way that the earth is accomplished.
One should meditate upon her who is black in complexion and adorned with a pair of arms holding parrots and grains of rice;
there, one should mentally visualize a pavilion decorated with jewels,
and therein, one should meditate upon the wish-fulfilling tree (*kalpavṛkṣa*) which grants the fruits of all desires.
One should contemplate a great golden lion-throne situated below that;
there, one should visualize the Goddess, the sovereign of the gods, residing within the heart-lotus.
Thus ends the specific [instruction] regarding Chinnamastā.
Although the fruit has been stated specifically for the *Surīkramastava* and not for [the hymns of] Chinnamastā and others,
nevertheless, according to the maxim that "a scriptural meaning established in one place applies elsewhere as well, provided there is no subverting factor," it applies everywhere to the *Kramastava*.
The result of that [objection] should be inferred.

Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) that the *Kramastava* is non-eternal. If it is argued that this is acceptable as a desired conclusion (*iṣṭāpatti*), we say no; for such a suspicion applies only to that which was not written by the ancient authors of compendia.
But as for Dakṣiṇakālī:
Having risen during the *muhūrta* of Brahmā and purified his hands and feet,
the best of practitioners should perform the meditation on the Guru as previously described;
having prostrated according to the rules before the Goddess, he should indeed meditate upon that eternal one.
Having recited [the mantra] one thousand and eight times according to this rite,
the preceptor should daily recite the Krama-stava according to this procedure:
"Oṃ, salutations to the gurus, to the gods, and likewise to the Supreme."
Likewise, having saluted those who are higher and lower, as well as the one higher than the highest,
and having remembered Kṣetrapāla according to the prescribed rule, [one should salute] the deities of the door:
Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī, Durgā, Gaṅgā, and likewise Godāvarī.

Having paid obeisance to Bhogavatī, one should then worship the deities of the site (vāstudevas). O beloved! I bow down to Vighnarāja, the Lord of the Site (Vāstvīśa), and Kṣetreśa, as well as Nairṛta and Brahmā, whose nature consists of the Brahma-karma.
Having prostrated before the obstacles according to the prescribed rite, one should then bow to those deities;
having saluted that Ādhāraśakti, who bears two lotuses, who is blue in color,
the Great Illusion (Mahāmāyā), and whose form consists of twelve syllables.

Then, I bow to that Goddess in the form of Śakti, who is served by hosts of Dharma; to Viṣṇu, whose body is all-powerful Śakti, who has assumed the form of a tortoise, who is dark blue in color, possesses a massive body, and resides upon the Himalayas.
I bow to that Lord Ananta situated upon his back;
salutations to Hari in the form of a serpent, endowed with a thousand hoods.
I bow to the all-pervading Viṣṇu, who resembles the Himalaya mountain and holds a single staff.
I bow to him who is adorned with thousands of hoods and jewels;
one should meditate upon his left side as having a plough that brings about inauspiciousness,
and there, on the left portion, a mallet joined with eleven [parts].
One should meditate upon the imperishable Viṣṇu in the form of Varāha situated upon his head—
having a single tusk, a massive body, and a luster like a dark rain cloud.
Upon his tusk, one should always meditate on the Earth, who rests upon that lotus.
The great goddess is blue in color and adorned with the awn of rice.

One should always meditate upon her head as being endowed with the powers such as *aṇimā* and adorned with all the principles (*tattva*). With the intellect, one should contemplate the earth, complete with various mountains and joined with oceans filled with jewels.
One should contemplate mountains adorned with noble lineages everywhere within that [meditation]; having paid homage to the elephants of the quarters, one should always bow down to the yogas,
to the lords of sages, to the seers, and to those who uphold the Yoga scriptures.
One should always pay homage to the Śākta, Vaiṣṇava, and Śaiva [deities], to the yantras,
to the deities of the mantras, and to those devoted to all the scriptures;
likewise to Candra, to the lunar dynasties, and to the solar dynasties as well.

One should always bow down to those born of the lineage of Manu and to human beings, as well as to the five elements, the great elements, the elemental beings, and the constituent parts (kalās). Having paid homage even to the tastes, one should always bow down to the fragrances.
Salutations again and again to the Gandharvas who smile with flowers;
salutations to the Yakṣas and the hosts of Bhūtas, and to the Pretas in all rites.
O Beloved! I always bow down to those whose nature is the Śabdabrahman.
Salutations again and again to the Rudras, to those of the Rudra lineage, and to the Bhairavas;
salutations to the Liṅgas, to the deities within the Liṅgas, and likewise to the Vedas and the Śāstras;
and to those Vedas and Śāstras as well, eternal salutations, salutations!
Having paid homage to the immovable ones, one should always bow to the sages;
I bow to the eternal goals, and salutations again and again to the dwellings.
Having paid homage to the mantras, salutations again and again to the meanings of the mantras.
Salutations again and again to the Brahmins who provide the materials for worship; having paid homage to the Yoginīs, salutations again and again to the Śaktis as well;
and having paid homage to the jewels, one should always bow down to the rivers.
Having paid homage to the sacred seats (pīṭhas), one should always bow to the Mothers;
having paid homage to the offerings of food (annas), [one should say] "Homage, homage to the Indras";
and having paid homage to the fields (kṣetras) as well as to the guardians of the fields (kṣetrapālas).
Having bowed to the Kulācalas and to the various manifestations,
I offer perpetual salutations again and again to whatever has been said and whatever remains unsaid concerning them.
Om, I bow to the Goddess Kālikā, the destroyer of the impurities of the Kali age.
I bow to the consort of Śambhu; I bow to Bhavasundarī.
Having paid homage to the primordial Goddess, I bow to her who deludes the three worlds. I bow to her whose resolve is ever true, who dwells upon all mountains.
Having bowed to Pārvatī, [he said]: "O Daughter of the Mountain! Salutations to you eternally!
O Mother, your feet grant to the gods—whose very state is the object of meditation—the desired object of all longing.
Those in whose hearts that lotus-foot of yours shines forth are truly blessed; they are certainly worthy of worship by the world of the gods."

O Mother! Devoted ones remember Your feet, which are smeared with auspicious fragrances and saffron paste; they hear of them and roll upon the ground. O Bhavānī! for them, old age shall never come to pass.
Your lotus-feet are the refuge of the gods; You are the supreme, the highest, the primordial nature (Prakṛti) beyond both the manifest and the unmanifest.
O Goddess! Day by day, everything shall come into the palm of one's hand; what more need the virtuous say?

O Daughter of the Mountain, my shanks dispel the pride of the lords of poets, which was once familiar with the beauty of their lotus-like hands, and they now encompass this entire assembly of the Gaṇas.
Therefore, O Mother! Your lotus-feet, which have become female and yet possess the state of Śiva, are fixed in my heart as a source of welfare.
For those who are poor always bow their minds to Your feet, O Mother.
By your grace, all the gods, asuras, and the foremost of the Siddhas constantly roll [in bliss].

Hari meditated upon your lotus feet, which became the source of prosperity for all the worlds; Śiva, the Lord of creatures, meditated again and again upon that certain supreme reality beyond the highest; and thereafter, this Lord of the world performed the creation of the universe—O Mother, what else is there to be said of your pair of feet?
As for the result:
O refuge of the gods! Indra is the protector of the deities, and Kāśyapa Prajāpati alone is such—none other.
O Supreme Goddess! Viṣṇu and Śiva are your chosen husbands; all this is the fruit of your lotus feet.

O most excellent one! May your navel, ever blossoming with fresh sprouts in the form of exquisite body hairs, grant me refuge; what else could be conceived by the best of minds? Śambhu, who originated from the substance worshipped at your feet, has attained a state of worship by gods and asuras alike.
Hari, being intent upon the worship of your feet, attained the sovereignty of the Sudarśana discus;
the earth was sustained by you in the form of fragrance and water in the form of taste;
fire was sustained by you in the form of heat, and within the *praṇava*, you assumed the form of Brahman.
O Mother! He who avoids my face—which has the form of the moon, which is accompanied by Yama, and which possesses three eyes within the sphere of the three worlds—is indeed a beast.
For him there shall be no success; O Mother, the entire universe is constantly [enjoyed] through your amorous side-glances.
He obtains the lotus-feet that bear fruit.
You are the sacrifice, you are the oblation, you are the *svadhā* offering; in ancient times you were the supreme power of Murāri, and you are the eternal blessing of Murāri.
You are Hara, you are Hari, you are Śiva, and you are the refuge of the auspicious; O Bhavānī, you are the goal, you are the goal, you are the goal!

You are ever-new, you are new, or you are the ever-fresh fruit of ritual action; you are the sacrificial oblation, the refuge of the earth, the river, the stream, the goal, and the treasure of all treasures. You are the son, you are the daughter, and you are the father of householders.

O Bhavānī! Having placed in their hearts the garland known as your "Muṇḍamālā," the lords of gods such as Brahmā and the great sages attain sovereignty over the deities. This is some other supreme refuge here; for those who mentally recite [this mantra] while holding a human skull and a sword in their two hands, [they likewise attain success].

O Goddess! On your left and right sides are the gestures of granting boons (*varada*) and fearlessness (*abhaya*). Siddhas and the lords of sages, having placed you above Śiva upon their hearts, sometimes mutter the *vidyā* within their hearts.
One shall always become a knower of the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) of poetry, and in the end, one should take refuge in your pair of feet.
Meditating upon you as the sky-clad one (Digambarī) in the mind, one should mutter the mantra known as Parā, the mother of the worlds.
One should mutter Parā, the intellect of the worlds; or rather, shall we take refuge in her who is called Parā?
Placing you—who are surrounded by the resonant cries of Śiva—within their hearts, they mutter [her name] constantly.
O Goddess of gods! O Goddess! They call her "Parā," she who is the state of being beyond both the supreme and the non-supreme, and devoid of a lord.

O Goddess, if the foremost among the knowers of the Vedas were to recite their mantras while holding your erotic sentiment within them, they would become objects of public reproach— even the poet among poets and the first-born (the Brahmin).

Mentally visualizing her with disheveled garments, if one sometimes recites this mantra with trepidation, that man attains sovereignty over the nectar of immortality; O Kālakālī, listen! Is there anything else on earth [greater than this]?
O Mother, the Siddhas indeed chant these three seed-syllables of yours for the sake of liberation; O Mother, those who take refuge at your lotus feet attain perfection even within three days.
O Goddess! Because one recites the two *kūrca* mantras belonging to you, one shall obtain excellence even over gods and demons;
all shall attain wealth and wisdom—what more need be said, O Goddess, regarding that which is known as the Supreme-Non-Supreme (*parāparā*)?
O Maheśānī! Because it makes known your two-fold modesty, there shall be the fourth siddhi;
by the grace of your boon of true siddhi, a lord of men attains sovereignty over you.

Therefore, O Mother, hear from me the fruit of your own name; the virtuous declare it to be the fourfold aims of life (*caturvarga*). Furthermore, by worshipping these three seed-syllables (*bīja*), even a lord of sages attains sovereignty over the gods.
Furthermore, the Siddhas, having the form of Narasiṃha, mutter and bow to the pair of *kūrca* mantras;
by reciting those two *lajjā* mantras as well, those people attain the perfection of their minds.
At the end, having added the word *vibhā*, they declare this extraction of your mantra: *vibhāvasoḥ*.
O Mother! Constantly contemplating you together with the *siddhis* upon the wheel of fifteen spokes, and gathering the supreme nectar at the southern step,
one who always meditates on Kālī and is intent on the equipment for worship performed according to the rules— truly, there is no further need for a detailed exposition to you.
The state beyond fear of the destruction of existence.
You are Śrī, you are Īśvarī Kālī, you are Hrī, and you are Karālikā;
you are Lajjā, Lakṣmī, Satī, Gaurī, Nityā, Acintyā, Cit, and Kriyā.
The first is Parā, then Parākhya, then Paramā, and Paramāvasu;

having always recited and praised with the mind these [mantras] beginning with Akulī, which are joined with words consisting of accumulations of syllables, the knower of mantras mutters the mantra within his heart.
O Goddess! their minds do not for even a moment find the strength to oppose the crushing destruction of their prosperity within this cycle of existence.
If one recites the mantra with these thirty-three verses, praises, and bows to these [deities], who are like the supreme nectar and the best of gods,
there shall be accomplishment in this pure world; having bowed one's head to your pair of feet, one attains the power of irresistible will (*prākāmya*) along with the most excellent of the gods.
The multitude of those worthy of worship.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Hymn to the Sequence of Dakṣiṇakālikā," in the Viśvasāra Tantra.

Since the general rule (*utsarga*) applies once the scope of exceptions (*apavāda*)— namely, those [mantras] for which a specific sequence-stotra (*kramastotra*) exists— is set aside, the fulfillment of that fruit is achieved simply by reciting the *dakṣiṇakālikākramastotra* for each respective [mantra].
Now, a specific [instruction] regarding Guhyakālī has also been stated in that very same sixth chapter, following her armor (*kavaca*).
I shall proclaim the sequential hymn of praise; listen, O lotus-faced one!
Having risen during the *brāhma* hour, one should always bow to the Guru and the deities.
Facing the west (*vāruṇī-mukha*), one should offer salutations above and below.

One should offer perpetual salutation to the gurus and to their sandals; salutation be to those who are supreme, to those who are both supreme and non-supreme, and to those who are even beyond the supreme. Having prostrated before the Support-Energy (Ādhāra-śakti), one should salute the Kulācalas.
Having paid homage to Dharma-karma, and indeed salutations to Kūrmarāja;
constant salutations to Ananta, and repeated salutations to Varāha;
constant salutations to Pṛthivī, and repeated salutations to the Kulācalas.
Homage ever to the oceans with their waters of nectar and jewels;
homage ever to the family trees, and repeated homage to the wish-fulfilling trees (kalpavṛkṣas).
Homage, repeated homage, to the golden lion-thrones and the jeweled altars.

One should pay homage to the four directions; then, one should offer salutations to all the gods. One should always offer salutations to the Vedas, repeated salutations to the meanings of the Vedas, constant salutations to its branches, and repeated salutations to its feet.
Homage always to those phonemes; homage again and again to the meanings of the phonemes. Homage indeed to the unconditioned words, and to the Supreme Self.
Homage always to the sciences, and homage again and again to the non-sciences.
Homage always to the scriptures, and homage again and again to those that are not scriptures;
homage always to the dharmas, and homage again and again to the non-dharmas;
homage always to the devotees of the Lord, and homage again and again to the sciences.
One should always bow down even to the Vedas; salutations again and again to the meanings of the Vedas.
One should always prostrate like a staff before the devotees of Śrī Rāma.
Salutations eternally to the devotees of the Lord; salutations again and again to the meanings of the Bhāgavata.
Homage always to the meanings of the principles, and repeated homage to the principles themselves;
homage always to the yogas, and repeated homage to the objects of yoga;
homage always to the compendiums, and repeated homage to their meanings.
Salutations eternally to the *mātṛkās*, and salutations again and again to their meanings; salutations eternally to the *kalās*, and salutations again and again to the *śaktis*;
salutations eternally to the vowels (*svaras*), and salutations again and again to the *rāgas*.
Homage always to the passionate ones; homage, repeated homage, to those who possess their objects.
Homage always to the missiles; homage, repeated homage, to the weapons.
Homage always to the living beings; homage, repeated homage, to the seed-syllables.
Homage always to those who move upon the earth; homage, homage to those who move through the sky.
Homage always to the yogas; homage, homage to the karaṇas. Homage always to the muhūrtas; homage, homage also to the watches of the night.
Constant salutations to the seasons; salutations, salutations to the years.
Constant salutations to the ḍākinīs; salutations, salutations to the Rudras. Constant salutations to the bhūtas; salutations, salutations to the pretas.

Homage always to the yakṣas; homage again and again to the obstacles. Homage always to the spirits; homage again and again to the great elements. Homage always to the teachers; homage again and again to the Śaṅkaras.
Constant salutations to the devotees of Viṣṇu, and to those who are deluded by Māyā;
one should bow constantly to Māyā herself, and repeated salutations to the individual souls (prattvas).
Constant salutations to bodies, and repeated salutations to the all-pervading ones.
Salutations eternally to the mantras, and salutations again and again to the yantras;
salutations to the deities who consist of the phonemes, and salutations again and again; salutations eternally to those words, and salutations again and again to the true words.
Salutations eternally to the meditations and indeed to the treatises on meditation;
salutations again and again to the hymns, the armor-protecting mantras, and even to the names.
Salutations eternally to the scriptures and salutations again and again to their meanings.
Homage always to those who perform those actions; they are proclaimed as the supreme teachers. Homage always to the tastes, and homage, homage, to the fragrances.
(p. 321) Homage always to the sacred seats (pīṭhas), and homage, homage, to those who reside therein.
Homage always to the *sattvic* beings; homage again and again to the *rājasic* ones.
Homage always to the *tāmasa* ones; homage again and again even to the *guṇas*.
Homage again and again to the perfected ones (*siddhas*) who are the incarnations of all branches of knowledge.
Having paid homage to the bulb of bliss (Ānandakanda), salutations again and again to Kandanā;
to the lotus whose essence is all principles (tattva), and to the petals which are the primordial nature (prakṛti);
to the seat of the perfected ones (Siddhapīṭha), and to Śiva in the form of a corpse for the sake of the living being (sattva).
Homage, constant homage, to the wheel with fifteen spokes;
homage to Kālikā who resides therein, the secret one whose form is desire.
Homage again and again to the powers beginning with Gurukula and to Kālikā.
Homage, homage, let there be homage to You; homage, homage to those who are both supreme and non-supreme!

To her with wide eyes, worshipped by the hosts of gods, whose lotus-feet are adored by gods and asuras—to You, the Supreme and the Non-Supreme, the Siddhas attain mastery through their bodies adorned with garlands of human skulls.
Some perfected ones proclaim her as gross, while other sages declare her to be subtle;
I bow to that Mother Ambikā—bestow great auspiciousness upon my body!

Having thus served this lotus-foot of yours, the perfected ones (siddhas) attain supreme power. O Mother, source of joy for the people of the world, those who meditate upon you in their minds with devotion shall all be endowed with every fruit, even from the midst of sin, all grief, and all suffering.
Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Krama Praise of Guhyakālī," in the Viśvasāra Tantra.
Now, the Krama-stava of Tripurāsundarī, in the seventh chapter.
I shall proclaim the Krama-stava; listen, O lotus-faced one! Om, salutations eternally to the gurus, and to that which is higher than the highest;
salutations eternally, salutations again and again, to those who are both supreme and non-supreme, and to those who are beyond the supreme.
Homage to the cows, homage to the Brahmins, and indeed homage to the sons of Brahmā; homage to the sages, to the wives of the sages, and indeed homage to the sons of the sages;
homage to the directions, to the lords of the directions, and indeed homage to those who are clothed in the directions (the naked).
Salutations eternally to the wandering mendicants, and salutations indeed to the tongues;
salutations again and again to the Vedas, to the Vedic scriptures, and to the meanings of the Vedas;
salutations eternally to the devotees of the Lord, and salutations again and again to the glorious Bhāgavatas.

Salutations always to the illustrious devotees of Rāma; salutations again and again to the followers of the Lord. Constant salutations to the sacred fords, to the mountains, and to the spiritual seats (pīṭhas).
Salutations indeed to the male yogis, to the female yoginis, and to the practices of yoga and the like.
Salutations again and again to the meditations, to the syllables of the mantras, and to the *mātṛkās*; salutations eternally to the teachers, and salutations again and again to the Bhairavas;
salutations again and again to the Rudras, to the wives of the Rudras, and to the Gandharvas.
Homage, repeated homage, to the Kinnaras, the Piśācas, and the Kuṣmāṇḍas;
homage, repeated homage, to the incarnations, the forms, and the Ādityas; homage to the years and to the days, homage, repeated homage.
Salutations indeed to the conjunctions of the lunar mansions and planets, and to the astronomical instruments;
salutations, repeated salutations, to the lunar days, to all times, and also to the seasons. Salutations, repeated salutations, to Mahādevī Kālikā, who begins with the letter 'ka'.
To the Great Goddess residing in the letter *e*, whose nature is the support of all; to the Great Goddess residing in the letter *ī*, Rati, beautiful as the limb of Kāma;
and to the Great Goddess Indrāṇī residing in the letter *la*, for the sake of all spiritual accomplishments.
Salutations from all sides to Mahādevī Śivā, who resides in the letter *ha*;
may the auspicious Sundarī, the Great Māyā, protect me with these syllables. May Sāvitrī, the Great Māyā residing in the letter *sa*, protect me always.
May Śiva protect me, O Goddess of gods; may the Sovereign of the Suras, whose name begins with the letter *Ha*, protect me.
May Śivānī, the source of great prosperity who dwells in the letter *Ha*, protect me always. May the Great Goddess who dwells in the letter *Va* protect me, she who grants all desires.
May Makudevī, who resides in the letter *la*, and Indrāṇī protect me at all times.
May the goddess Sarvāṇī, the most beautiful of all, protect my entire body.
With these syllables, may Mahāmāyā, the beautiful one, always protect me.
May Mahāmāyā, residing in the syllable *ka*, protect me always as Brahmāṇī;
may Śivā, the messenger of Śiva, residing in the syllable *ha*, protect me everywhere.
May Śivā, residing in the syllable *ka*, protect me, and may Sureśvarī, residing in the syllable *ha*, protect me.
May Sāvitrī, the bestower of happiness, residing in the letter *sa*, always protect me; may the Great Goddess Lakṣmī, residing in the letter *la*, protect me at all times;
and may Bhavānīsundarī, the Mistress of the World, always protect my every limb.
May the Sovereign of the Gods, abiding in the letter *A*, protect [me] eternally and boundlessly;
may Śivadūtī, the Sovereign of the Gods who begins with the letter *A*, protect [me] always;
may Kāminī, the bestower of desires, abiding in the letter *Sa*, protect [me] forever.
May the Mistress of the Three Worlds protect me in all fields at the letter *la*;
may Indrāṇī, residing in the letter *la*, always protect me;
may the Queen of the Gods, residing in the letter *ma*, always protect me everywhere.
May the Goddess Bhuvaneśvarī, established in these syllables, protect me;
may Śivānī, the beautiful consort of Hara, always protect me everywhere;
may the Vidyā Sāvitrī, who abides in the seed-syllable of the Moon and possesses the form of Śambhu, protect me.
May the goddess Bhuvaneśvarī protect me in all fields;
may Mahāmāyā, consisting of these twenty-five syllables,
and Tripurāmbikā, as Bhuvaneśī, always protect me in every limb.
One should employ Bhuvaneśvarī everywhere among all the seed-syllables.
May the Goddess, the Sovereign of the Three Worlds, always protect me in every limb.
[She resides] in the crest-lock, the pair of eyebrows, the two eyes, the two lips, the two cheeks, and the nose.
And likewise: on the chin, the teeth, the tongue, the root of the palate,
the heart, the two sides, the back, the navel, as well as the belly, the hips, the generative organ, the secret parts, and the pair of knees.
May the Goddess Śrī Tripurasundarī protect me at the wheels of the knees, in the shanks, at the hips, and again in the feet; may she protect me in every limb—
whether in the study of scriptures, in debate, in battle, at the royal court, or in the worship of the gods.

May Tripurāmbikā protect me in the wilderness, in mountain fortresses, and likewise in the midst of enemies; in thieves, tigers, and lions; in fears of poisons and the like; and in those afflicted by extreme disease.
May Sundarī protect everywhere; may Sundarī preserve [me].
This is declared to be the Krama-stotra of Tripurasundarī.
It must not be spoken anywhere and at any time if one desires one's own welfare.

O Maheśvarī! One should never reveal [this] to one who is deceitful, devoid of devotion, or a slanderer; nor to one with missing limbs or extra limbs. O Maheśvarī! One should not give this King of Hymns (Stavarāja) to a Śūdra.
Whether one recites or even demonstrates that which was spoken by Śaṅkara—
be it a single verse or a single hymn— or even worships while reciting it,
[one is purified of] the killing of a Brahmin, the drinking of liquor, theft, and violating the teacher’s wife.
By the grace of this hymn, one quickly overcomes everything:
the childless obtains a son, the poor man obtains wealth,
and even by its mere touch, one becomes free from disease and endowed with strength.
O Goddess, what more need be said? Whatever one desires for oneself, all that is obtained, O Goddess, through the grace of this hymn.
Thus ends the "Hymn to the Sequence of Tripurāsundarī" in the Viśvasāra Tantra.
Thus, in the third section (Arthakāṇḍa) of the Śrī Prāṇatoṣiṇī, this is the second chapter, titled "The Description of the Branch Consisting of the Rules for Morning Duties."
In the Jāmalam.
"All rites for human beings prescribed in the Śruti and Smṛti have bathing as their root;
therefore, one should practice bathing, which increases prosperity, nourishment, and health.
This statement also appears in the tenth chapter of the Matsya Purāṇa.
The fault incurred by not performing the ritual bath has been stated by Rāghavabhaṭṭa.
And because deities do not preside over a person who wears unclean clothes, does not bathe, and is without ornaments.
The classification of baths is stated in the twenty-first chapter of the Uttarakhanda of the Rudrayamala.
Bathing is said to be of two kinds: immersion and the cleansing of the body.
Bathing with mantras, water, and other such means is proclaimed to be the superior one.
O beloved of my life! Listen to that manner which is the cause of my joy.
In the second chapter of the Viśvasāra Tantra.
The mantra, the terrestrial, the fiery, the aerial, and likewise the celestial.
The Vāruṇa and the Mānasa are proclaimed as the sevenfold bath;
having bathed in this manner according to the rule, one becomes pure, and not otherwise.
In that very context, he specifies the mantra-bath and so forth.

The ritual bath with mantras beginning with *āpo hi ṣṭhā* is considered the earthly (*bhauma*) bath; wiping the body [with earth] is the earthly bath; bathing with ashes is the fiery (*āgneya*) bath; the dust raised by cows is remembered as the windy (*vāyavya*) bath;
and that which is performed with sunlight and rain is here called the celestial (*divya*) bath.
The ritual bath for Varuṇa consists of immersion [in water] and the mental contemplation of Viṣṇu.
In that regard, the mantra-bath is of two kinds: internal and external.
Among these, the internal Vaiṣṇava bath has been described in the *Vasiṣṭhasaṃhitā*.
One should meditate upon the all-pervading Lord Nārāyaṇa, who resembles infinite suns, who has four arms, who bears the conch,
discus, mace, and lotus, who wears a crown and a forest garland,
and who resides within the lotus of the twelve-syllable mantra.
In the second chapter of the Viśvasāra-tantra.
Meditating on the lotus-eyed Lord, who stands firm and is embodied,
one should contemplate the stream of water arising from His feet falling upon one's own head,
entering one's body through the aperture of Brahma (brahmarandhra).
By means of that [water], one should wash away all this impurity residing in the body;
at that very moment, the practitioner becomes free from dust and resembles a crystal.
This excellent bath is remembered as being a thousand times superior to [the power of] mantra.
Thus ends the internal Vaiṣṇava bath.
The internal bath of Śākta nature is taught in the venerable Pañcamīmata.

The method of bathing is twofold, distinguished as external and internal. I shall explain with reverence the internal bathing, which is extremely secret, for the destruction of your [sins] and for the attainment of the fruits of the four aims of life.
Having recollected the threefold consciousness from within the midst of the three feet,
one should contemplate the flowing stream of Being-Consciousness-Bliss,
which is the object of meditative realization and the means for the liberation of men through mere remembrance by yogins.
By that, one should contemplate oneself as being washed, for the sake of the pacification of existence.
Thus ends the internal bath according to the Śākta tradition.
The internal bath according to the Śaiva tradition is described in the Śaiva Āgama:
preceded by breath control (prāṇāyāma), one should perform it mentally with the root mantra.
One should perform the mental bath, which is prescribed for all occasions.
In the Gandharva Tantra, in the sixth chapter.
Bathing is declared to be threefold, and the twilight devotions (saṃdhyā) are likewise remembered as being threefold. O Goddess! There is the internal, the external, and the mental.
Indeed, the mental bath belongs to one whose mind is always pure.
Indeed, one should always remain free from conceptual construction regarding touch, smearing, and so forth.
Having been told about the external mantras, now hear the internal [practice].
The wise one, intent on breath control (prāṇāyāma) according to the sequence previously described, [should proceed].
Having united Śakti with Paraśiva according to the prescribed method,
one should repeatedly immerse her in the nectar arising therefrom.
Now, the fruit of the daily bath is described in the tenth chapter of the Matsyasūkta.
Indeed, one who bathes daily does not experience the agonizing suffering of Yama;
even those people who are doers of evil are purified by daily bathing,
as well as those guilty of approaching forbidden women, accepting gifts from the wicked, and other such sins.
By performing the ritual bath, one is liberated from the sin committed in secret.
Now, the external bath.
In the second chapter of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa of the Rudrajāmala.
Furthermore, a man should bathe according to the prescribed rules in rivers, lakes, ponds, wells, or tanks, in the morning, at midday, or in the evening.
In the second chapter of the Viśvasāra-tantra.
Having intended the bath according to the prescribed rule, one should perform the morning rites at a river,
a natural pool dug by the gods, a large pond, or likewise the ocean.
The syntactical connection is as follows: having reached these [waters], one should perform the morning rites with the intention of bathing.
In that very same [text], it is stated that the water remaining in its place is more excellent than water drawn from rivers and other sources.
All rivers, beginning with the Gaṅgā, are praised by the wise according to their locations;
indeed, all the sacred fords (tīrthas) that exist in Bhārata, beginning with Kāśī,
are praised in their respective places as they are truly removers of all sins.

Thus, according to the statement to be explained, since the region extending as far as a *yojana* possesses the nature of the Gaṅgā, the excellence of even the water of the Gaṅgā when drawn out is established by the logic of "how much more so" (*kaimutikanyāya*).
And so, in the phrase "the Gaṅgā and others" (*gaṅgādyāḥ*), it should be understood that it is a *tadguṇasaṃvijñāna-bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "those distinct from the Gaṅgā."
In the second chapter of the Nīlatantra.
Then, having taken up earth and kusha grass and gone to the water's edge,
one should bathe to remove impurities and perform the ritual bath with mantras.
The *Śyāmārahasya* specifies the *kuśa* grass for the *śākta* [rite].
Silver should be worn on the index finger, and gold should be worn on the ring finger.
This alone is the *kuśa* for the Śākta; the *darbha* grown in the forest is not [to be used].
Thus ends the section on the Śākta-kuśa in the fifth chapter of the Mahānirvāṇatantra.
First, having touched water, one should then enter the water;
standing in water reaching to the navel for the removal of impurities,
one should bathe once, emerge, and then perform the ritual bath with mantras.

By this it is shown that bathing merely by means of formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*), without the removal of impurities (*malāpakarṣaṇa*), is contrary to the injunctions. However, some— citing the previously mentioned statement from the *Viśvasāra* which shows bathing immediately after the morning rites (*paurvāhṇikakriyā*)— maintain that even those who have not performed those rites, and who are anointed with oil, may [bathe] prior to the bath.
They perform the morning rites;
however, that is not pleasing,
because according to the previously cited statement of Jāmalā, every ritual action is rooted in bathing, and for this very reason, Rāghavabhaṭṭa [states]:
Having performed the ritual bath with mantras and having come to the temple, one should perform the sweeping and so forth, as previously described.
In the Nīlatantra:
Having thus immersed oneself three times with the *vidyā* mantra and likewise with water,
one should immerse again in the water and complete the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*).
For the purpose of worshipping the chosen deity (*iṣṭadevī*), one should perform the ritual bath in a body of water.
In the *Mantratantraprakāśa*.
When the dawn has not yet risen, the practitioner (mantrī) should perform the Vedic bath at a sacred ford or in pure water,
and then perform the Tantric bath. Thus concludes the Tantric bath following the Vedic bath.
In the Gandharva Tantra, in the first chapter.

Having first extracted the Praṇava (Om), then saying "tat," and then addressing it as "sat," the wise man should perform his action. By remembering this at the beginning of actions, one becomes fit for union with Brahman.
Thus is the fruit of the designation "Tatsat," according to the second chapter of the Toḍalatantra.
Having recited "Today," and so forth, one should then recite the solar month;
thereafter, for the pleasure of the deity, one should bathe with pure water.
In the *Kulacūḍāmaṇi*.
My forms are black, red, yellow, blue, and various others; therein,
whichever disciple belongs to a particular family, perceiving that very form,
[he perceives] the entire heaven, the earth, the netherworld, and the origin of all beings.

Having sipped water with *darbha* grass from his family lineage, and having applied a sectarian mark (*puṇḍraka*) with *darbha* and family materials, he should then take his family vessel containing *dūrvā* grass, sesame seeds,
and water, and perform the ritual bath for the pleasure of his family deity.
Having first formed this resolve, one should place the *kulacakra* in the water.
A vessel for the family is a copper bowl;
a wheel of the family is a triangle—this is the procedure for the ritual visualization (saṅkalpa).
In the Matsyasūkta:

In rites performed for ancestors or deities—whether obligatory, occasional, or for the sake of specific desires—an action preceded by a formal resolve (saṅkalpa) is required; otherwise, it is traditionally held that no fruit is obtained.
Thus, there is a fault in failing to form this resolve.
For the purpose of formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*), even a vessel that is prohibited or prescribed is [permissible] in that very context.
One should never make a formal resolve (saṅkalpa) using mother-of-pearl, conch, stone, or hand-held vessels made of bell-metal, silver, and the like, nor ever with those made of clay.
