Thus, in this resolve, [one should avoid] a prohibited vessel.
Having taken an udumbara vessel, and especially one made of gold,
the wise man should perform the formal resolve (saṅkalpa), or else with a cup formed from pure leaves.
Thus, in this resolve, the vessel is prescribed right there.
At the time of bathing, however, one should use either the hand or a copper vessel;
for rites concerning the ancestors, a śrāddha-vessel is used, while for rites concerning the gods, a conch shell is recommended.
Thus, there is a distinction of recipients according to the distinction of the action.
He describes the manner of immersion in that very same [text]:

One should immerse oneself facing the current or else facing the sun; thereafter, one should remember Nārāyaṇa, Gaṅgā, and one's chosen deity (iṣṭadeva). While immersed, one should have the hair loose, and upon emerging, one should bind the topknot (śikhā) once again.
Then, having joined his palms in reverence, he should invoke the sacred fords (tīrthas) with this:
"Oṃ, Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Godāvarī,
Sarasvatī, Narmadā, Sindhu, Kāverī— be present in these waters!"
O Sun, the divine holy places in the cosmic egg have been touched by your rays;
by that truth, O Lord, O Maker of Day, grant me a sacred bathing place!
And the beloved holy places situated within the rays of the sun—
Having arrived and accepted the *arghya*, say: "Bestow all spiritual accomplishments (*siddhi*) upon me.
Then, having fashioned a square, the wise one should provide for the ritual bathing (*snāna*) therein.
As cited by Rāghavabhaṭṭa:
"O Goddess! O beautiful one! I invoke you here for the purpose of bathing. Come, O Gaṅgā! Salutations to you, who are accompanied by all sacred fords (tīrthas)."

Thus, having invoked the *tīrtha* from the solar orb (*ādityamaṇḍala*) with the mantras and the goad-mudrā (*aṅkuśamudrā*), and having joined it with the water while reciting "vaṃ," one should visualize the lunar, solar, and fiery orbs therein; then, consecrating it twelve times with the nectar-seed syllable "vaṃ," veiling it with the armor-mantra (*kavaca*), protecting it with the weapon-mantra (*astra*), one should consecrate it eleven times with the root-mantra (*mūlamantra*).
Its authoritative source is found in the Vaśiṣṭha-saṃhitā.
Having drawn forth the sacred water (tīrtha) from the mandala with the heart-mantra and the goad-mudrā (aṅkuśamudrā), the practitioner of mantra,
having invoked it and united it with the lunar, solar, and fiery mandalas within the water,
should immerse himself in its midst with perfect concentration.
Having recited the root mantra, one should mentally delineate the form.
In the Jñānārṇava.
Having performed the assignment of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) upon one's own body preceded by breath control (*prāṇāyāma*),
one should draw forth the sacred water (*tīrtha*) from the orb of the glorious Sun using the hook-gesture (*aṅkuśamudrā*).
Having bathed it with the syllable *vaṃ*, one should veil it with the armor-mantra (*kavaca*).
Having protected it with the Astra-mantra, one should consecrate it with the Mūla-mantra eleven times (the number of Rudras).
Having immersed the Śrī-deva therein, one should meditate upon Him and recite the mantra according to one's capacity.
Also, in the Matsyasūkta:
One should recite the mantra eleven times while covering [the vessel] with the fish-mudrā (mīnamudrā).
Then, facing the sun, one should cast water into it twelve times— the number of the sun being twelve.
Having recited the root mantra, one should wash both hands;
then, having immersed oneself three times in the water flowing from the feet, one should mutter the mantra.
Now follows the ritual of applying clay, as described in the Viśvasāra Tantra:
Having smeared himself with the mud and water of the Gaṅgā according to the prescribed rule,
he should perform his bath according to the ritual, as per the word of Mahākāla.
The method for touching the clay, however, is found in the *Mantratantraprakāśa*.
Having brought the clay with the root mantra, one should divide it into three parts there;
one part should be cast with water while reciting the mantra.
In this manner, one should likewise smear [the body] from the head down to the navel.
In the same manner, one should smear the lower part with another portion; this is the remainder of the instruction.
The method of smearing is described in the Matsyasūkta.
The procedure for applying earth to one who has no fire is as follows: on the nose, forehead, cheeks, chin, sides, feet, back, navel, thighs, and shanks.
The mantra for casting [the arrow], however, is in that very same place.

For this mantra, "idaṃ viṣṇuḥ," Medhātithi is the seer (ṛṣi), Gāyatrī is the meter (chandaḥ), Viṣṇu is the deity (devatā), and its application (viniyoga) is for the application of earth upon the water.
Oṃ, Viṣṇu strode across this; in three places he planted his step; his footstep is firmly set in the dust.
The mantra for anointing the limbs is found in the Viśvasāra.
Oṃ! O Vasundharā, trodden by horses, trodden by chariots, and trodden by Viṣṇu!
O Earth, take away my sin, whatever evil deed has been committed by me.
Oṃ! You were lifted up by the boar, Kṛṣṇa, who possesses a hundred arms.

Salutations to you, O Aruṇī, source of all the gods, O lady of excellent vows! Then: "Oṃ, I bow first to those who are the support of Viṣṇu, who possesses incomparable splendor and every form, and from whom those forms were subsequently born."
Having thus instructed, the wise man should then immerse himself three times in the water.
In the Vaśiṣṭha-saṃhitā.

Having risen and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), he should thereafter perform the placement of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa). Then, having consecrated himself seven times with the root mantra using the mudrā called the "water-pot" (kalaśamudrā) and with waters empowered by the root mantra, he should proceed.
The mudrā of the jar is as described in the Jñānārṇava.
O Pārvatī, when a fist is formed with the left hand and [the right hand is positioned] over it,
this auspicious mudrā called Kalasa destroys all sins.
In the Vaśiṣṭha-saṃhitā.
Having emerged from the water and formed the *kumbha-mudrā*, one should then bathe with the syllable *vaṣaṭ*.
Having placed the water from the *śālagrāma* stone, mixed with the fragrance of *tulasī*,
into a conch shell and whirling it three times, one should pour it over one's own head.
Then, having pressed his own thigh and having carefully washed it and sipped water (performed ācamana), he should briefly satisfy the Brahmins, the humans, and the ancestors.
Thus concludes the abbreviated libation.
However, there is a specific distinction regarding the *parakhaṭa* (the other's account) in the second chapter of the *Viśvasāra*.
In the case of another's account, one should always perform the removal of the mud-clod, [saying]:
"Arise, arise, O Mud! Abandon the merit of another;
destroy my sins and grant me constant peace."
Thus concludes the procedure for the *parakhāta* (the secondary pit).
Now follows the prohibition against bathing with oil at the beginning of the solstices.
In the *Yoginītantra*, in the Northern Section (*Uttarakhaṇḍa*), in the ninth chapter.
One should not perform an oil bath during the solstices, at the equinoxes, on Tuesdays, on the day of the new moon, on the twelfth lunar day, or when the sun is eclipsed by Rāhu.
Now, regarding the wiping of the body, it is in that very same place.
O Goddess! One should wipe [the image] with cloth made of cotton or with bark-fibers.
By using red garments, one becomes afflicted with leprosy; by using white ones, one incurs disease.
One should not use flowers at all, for by doing so, one meets with destruction.
By wearing blue cloths, one attains the eye; by wearing red ones, one reaches the destruction of [one's] enemies.
However, in the tenth chapter of the Matsyasūkta, bathing at midday and the wiping of the body are prohibited.

O Queen of the Gods! At midday bathing, one should not wipe the body with a cloth or with the hand; however, that which was used in the morning does not cause defilement. This applies to bathing for the deceased, at sacred pilgrimage sites, and at the Gaṅgā at all times.
One should not wipe the body with the husk of a cotton seed;
one should not wipe the body with these at all.
It is stated "not with the husk of a cotton seed" in order to demonstrate that there is an even greater fault [in using other such materials].
The reason for the prohibition against body-cleansing at midday is also stated in that very same place.
The gods drink from the head, the ancestors likewise from the mouth;
the Pitṛ-gandharvas from the chest, and all living beings from the lower parts.
Therefore, one should not wipe the body, especially at midday.
In the *Puraścaraṇarasollāsa*.

O Goddess! O Maheśānī! If one worships Kālikā without bathing in the Gaṅgā, or if one worships the ten Vidyās with devotion, all of that is in vain for him, O beloved Goddess, without bathing in the Gaṅgā.

O Pārvatī! Having recited the Gaṅgā-mantra at a sacred site or by a river, even a sinful person who performs an ablution is liberated from all sins. O beautiful one, listen now to the meditation and the mantra of Gaṅgā.
The meditation and mantra taught in the Tantras are highly recommended in the Kali age in Bhārata.
Now, meditation.
Resembling pure crystal, adorned with white garments,
graced upon her heart with a necklace of white pearls,
the Goddess wears white garlands and is embellished with white ornaments.
O Śaṅkarī, listen! Having thus meditated upon Gaṅgā—who is eternally sixteen years of age and attended by Brahmā and the other gods—one should recite the Vidyā.
First, having uttered the Praṇava, one should extract the Māyā-bīja.
O Supreme Goddess, [one should say] "to Gaṅgā.
After that, one should utter further:
having spoken the two preceding seed-syllables, one should extract the wife of Fire (svāhā).
This nine-syllabled vidyā is established upon the path of the suṣumṇā. || 1 ||
I shall now proclaim another mantra, a supreme secret:
having first extracted the *praṇava*, then [the word] *gaṅgāyai*, and again extracting the *praṇava*, one should utter this mantra. (2)
I shall now describe another [mantra] situated on the path of Suṣumṇā:
having extracted the seed-syllable of Māyā (Hrīṃ), one should again extract the Praṇava (Oṃ).
Then, O Goddess, O Beloved! make the word "Gaṅgā" end in the dative case.
Having first uttered the two seed-syllables, recite this mantra;
this seven-syllabled vidyā always resides upon my head. (3)
I shall now proclaim another mantra that is exceedingly difficult to obtain:
having extracted the seed-syllable of Māyā (Hrīṃ), one should then say "Gaṅgāyai," and having again extracted Māyā, one should utter this mantra. (4)

O Pārvatī! By this path of meditation and the path of mantra, one should constantly worship Gaṅgā; for such a person, spiritual perfection is not far off. By reciting [the mantra] day after day, one indeed obtains the fruit of bathing in Gaṅgā.
Likewise: "Therefore, O Goddess worshipped by the gods, one should first recite the mantra of Gaṅgā;
then Gaṅgā herself comes for the sake of purifying the practitioner."
Thus ends the fruit of the Gaṅgā-mantra.
That Gaṅgā who is the great illusion (māyā), the coiled one (kuṇḍalī), and the supreme coiled one—O Supreme Goddess! that Gaṅgā remains pervading the entire universe;
indeed, in the form of the great river, she remains pervading everything.
The greatness of the Gaṅgā-kṣetra is also described in that very same place.

O Goddess! O Beloved! in whatever field that river exists for even a single *yojana*, it is indeed the Gaṅgā, O lady of tremulous glances; of this there is no doubt. Indeed, in my knowledge, no merit equal to the Gaṅgā is found.
In the *Yoginītantra*, in the first section, the eighteenth chapter.
O Goddess of the Suras, how can I describe the majesty of Gaṅgā,
by the mere remembrance of whose name even sinners become partakers of liberation?
Even a sinner who says "Gaṅgā, Gaṅgā" among other sinners [is purified].
And having abandoned their sin, he shall indeed go with them to the city of Viṣṇu.

Thus ends the majesty of the name of Gaṅgā. O Maheśvarī! Whatever sins have been described—those for which no atonement has been prescribed, as well as those for which atonements exist—[are all removed by it].
All of those perish through ablution in the waters of the Gaṅgā.
Thus ends the majesty of the waters of the Gaṅgā.
O Śivā! By the majesty of the mantra, even if water from the Ghargharā river falls into the city, it all becomes the Gaṅgā;
indeed, whatever region the Gaṅgā flows through, that region becomes a vessel of merit.
This sacred field is declared to be pure for two yojanas;

whatever action is performed there is equivalent to an action performed at the Gaṅgā, of this there is no doubt. O Goddess, whatever is done at the Gaṅgā, one obtains the fruit of that which is inexhaustible.
O beloved of Śambhu! Whether it be a confluence or a sacred site, it has been described [as such];
all living beings situated there have emerged from the world of the gods.
Having always performed meritorious deeds and having enjoyed various pleasures, they [attain liberation].
Without effort they shall go to that place which is most difficult to attain;
such is the fruit of the Gaṅgā region.
Where the Gaṅgā does not grieve, being praised by hosts of celestial sages—
he who gives up his life in the Gaṅgā through the power of merit attains liberation through knowledge; in the absence of that [knowledge], he attains Vaikuṇṭha.
O Great Goddess! Gaṅgā [leads one] from the world of heaven onwards, [rendering one] free from sin.
Thus is the fruit of relinquishing one's life in the Gaṅgā.
If one gives up their life on the road while traveling toward the Gaṅgā,
even if they are a sinner, they go to the world of Viṣṇu, which abounds in virtues.
Thus is the result of death for one traveling on the road to the Gaṅgā:
whoever gives up their life on its bank, whether by lawful or unlawful means,
even they attain heaven endowed with every provision.
Thus is the fruit of dying on the banks of the Gaṅgā:
as long as the bones of the deceased are cast into the Gaṅgā,
for that many thousands of years he is honored in the heavenly world.
Thus ends the fruit of casting the bones of the deceased into the Gaṅgā.
"Wherever one dies through contact with the waters of the Gaṅgā,
being liberated from all sins, one is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
Thus, elsewhere, [is stated] the fruit of dying in conjunction with the waters of the Gaṅgā.
On the bank of the Gaṅgā, one who is composed should offer a funeral ball (piṇḍa) on a space measuring four cubits;
having thus fulfilled his debt to the ancestors, he is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
Thus ends the fruit of offering funeral cakes within the four-cubit area.
O Goddess, for that meritorious person who performs the libation (tarpaṇa) in the Gaṅgā,
there shall truly be great satisfaction for the ancestors for a hundred years;
it is likewise declared to be so for the sages and the deities as well.
Thus ends the fruit of the libation performed in the Gaṅgā.

O Śivā! Whether by day or by night, at twilight or in the dead of night, one should perform bathing, giving, austerity, fire-offerings, libations, and worship in the Gaṅgā; one should do all these without regard for distinctions of time.

Thus ends the section on the absence of prohibited times regarding the Gaṅgā. O Śivā! If, having observed a specific time, one should abandon the rite, he shall thereafter become an immobile being in the forest.

His crest was quickly consumed by the forest fire and reduced entirely to ashes. Thereafter, O Supreme Goddess! he is born as a Cāṇḍāla suffering eternal misery for seven births; at the end of that, he becomes a washerman.
O Maheśānī! [He remains] for three births; at the end of that, he is born among Śūdra wombs.
O Maheśānī! For ten births, he then attains the status of a Vaiśya.
When four births have passed, he becomes a Kṣatriya after three more births.
"Having thereby attained the status of a Brahmin, a man shall obtain a meritorious rebirth.
Thus ends the censure of deliberating over whether it is the right or wrong time for bathing in the Gaṅgā.

O Supreme Goddess! For whoever steals anything from the Gaṅgā, there is no atonement for that person blinded by the darkness of delusion other than Raurava. O Goddess, O Sovereign of the Gods! I have thus described to you [the fate] until the dissolution of all beings.
Thus, there is a slight fault regarding the carrying [of water] in the Gaṅgā.
O passionate woman! That man who accepts [gifts] on the bank of the Gaṅgā or from the Gaṅgā itself is born constantly as a dog-eater (outcaste) for ten births;
thereafter, due to the affliction of poverty, he wanders the earth.
O Great Goddess! [This lasts] for seven births; at its conclusion, one shall obtain liberation.
Thus ends the section on the fault of accepting gifts at the Gaṅgā and other such places.
Thus, O Maheśānī, has the supreme majesty of that mantra of Kālikā been described to you, as well as the cause for the majesty of the Gaṅgā.
Thus ends the glorification of the Gaṅgā in the Yoginītantra.
Oṃ! For one desiring to emit the entire universe, semen is repeatedly produced.
May the divine Waters, the mothers of all beings, purify me.
One should recite that [mantra] enclosed by the seed-syllables of Tāra (oṃ) and Varuṇa (vaṃ).

Having sprinkled oneself with the two mantras held by Rāghavabhaṭṭa: "May the waters, which constantly wash away misfortune in the form of impurity residing within all beings through their very touch, purify me."
Oṃ! Whatever misfortune is in my hair, at the parting of my hair, or on my head;
whatever is on my forehead, in my ears, or in my eyes—O Waters, may you remove that. Salutations to you!
[Grant me] long life, health, sovereignty, the destruction of the enemy faction, and happiness.
"May contentment, forbearance, faith, and knowledge be yours; salutations to you.
With this verse, as recorded by Rāghavabhaṭṭa, one should bow to the water.
Now, the mental bath (mānasasnāna).
In this regard, he first demonstrates that the mind is the cause in matters such as bondage and liberation.
In the *Yoginītantra*, in the third part, the eighth chapter.
The mind alone is indeed eternal; the mind alone is the cause.
The mind alone is the cause of bondage and liberation for human beings.
By the mere restraint of that [mind], one shall never again be subject to worldly existence.

"If one says one thing, does another, and likewise displays something else residing in speech and mind, his action shall be in vain. Thus it is stated additionally in the twenty-sixth chapter of the Matsya Sūkta.
"What need has he who contemplates the evil he has committed for bathing at sacred fords?
Even if washed a hundred times with water, it remains impure like a liquor jar," so it is said in the Matsya Sūkta.
In the Yoginītantra.

That [external ritual] has become secondary; that primary cause of suffering—the mind—is corrupted within. Even if it is constantly washed with water, it remains as impure as a vessel that once held liquor. Thus, bathing at sacred fords is prohibited.
Whether one dwells for a long time in a cave on a mountain peak, or whether one possesses a triple-segmented alchemical pill or a sacred cloth;
whether one recites the Purāṇas or the essential principles of Vedic doctrine— if the heart is impure, all of this is in vain.
Neither sacred fords, nor gifts, nor vows, nor stages of life can ever purify one who is evil-intentioned and of corrupt mind. Thus ends the description of the faults of the wicked-minded.
In the same way.
Having thus brought the mind under control, wherever a man may dwell,
there for him is Kurukṣetra, Prayāga, Puṣkara, and Gayā.
Thus ends the description of the fruit for one of pure mind,
from the *Jñānasaṅkulyā*.
"Deluded people wander from one sacred ford to another; they do not know the sacred ford that is the Self. O fair-faced one, how can such people be liberated?"
In the Rudrajāmala, in the Uttarakhanda, in the twenty-first chapter.
Merely by bathing, one shall be liberated from the mountain of sin that extends to infinity.
One should bathe in the stainless sacred ford (tīrtha) within the lotus-pool of the heart,
or else one should bathe in the Bindu-tīrtha for liberation from the sins of all births.

In this body, which is a sacred ford of Śiva filled with the water of wisdom, the two channels, Iḍā and Suṣumnā, flow; for one who always bathes therein with the waters of Brahman, what need is there for the waters of the Gaṅgā or even those of Puṣkara?
These two statements were written as being from the *Kalpasūtra-ṭīkā* and the *Udayākara-paddhati*.
In the *Jñānasamuccaya*.
The *iḍā* is the Bhāgīrathī Gaṅgā, and the *piṅgalā* is the river Yamunā;
the channel situated between them is called the *suṣumnā*, which is the Sarasvatī. Where these three confluence—that is called the King of Holy Places (*tīrtharāja*).
One should perform a bath there; one is liberated from all sins.
Thus concludes the mental application.
In the Rudrajāmala:
Iḍā, which dwells in the seat of impurity and is the flowing Yamunā whose essence is the Sun,

and likewise Suṣumnā, which goes to the region of impurity— Sarasvatī protects the nature of immersion for the person intent on bathing within the mind, who knows the reality distinguished by the yoga of mantra-rituals.
One who joyfully bathes in the pure water of the earthly sacred site within the root-lotus shall become a partaker of perfect liberation.
The Gaṅgā, the purifier of all sacred sites, having emerged from the Great Being (Viṣṇu),
destroys all sins and bestows liberation itself, directly granting the merit of stainless goals.
Thus ends the sacred site (tīrtha) located at the mūlādhāra.
To whatever extent the sacred ford resides in heaven, it likewise resides within one's own lotus of the self-abiding center.
"Just as the lord of yogis, having fixed his mind [there], bathes in the waters of the Gaṅgā"—
thus is the sacred ford (tīrtha) located in the Svādhiṣṭhāna.
In the Maṇipūra, there is the divine sacred ford (devatīrtha), the lake of the five pools (pañcakuṇḍa-sarovara).
There, he who desires liberation bathes at the Śrīkāmanā-tīrtha.
Thus ends the description of Maṇipūra-tīrtha.
He who desires liberation and bathes in all the sacred fords (tīrthas), having visualized them as being within the solar orb in the Unstruck (anāhata) center—
this is the sacred ford of Anāhata.

Having meditated upon the great lotus called Viśuddha, which is the source of the eight sacred fords (tīrtha) and bestows the liberation of absolute isolation (kaivalya), the hero bathes therein for the sake of release. Thus ends the sacred ford situated in the Viśuddha [cakra].

Having always meditated upon Mānasa, Bindutīrtha, Kālīkuṇḍa, and Kalādhara within the Ājñā-cakra, one bathes for the sake of attaining liberation (nirvāṇa). Thus ends the section on the Tīrthas situated in the Ājñā.
Yogins joyfully perform this bath dear to the Kula;
therefore, the heroes who are endowed with sattva and possessed of all siddhis, O gods,
having always committed various sins including even the murder of a Brahmin, [are purified].
Having performed their ablutions in these great sacred fords (tīrtha), the perfected ones (siddhas) attain powers such as atomization (aṇimā).

Merely by bathing, one becomes free from sin; however, one who is incapable of controlling the vital breath (vāyu) shall certainly become a liberated yogi simply through the sight of these sacred fords.
Thus ends the fruit of the mental bath.
In the tenth chapter of the Matsyasūkta.

That which ought to be performed after rising from the water, and that which ought to be performed while seated in the water— if one performs these two in reverse, it is as if it were not done at all; likewise,
whatever is performed in the water with a dry garment, or on land with a wet garment, is likewise ineffective.
"One should not perform daily rites (āhnika-karma) either in water or on dry land.
This prohibits performing the rite in water while wearing dry clothes, or on land while wearing wet clothes.
In the Gautamīya [Vinaya].
Having wrung out his garment and washed his thighs, and having sipped water while remaining silent,
he should put on two pure garments, an undergarment and an upper cloth,
which are uncut, with their fringes intact, and white; then, seated upon a seat, he should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana).
In the Matsya-sūkta.
Having crossed over and put on two washed garments, the wise man should do so;
neither dyed, nor dirty, nor blue clothing is praised.
The lengths should be eight, seven, six, and four cubits respectively.
The upper garment (*pidhānāmbara*) is prescribed according to the sequence beginning with the Brāhmaṇas. Thus ends the measurement of the cloth to be worn around the body.
In the Matsya [Purāṇa].
White, red, yellow, and black—these [colors] in their proper sequence;
"in proper sequence" means according to the order of the Brāhmaṇas and the other castes.
One should always avoid wearing clothing that has already been worn by another.
Having raised the base of the cloth six finger-breadths along the spine and leaving three finger-breadths at the fringe, one should designate the measurement at the level of the navel;
it must not be less than ten finger-breadths, nor should one cause it to be turned over.
Thus ends the method for putting on the garment.
Now, the specific garments for specific rites.
In the *Kṛṣṇārcanacandrikā* composed by Udayabhānunātha.
In the Svatantra Tantra held within the Śyāmārahasya.
"One seeking liberation wears two red garments; one seeking enjoyment wears two white garments;
for killing, one wears black garments, but for subjugation (vaśya), one always wears red.
Thus, as for the impropriety of wearing red garments mentioned in the previously cited statement from the *Matsyasūkta*:
This refers to rites other than specific acts such as liberation (*mokṣa*), according to the principle of the general and the particular.
For this very reason, the wearing of red garments will be mentioned in the passage to be cited from the *Annadākalpa*:
"In the rite of eradication (*uccāṭana*), tiger skins; in the rite of immobilization (*stambhana*), tree bark. (p. 336)
Then, having dressed himself, the practitioner of mantra should enter the sacrificial ground;
thus it is stated in the *Matsyasūkta*.
One should not shake one's garment in this manner, nor should one ever shake one's hair.
Whatever rite a twice-born man performs with a garment dyed with indigo—
whether it be bathing, giving gifts, recitation, or fire-offerings— all of that shall become fruitless.
Thus is the prohibition against performing ritual actions with garments that are blue or otherwise colored.
In the Kali age, cotton cloth, silk, and linen are recommended. One should always wash it with water to remove impurity; "washed" means cleansed by water.
Thus concludes the praise of garments made of cotton and other materials in the Kali age.
O Goddess of Devas! A twice-born man who wears a garment pierced by a needle, bitten by a rat, or lacking a waistband, takes away the entire fruit of his bath.

Thus ends the prohibition regarding cloth pierced by a needle and the like. If a garment made of silk (kṛmija) or one produced from a storehouse (koṣṭhaja) is seen through another layer of cloth, it should not be offered in rites for the gods or the ancestors; however, that which is produced from a storehouse is praised [when used as the outer layer].
Thus ends the prohibition against garments of different origins.
However, if a man performs his bath wearing a garment made of silk (kṛmija),
all the merit acquired at any time perishes by that very act of bathing.
Thus is the prohibition against bathing with cloth produced by worms.
This very same [prohibition] does not apply to cloth produced from white-grown trees;
that which is produced from white worms is commended for rites dedicated to the gods and the ancestors.
Thus ends the praise of white cloth produced by worms.
Now follows the upper garment.
In the Matsya-sūkta.
With a cord of two hundred [units], you should measure the circumference.
Alternatively, if [the full measure] is unavailable, it should be made with half of that size in all respects.
Since the *yogapada* and other such items are utilized in worship and other rites, their characteristics are described in the *Siddhāntaśekhara* as cited in the *Vīramitrodaya*.
The first type of yoga-mat is made from a tiger skin;
the second is enriched with a deer skin; and the third is woven from threads.
It should be four finger-widths in width and in length, like a sacrificial thread (yajñopavīta).
Four mātras means a measure of four finger-breadths.
The requirement that the wiping of the sacred thread (yajñopavīta) must be performed after bathing is now set forth here.
In the fourth Brāhmaṇa-paṭala of the Gāyatrī-tantra.
Having wiped it with great effort using curd, milk, and ghee—O lovely-limbed one!
in the absence of ghee and the like, one should wipe it with rice-flour;
in the absence of that, with mustard oil, while avoiding sesame oil.

"The best of the twice-born should cleanse [the thread] with the fruits and exudations of the *vilva* tree; then, day by day, the sacred thread becomes composed of pure *sattva*. Thus [are described] the substances for cleansing the *yajñopavīta*. (p. 337) Thus ends the section on the materials for cleansing the sacred thread.
The method for wiping the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) is described in that very same place.
Having drawn [the thread] up from the left shoulder, one should fix it upon the left thumb;
the left thumb and the left shoulder should be joined in this very manner and not otherwise.
Having thus made the thread joined with the left thumb, the twice-born should sweep [the area].
Thus concludes the method for adjusting the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) and wiping [the face];
the fault of wearing the sacred thread around the neck and so forth is also explained in that same [text].
Having placed [the sacred thread] around the neck, on the head, or on the right hand, one becomes a Śūdra;
by reciting the Gāyatrī ten thousand times, one is liberated from that sin. Likewise:
For a Brahmin, a Bhaṭṭa, and likewise for a Vaiśya, ritual cleansing (mārjana) is not always beneficial;
the wearing of the sacrificial thread (yajñasūtra) is distinct for each of these different castes.
Those of the Kṣatriya caste should perform the cleansing with water mixed with red sandalwood.
"A Vaiśya should cleanse with turmeric"—this is the settled conclusion of the scripture.
Now, regarding the *tilaka*, it is found in the tenth chapter of the *Matsyasūkta*.
Then, having sat down facing the eastern direction and being well-composed,
the practitioner of mantra should apply a tilaka while facing either the north or the east,
using either gopīcandana or yellow pigment (rocanā) mixed with saffron.
With clay, sandalwood paste, or with *tulasī* and *bilva* leaves.
In the *Yoginītantra*, in the third part, the ninth chapter.
With the fragrance of *malayaja* sandalwood, or with *gopīcandana*, or with wood produced from the *bilva* tree, or with *tulasī* wood, or with lotus, *tamāla*,
or likewise with *rocanā*.
Or, having applied one of these as an excellent forehead mark (tilaka).
The phrase "arising from *vilva* wood" refers to one who is indifferent [to worldly concerns].

This is because of the statement found in the fifth chapter of the first section of the *Yoginītantra*: "He who, out of devotion, wears that *vilva*-wood sandal paste upon his forehead," and so forth.
The results of clay and other materials are described in the Matsyasūkta.
One attains liberation through clay, while longevity is gained through sandalwood. With saffron, one’s purpose is accomplished, and *rocanā* is said to bring subjugation.
Clay situated in water should be avoided; that found on the bank bestows merit.
Therefore, reciting the mantra "aśvakrānte," a wise man should joyfully take [the clay] produced on the bank of a river frequented by women; he should not rise up to apply the *tilaka*,
nor should he do so with *gopīcandana* from the banks of the Ganges, which is also highly recommended.
Thus end the rules for the application and prohibition of clay for the *tilaka*.
As for the mantra for making the *tilaka*, it is found in the *Matsyasūkta*:
"O Keśava! O Ananta! O Govinda! O Varāha! O Puruṣottama! May this *tilaka* bring me merit, fame, and long life."
May [he/it] be gracious.
The mantra for wearing sandalwood paste is also found in that very same place.

"May sandalwood grant me luster, fortune, fortitude, happiness, and incomparable good fortune; I shall wear it constantly and perpetually. With this mantra, the most excellent knower of mantras should apply it.
The locations for wearing the *tilaka* are described in the *Matsyasūkta*.
One should first apply it on the forehead, then on the head, and then on the heart;
one should also apply it on the throat, the two ears, the two arms,
the two armpits, the navel, the back, and on both sides in pairs.
One should indeed apply sectarian marks (tilakas) and is thereby liberated from all sins:
a mark shaped like a lamp-flame on the forehead, one like a bilva leaf on the two arms,
one shaped like a lotus on the heart, and one representing the moon on the neck.
However, there is a specific distinction regarding the Vaiṣṇava tilaka.
On the forehead, a mace should be made; likewise, a bow and arrow on the head;
Nandaka [the sword] in the middle of the heart; and a conch and a discus on the two arms.
Even if a Brahmin marked with the conch and discus dies in a cremation ground, [he attains liberation].
O Nārada, the destiny that is proclaimed for Prayāga belongs to him as well;
thus it is stated in the second chapter of the Śyāmāpradīpa:
"One should not perform ritual acts while wearing a sectarian mark (tilaka) on the side of the sacrifice."
Therefore, wise men should apply the *tilaka* with either clay or water;
otherwise, it should be known as fruitless, like sowing seeds in barren soil.
A censure regarding the failure to apply the *tilaka* is also found in that same *Matsyasūkta*.

He who looks upon a Caṇḍāla without having applied a sectarian mark (tilaka) on his forehead must bathe again; likewise, after voiding feces or urine, he must bathe. Having observed his reflection in water, in a jar, or in a shadow, he should apply the tilaka.
One should carefully examine it in a mirror, but one should avoid doing so on the new moon day.
Thus is the prohibition against applying *tilaka* on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*). Likewise:
"In the *tilaka*, one should draw the weapon of one's own deity, starting from the right."
The seed-syllable, preceded by the *praṇava* (oṃ), [should be placed] on the arms, the belly, or the forehead;
"on the lap" (*utsaṅge*) means on the chest.
In the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa as cited by Rāghavabhaṭṭa.
He on whose forehead an upright, straight, and gentle *ūrddhvapuṇḍra* is seen—even if he is a *caṇḍāla*, he is a pure soul and is indeed worthy of worship; there is no doubt about this.
In the first quarter of the verse from the *Padmapurāṇa*, the reading is "saumyam" (gentle) rather than "saumyaiḥ" (with clay).

Even a person who is impure, lacking in proper conduct, and who commits evil with the mind, shall always remain pure if he is endowed with the vertical *ūrdhvapuṇḍra*. O Four-faced One! [One should wear it] for my pleasure, for the sake of auspiciousness, or for protection.
My devotee, free from sloth, should always wear the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra);
likewise, at the time of my worship and fire-offerings, being composed in mind both morning and evening,
my devotee should always wear the vertical mark that destroys worldly existence.
This is further detailed in the Padma Purāṇa as cited in the *Bhagavadbhaktivilāsa*,
and in the Skanda Purāṇa as cited therein, in the context of the month of Kārttika.
He on whose forehead a bright vertical mark (*ūrdhvapuṇḍra*) made with clay is seen—even if he be an outcaste (*caṇḍāla*), being pure in soul—he attains the eternal Brahman.
Prosperity resides in the vertical mark; glory resides in the vertical mark.
"Liberation resides in the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra); Hari resides in the vertical mark," as stated in the Uttarakhaṇḍa in the dialogue between Śiva and Pārvatī.
Within the broad and most beautiful center of the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra),
Janārdana, the God of gods, sits together with Lakṣmī;
therefore, he upon whose body this vertical mark is worn [is truly blessed].
The body of that Blessed One is remembered as a stainless temple;
the Brahmin who wears the vertical *ūrddhvapuṇḍra* is honored in all worlds.
Ascending a supreme celestial chariot (*vimāna*), he goes to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
Upon seeing a Brahmin wearing the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra), one is liberated from sins;
likewise, by remembering his name and through devotion, one obtains the fruit of all gifts. Whoever shall feed a Brahmin wearing the vertical mark at a Śrāddha ceremony [attains great merit].

O lady of auspicious countenance, there is no doubt that his ancestors remain satisfied for ten million kalpas; indeed, he who wears the vertical sectarian mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) and performs the ancestral rite (śrāddha) shall attain residence in Vaikuṇṭha for thousands of millions of kalpas.
One should perform sacrifices, charity, the practice of austerity, recitation of mantras, fire oblations, and so forth;
wearing the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra), one shall obtain infinite merit from such acts.
The words of Viṣṇu in the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa:
Wherever a mortal wearing the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) dies,
even if he be an outcaste (śvapāka), he is honored in my world, seated upon a celestial chariot (vimāna). In whosever house a mortal wearing the vertical mark eats food, [that house is purified].
At that time, I shall deliver his twenty generations of kin from hell.
Thus ends the majesty of the vertical *puṇḍra*.
In the Padma Purāṇa, as spoken by Nārada.
Sacrifice, charity, austerity, fire-offerings, Vedic study, and libations to the ancestors—
all these become fruitless if performed without the vertical sectarian mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra).
In the Uttarakhanda.

If one performs any rite whatsoever while devoid of the *ūrddhvapuṇḍra*—whether it be sacrifices, charitable works, or other such acts—all of it shall be fruitless; it cannot be otherwise. Even if one devoid of the *ūrddhvapuṇḍra* should perform the twilight prayers (*sandhyā*) and other such duties, [they too are in vain].
All that should be known as demonic, and one goes to hell;
that body of men which is made without the *ūrdhvapuṇḍra* must not even be looked upon, for it becomes like that of a *caṇḍāla*.
In the Skanda [Purāṇa]:
Indeed, one should not even look at that man on whose forehead an upright *puṇḍra* is seen;
having seen him, one should gaze upon the sun.
Thus is the fault in not making the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra).
In the Uttarakhaṇḍa.
A learned Brahmin who follows the Vedic path should wear the vertical *ūrdhvapuṇḍra* mark with pure clay; he should never wear it horizontally, even in times of distress,
as declared in the *Bhagavadbhaktivilāsa*.
He who applies the Tripuṇḍra over an Ūrdhvapuṇḍra is the lowest of men;
having enjoyed the merit of Viṣṇu’s abode, he certainly goes to hell.
In the Skanda Purāṇa.
One should not apply the horizontal *puṇḍra* mark even when death has arrived;
nor should a man utter the name of any other [deity] except for Nārāyaṇa.
Thus ends the prohibition against applying the *tripuṇḍra* on the *ūrdhvapuṇḍra*.
As cited in the Śāktānandatarangiṇī.

Having applied either the vertical *ūrdhvapuṇḍra* or the triple horizontal *tripuṇḍra*, one should perform the twilight devotions (*saṃdhyā*). That very rule has been established in the *Skanda Purāṇa*.
The wise knowers of Brahman declare that for Vaiṣṇava Brāhmaṇas the ūrdhvapuṇḍra is prescribed, whereas for others the tripuṇḍra should be worn.
In the Padma Purāṇa.
If the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) is not seen upon the forehead of a Brahmin who wears the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra),
one should perform a bath with one's clothes on after merely seeing or touching him.
One should not apply the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) upon the vertical sectarian mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) of Vaiṣṇavas;
for the ritual acts of a mortal who has applied the triple mark do not lead to the pleasure of Hari.
Now follows the procedure for the preparation of the *ūrdhvapuṇḍra*, according to the *Brahmāṇḍapurāṇa*.
O highly fortunate one! He who, with great effort, observes this rule and applies the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) in a place where there is water, attains the supreme goal.
A mark measuring ten finger-breadths in length is said to be the most excellent of the excellent.
The middle [measure] should be nine finger-breadths, and beyond that, eight finger-breadths;
one should have it made according to these various finger-measures, and must not touch it with the fingernails.
The characteristics of the *ūrddhvapuṇḍra* are described in the *Matsyasūkta*.
The vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) is prescribed as extending from the nose to the hairline;
a hole should be made in the middle, for that hole is the abode of Hari.
In the Padma Purāṇa, in the Uttara-khaṇḍa.
Those of great fortune, who are devoted exclusively to the welfare of all beings,
apply the *puṇḍra* in the shape of Hari’s foot with an interval between the lines.
It is declared that a dark-colored mark brings peace, while a red one likewise brings subjugation (*vaśya*).
They say that yellow brings prosperity, while white is auspicious and bestows liberation.
Thus, for specific rites, there are specific types of *tripuṇḍra* according to one's caste:
circular, horizontal, with a gap, short, very long, or thin.

They say that a *puṇḍra* which is brownish, misshapen, having many tips, split at the base, displaced from its position, lusterless, rough, smeared, not fashioned with the fingers, foul-smelling, or placed counter-clockwise (apasavya), is useless and brings misfortune.
Thus ends the [section on] the censured sectarian mark.
The phrase "not fashioned by fingers" is an elliptical expression (upalakṣaṇa) for anything other than the prescribed wooden sticks.
Otherwise, the statement found in the tenth chapter of the Matsyasūkta would be meaningless. That statement, however, is as follows:
It should be made of gold alone, and never of wood or iron,
nor ever of conch-shell, copper, or bell-metal.
One should engrave it with Tulasī wood, Bilva wood, or silver.
The form of the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) is described in the Uttarakhanda.
Resembling the leaf of the *aśvattha* tree, likewise shaped like a bamboo leaf,
and resembling a lotus bud— this triad is known as the "Enchanting" (*mohana*).
Beginning from the base of the nose, one should joyfully draw it as far as the edge of the forehead.
The phrase "up to the forehead" serves to exclude any lesser measurement; otherwise, the mention of ten finger-breadths as the maximum would be meaningless.
As for the measurement of ten finger-breadths, it extends from the third part of the nose up to the *brahmarandhra*.
The word *mṛd* is an indicative mark (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the materials prescribed [for the ritual].
In the reading *mṛdam*, the same meaning is obtained through the transposition of case endings (*vibhaktivyatyaya*) according to the rule *vyatyayo bahulam*.
The three parts of the nose are declared to be the root of the nose;
beginning from there, one should determine the interval up to the middle of the eyebrows.
By the force of the instruction "three parts," the meaning of the ordinal suffix is understood, whereby "the third part" is obtained;
and that part is precisely where the nose, situated at the head, emerges.
Therefore, O lady of auspicious appearance, the upright *puṇḍra* mark, rod-like in shape and very beautiful, should always be made by Brahmins and by women;
it should extend from the nose up to the hair, being a most splendid *ūrdhvapuṇḍra*.
One should know that to be the temple of Hari which is provided with a cavity in its center.
Thus ends the description of the characteristics of the Hari-maṇḍira.
Brahmā is situated on the left side and Sadāśiva on the right side;
one should know Viṣṇu to be in the middle. Therefore, one should not smear [the ointment] in the middle.
In the Hiraṇyakeśīya branch of the Yajurveda.

He who wears the vertical *puṇḍra* with a central gap, having placed the treading of Hari’s feet within it, becomes dear to the Supreme Lord, he becomes meritorious, and he becomes a partaker of liberation.
Regarding the rule for the fingers in the fashioning of the *tilaka*, the *Smṛti* cited in the *Bhagavadbhaktivilāsa* states:
The ring finger is said to grant desires; the middle finger brings long life. The thumb is declared to bestow nourishment, while the index finger is the means for liberation.
Regarding the clay for the *ūrdhvapuṇḍra*, it is stated in the *Padmapurāṇa*:
On a mountain peak, on a riverbank, at the foot of a bilva tree, by a reservoir of water,
on the shore of the ocean, at an anthill, and especially in a field sacred to Hari.
One should take the clay from that place where the water used for Viṣṇu’s ablutions flows constantly, for the purpose of applying the *puṇḍra* marks—
at Śrīraṅga, on the Veṅkaṭādri mountain, at Śrīkūrma, and at the auspicious Dvārakā.

Having devoutly taken earth from Prayāga, Nārasiṃhādri, Vārāha, and the Tulasī grove, and having applied the *puṇḍra* marks upon one's limbs along with the water from Viṣṇu’s feet, one shall attain union (*sāyujya*) with Viṣṇu.

In the phrase "on the mountain peak" (*parvatāgre*) and so forth, since there is no distinction between the meanings of the genitive and locative cases according to the maxim [of grammatical equivalence], the sense of "of the mountain peak" (*parvatāgrasya*) and so forth is obtained.
This is then construed with the subsequent word, "having taken the clay" (*mṛttikām gṛhītvā*).

The locative case is used in the sense of the genitive due to the rule *vyatyayo bahulam* (various substitutions occur frequently). Thus, "on the riverbank" (*nadītīre*) should be understood as "of the bank of the Gaṅgā," because the previously cited statement from the *Matsyasūkta* prohibits the taking of earth from a female river.
Śrīraṅga is a particular sacred field situated in the middle of the Kāverī river, renowned in the southern regions.
Veṅkaṭādri, known by the name Śeṣācala, is renowned in the Telugu country.
Śrīkūrma is a particular sacred field renowned in the Kaliṅga country.
Regarding the greatness of *gopīcandana*, it is stated in the *Matsyasūkta*:
"In this world, the sandalwood created by Viṣṇu for the cowherd girls (*gopīs*) is difficult to obtain;
by applying it as a tilaka, one immediately dispels even the sin of killing a Brahmin."
By supplying the word "of one who stands" (*sthitasya*), there is a single agency [for both actions];
this is also the case in the words of Nārada in the *Padma Purāṇa*.
Whether one is a slayer of a Brahmin, a slayer of a cow, a rationalist skeptic, or a perpetrator of every sin,
one becomes purified at that very moment through contact with Gopīcandana.
Furthermore, whoever gives a piece of Gopīcandana here to a Vaiṣṇava—
By that, one's own family, increasing by one at a time, shall be delivered—a hundred in total.
Thus ends the fruit of the gift of gopīcandana according to the Vaiṣṇava tradition.
The words of Dhruva in the Skanda Purāṇa.
If one is seen with a body marked by the conch and discus, bearing a cluster of blossoms on the head,
and limbs smeared with Gopīcandana— then whence can there be sin?
[For] the clay from Vraja, Tulasī, the conch, and the Śālagrāma stone together with its discus [are the means of purification].
Even in the home of one who possesses these five, whence can there be fear of sin?
"With the wheel" (sacakraka) means "with the Śrīcakra";
as stated in the Kāśīkhaṇḍa.
Where is that fragrance in sandalwood, or where is such a color in gold?
Where indeed is that purity found in any sacred ford as it is in the auspicious Gopīcandana?

In the Garuḍa Purāṇa, the words of Śrī Nārada: "He who, having taken in his hand clay originating from Dvāravatī, constantly applies it as an *ūrdhvapuṇḍra* upon the surface of his forehead, shall always obtain the fruit of his religious rites multiplied ten millionfold."

Even if a rite is devoid of ritual action, devoid of mantra, devoid of faith, or performed at an improper time—should one apply Gopīcandana upon the forehead, one obtains the fruit of that action which is eternally inexhaustible.
O Lord of the twice-born! If a twice-born person always wears the beautiful sectarian mark (puṇḍra) produced from Gopīcandana on his forehead;

O King of Birds! whatever merit is obtained at Kurujāṅgala, at Ravigṛha, or likewise at Prayāga on the full moon day of Māgha—whether by night or by day, at all times—one attains that same merit here;
he dwells in the abode of Viṣṇu like a god.
O Bird! In whatever house a person dwells who wears Gopīcandana on his forehead with devotion, Hari—the slayer of Kaṃsa—always resides in that house, endowed with faith.

Whoever always wears on their forehead the sacred Gopīcandana originating from Kṛṣṇapura—which removes the impurities of the Kali age—accompanied by the mantra, shall not see Yama even if they are enveloped in sin. O Bird! At the time of death, [the merit of] that person on whose arms, forehead, heart, and head the Gopīcandana is present...
If one who has killed a cow or a child should become a slayer of a Brahmin, he goes to the world of the Lord whose abode is the lotus.
The planets do not afflict him, nor do the hosts of Rākṣasas, Yakṣas, Piśācas, Uragas, Bhūtas, or Dānavas— O Bird!—
for one upon whose forehead the Gopīcandana remains by the grace of Hari.
In the Padma Purāṇa.
O Ambarīṣa! For the sake of destroying great sin, look upon those who have daily applied the mark of Gopīcandana on their foreheads.
In the Kāśīkhaṇḍa, Yama says:
"O messengers! Listen: he whose forehead is marked with Gopīcandana should be avoided from afar with great effort, like a blazing piece of fuel."
Thus concludes the majesty of Gopīcandana.
In the Kāśī-khaṇḍa contained within the Bhagavad-bhakti-vilāsa.
Then, upon that [forehead], a beautiful vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) should likewise be made by Vaiṣṇavas using the clay from the root of the glorious Tulasī plant;
thus it is stated in the Skanda Purāṇa, beginning with the description of the clay from the root of the Tulasī.
Those men who, having taken that clay, have applied the *puṇḍra* mark upon their foreheads,
have indeed set out on the journey toward liberation.
O Nārada! Sin does not touch the body of one on whose forehead the sectarian mark made with Tulasī clay is seen, even while it is being committed.
In the Garuḍa Purāṇa.
For those people who apply the sectarian mark (puṇḍra) with Tulasī clay day after day,
the sins committed over a year depart simply by the sight of them.
Regarding the greatness of the clay from the root of the *tulasī* plant, the *Garuḍa Purāṇa* states:
"Above that [the forehead], one should likewise wear the remains of the Lord's garland and unguents;
for thus is the threefold *tilaka* prescribed."
By the previously mentioned statement, "then upon that," it means upon the *tilaka* made of *gopīcandana*;
and "there, upon that" means upon the *tilaka* made from the clay at the root of the *tulasī*.
Therefore, having first applied a tilaka of Gopīcandana, one should apply a tilaka of clay from the root of a Tulasī plant upon it.
And upon that, a tilaka should be made with the remains of Viṣṇu’s garland and ointment; thus, the tilaka is of three kinds.
Now follows the procedure for the twelve tilakas.
In the Brahmapurāṇa.
Then, a Vaiṣṇava should duly apply twelve vertical marks (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) upon the twelve limbs with the twelve names beginning with Keśava.
In the Uttarakhaṇḍa of the Padma Purāṇa.
One should meditate on Keśava at the forehead, Nārāyaṇa at the abdomen,
Mādhava on the chest, Govinda in the hollow of the throat,
Viṣṇu on the right side of the belly, and Madhusūdana on the arm.
One should place Trivikrama on the region of the shoulders, Vāmana on the left side,
Śrīdhara on the left arm, Hṛṣīkeśa on the neck,
Padmanābha on the back, and Dāmodara on the hips.
The water used for washing that [vessel] should be poured upon the head while reciting "Vāsudeva," according to the *Yoginītantra*.
Having covered the excellent *tilaka* with one or another of these—
namely, *catuḥsama*, *trisama*, or *dvisama*, O Goddess of the Gods!—
and having then anointed the body, one should avoid [the practice] during the *ayana*.
Regarding the previously mentioned "fourfold mixture" and so forth— namely, sandalwood, gopīcandana, vilva, tulasī wood, padmaka, kṛtamāla, and gorocanā—
one should not apply these fragrant substances during a cold bath at night;
however, one may apply them specifically on the forehead, but never on the head.
In the Matsya-sūkta.

One should not apply a *tilaka* at night, nor after eating, nor indeed [at other improper times]. Furthermore, upon the death of a great preceptor (*mahāguru*), a man should remove his *tilaka*. (From the *Bahvṛca-pariśiṣṭa*).
Therein, first, one should cleanse all the limbs with the unguent from the Blessed One’s lotus feet and with the grace of the flower-offerings (nirmālya).
In the Brahmapurāṇa:
One should always wear sandalwood paste adhering to a *śālagrāma* stone on all parts of the body for the sake of attaining great purity, O Lotus-seated One.
Thus ends the section on the *ūrdhvapuṇḍra*.
Now begins the procedure for wearing the *tripuṇḍra*.
As cited by Rāghavabhaṭṭa.
A wise person should bring purified ash produced from the *agnihotra* sacrifice,
or else, having brought cow dung that has not touched the ground, according to the truth.
By means of the truth and the syllable Om.
Having purified [the vessel] with the left hand, one should burn away [impurities] with the Aghora mantra.

Having extracted it with the Tatpuruṣa mantra, one should purify it with the Īśāna mantra. Thus consecrated, one should rub the ashes while reciting the mantra beginning with "agniriti," and touching the limbs, take them up again with the mantra.
Therefore, one should recite the mantra "Oṃ Brahmaṇe" eleven times with the Yajus formula;
then, using the Aghora and Īśāna mantras preceded by the Praṇava,
in the dative case and ending with the word "hṛdayāya," and beginning with the five-syllable [mantra], one should apply them to the forehead, shoulders, stomach, and heart.
One should apply the Tripuṇḍra on the head with the five-syllabled mantra;
by wearing the Tripuṇḍra, the practitioner becomes like another Śiva in person.
In the Vāyavīya-saṃhitā, another method for taking up the sacred ash is also stated.
For example:
"The ash of the Śiva-fire should be collected, or that produced from the Agnihotra fire,
or even that produced from the nuptial fire— cooked, pure, and fragrant."
The pure dung of a tawny cow, caught while falling from the sky—
neither moist nor hard, neither foul-smelling nor stale; "stale" (uṣita) meaning that which has been left overnight.

If [the offering] has fallen, one should discard what is above and below and take [what remains]; having formed it into a ball, one should cast it into the Śiva-fire while reciting the root mantra. One should discard what is undercooked or overcooked, and [take] the white ash.
For the *Kālāgnirudropaniṣad* has demonstrated that even the cow-dung of a bull is of this same nature, stating: "Because, when taken up, it becomes pure, just as ashes are produced."
"With the left" means:

Oṃ, obeisance to Vāmadeva; obeisance to Jyeṣṭha; obeisance to Rudra; obeisance to Kāla; obeisance to Kalavikaraṇa; obeisance to Balavikaraṇa; obeisance to Balapramathana; obeisance to Sarvabhūtadamana; obeisance to Manonmana.
The mantra beginning with "aghoreṇa" is: *Oṃ aghorebhyo 'tha ghorebhyo ghoraghoratarebhyaḥ | sarvataḥ śarvaśarvebhyo namaste rudrarūpebhyaḥ* ||
The mantra beginning with "tatpuruṣeṇa" is: Oṃ tatpuruṣāya vidmahe mahādevāya dhīmahi tanno rudraḥ pracodayāt.
The mantra for Īśāna is as follows:
(p. 346) Oṃ, Īśāna, lord of all sciences, sovereign of all beings, overlord of Brahman, overlord of the sacred word—may Śiva, the Sadāśiva, be mine.
As for the mantra beginning with "Agni":
"Agni is ashes, Vāyu is ashes, water is ashes, earth is ashes, space is ashes;
all this is ashes. O mind, these are the six eyes. Therefore, this is the Pāśupata vow."
One should touch one's limbs with ashes.
Therefore, this is that Brahman, the Pāśupata, for the sake of liberation from the bonds of the individual soul (paśu).
It is performed with the Yajus, that is, with the Yajur-mantra consisting of five syllables, namely the mantra "Namaḥ Śivāya."
The scriptural citation held in the commentary on the third section of the *Kulamūlāvatārakalpasūtra*.
Pure substance is the Tripuṇḍra made of sacred ash belonging to Agni, consisting of three lines and having the form of a half-moon.
Now, according to the measurement of Sanatkumāra, [the forehead] is divided threefold from the forehead down to the eyes, and subsequently from the middle of the eyebrows.
Of these, the first line here is the Āhavanīya fire, the Sun, and the Ṛgveda;
it is the morning libation (prātaḥsavana) and Maheśvara.
The second line here is the *āvasathya* fire, the syllable *ukāra*, the *Yajurveda*, and Sadāśiva;
the third line here is the *gārhapatya* fire, the power of knowledge of the Supreme Self (*paramātma-jñāna-śakti*), consisting of the letters beginning with *makāra*.
Now begins the Kālāgnirudra Upaniṣad.
The fire is Saṃvartta, the seer is Virāṭ, the deity is Rudra of universal form, the metre is Anuṣṭubh; the application is for the sake of pleasing Śrī Viśvarūpa.
Now, Sanatkumāra questioned the Blessed Lord Kālāgnirudra: "Please teach me, O Lord, the procedure for the triple mark (tripuṇḍra)."
"What is its true nature? What is the substance? What is the location? How many are the measures? What are the lines? What are the mantras?
What is the deity? Who is the agent? And what is the fruit? To him, the Blessed Lord Kālāgnirudra replied:
"It has been truly stated: that which is the substance is the ash produced by fire, [consecrated] with the five Brahma-mantras beginning with Sadyojāta and the Rudra-mantras."

Having taken up the ashes with the mantra "Agni," and having consecrated them with this [mantra], he should stir them together with "Mā nas toke. Then, with the three *tryāyuṣa* mantras beginning with "Tryāyuṣam," he should draw three horizontal lines across his head, forehead, shoulders, throat, heart, and both arms using the three *tryambaka* mantras.
This indeed is that *śāmbhava* [initiation] which has been declared by the knowers of the Vedas in all the Vedas.
Practicing that for the sake of liberation, one should not [seek] rebirth.
One should draw three horizontal lines: from the forehead to the eyes, from the eyebrows to the middle of the face, and from one ear to the other.

That which is the first line is the Gārhapatya fire, the letter *A*, the Bhūr-loka, the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*), and the Ṛgveda; it is the first pressing (*prathama-savana*) and Maheśvara. That which is the second line... [p. 347] ...is that.
The Dakṣiṇāgni fire is the syllable *ukāra*;
truth is the intermediate space, the inner self, the power of will (*icchā-śakti*), and the Yajurveda;
and midday is the second libation (*dvitīya-savana*) and the deity Sadāśiva.

That which is the third line is the Āhavanīya fire, the letter *M*, darkness, heaven, the Supreme Self, the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*), the Sāmaveda, the third pressing (*tṛtīyasavana*), and Lord Śiva. The wise man— whether a student, a householder, a forest-dweller, or an ascetic— who applies the triple mark (*tripuṇḍra*) with ashes [attains liberation].
He becomes purified from all major and minor sins; he becomes as one who has studied all the Vedas;

he becomes as one who has bathed in all sacred fords; he becomes a constant reciter of all mantras. Having enjoyed all worldly pleasures, upon casting off the body, he attains union with Śiva and does not return again.
"He is indeed Viṣṇu, he is Śiva, and he is Brahmā, the Lord of Creatures;
he is liberated from all sins and is not subject to rebirth.
Thus spoke the Blessed Kālāgnirudra once again.
"Agni is ash; water is ash; wind is ash; the earth is ash; the entire universe is ash.
That which is sacred to Agni is the ash of the sacrificial cow-dung. With that, one should apply the triple mark (tripuṇḍra).
With that, the venerable Lord Bhava said: 'Whatever sacrificial rite there may be, it is this.'"
Thus ends the Kālāgnirudra Upaniṣad.
In the Vāyavīya Saṃhitā, the wearing of the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) is prescribed for thirteen locations on the body.
As cited by Rāghavabhaṭṭa:
Brahmā is to be known in the forehead; Havyavāhana (Agni) is in the heart;
Pūṣan is in the navel, the shoulder, and the throat; Rudra is in the right arm;
Āditya is in the middle of the arm; and Śaśin (the Moon) is at the wrist.
Vāmadeva is on the left arm, Prabhañjana is in the middle of the arm,
Vasava is at the wrist, and Hara is said to be in the region of the back.
Śambhu is proclaimed to be on the hump [of the spine], and the Supreme Self (Paramātman) is remembered as Śiva.
Therefore, there is an option based on one's preference regarding the locations mentioned in the Kālāgnirudra Upaniṣad and the Vāyavīya Saṃhitā.
In the second chapter of the *Puraścaraṇalaharītantra*.
The ash produced from burnt cow dung is said to be of the nature of Agni;
it should be purified with the six-syllable mantras, excluding the Vedic mantras,
[by applying it] to the region of the head, the forehead, the shoulder, and the brow.
Then, one should apply a *tilaka* with the thumb upon the middle and ring fingers. (p.
348) A *tilaka* consists of three lines; for these lines, there are nine deities:
Earth, Fire, the Self (*ātman*), the Power of Action (*kriyāśakti*), and Maheśvara.
The deities of the first line have been proclaimed by you with devotion;
O fortunate one, you should now receive those who are the deities of the second line,
and Paramātman, the god Śiva, is the deity of the third line.
Having constantly paid homage to these [deities], if one should wear the triple mark (tripuṇḍra),
having performed this vow of Maheśvara, one shall become a lord of perfection (siddhīśvara)—
whether as a student, a householder, a forest-dweller, or even an ascetic.

O Subhageśvarī! One is liberated from the multitude of great sins (mahāpātaka) and from all other transgressions; likewise, one is freed from the sins of killing a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, a Śūdra, or a woman, as well as from the killings of a hero and a Brāhmaṇa.
Even if one performs an act without mantras, having attained great eminence through it,
one who wears the Tripuṇḍra and the Tilaka on the forehead is liberated from all sins—
including the theft of another's property and the violation of another's wife.
Censuring others, seizing another's field, causing pain to others,
speaking untruths, backbiting, harshness, selling [the image of] the gods,
giving false testimony, abandoning one's vows, gambling, and serving the base;
The acceptance of gifts from low-born persons for cows, land, gold, buffaloes, sesame, blankets, clothing, food, grain, water, and the like;
as well as [acceptance from] slave-girls, prostitutes, women of the plowmen, Śūdra women, and actresses.
Sexual union with women in their menses, with maidens, or with widows;
the sale of meat, hides, fat, and salt—
such are the various and innumerable sins of this kind.
They perish instantly by the wearing of the *tripuṇḍra*. One is not purified by penances for the theft of Śiva’s property, for reviling Him anywhere, or for reviling His devotees.

Families are swiftly destroyed by the misappropriation of divine property, by the seizure of a Brahmin’s wealth, and by showing contempt toward Brahmins. He upon whose body Rudrākṣas are worn and who bears the Tripuṇḍra on his forehead [is purified].

Even if he were a Cāṇḍāla, he would be the most excellent among all castes; for wherever the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) is on his forehead, he is as if bathed in all the sacred sites (tīrthas) and rivers such as the Gaṅgā that exist in this world.
Seven crores of great mantras, as well as the secondary mantras (upamantras),
the crore of mantras of Śrī Viṣṇu, and the crore of mantras of Śiva—
all these are recited by him who wears the triple mark (tripuṇḍra).
He who wears the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) shall uplift a thousand ancestors and a thousand future descendants born of his own lineage;
having attained the divine tripuṇḍra, he becomes endowed with the eightfold sovereign powers (aṣṭaiśvarya).
Having ascended a celestial chariot and attended by hundreds of divine women,
he proceeds in due order through the worlds of the Vidyādharas, Siddhas, and the highly effulgent Gandharvas,
as well as the worlds of Indra and the other world-protectors.
Having enjoyed vast pleasures in the cities of the ancestors,
and having attained the station of Brahmā, he rejoices there for the duration of ten thousand kalpas;
and in the world of Viṣṇu, he delights until the end of a hundred lifespans of Brahmā.
Having reached the world of Śiva from there, he rejoices for imperishable time;
he attains union with Śiva and is not born again.
Thus ends the fruit of wearing the triple mark (tripuṇḍra).
In the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa, as cited in the Śāktānandataraṅgiṇī.
O Goddess! Any Vedic rite whatsoever that one performs without the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) shall be fruitless, even if it were performed by Brahmā himself.
In the Śyāmāpradīpa, however, it is recorded as being from the Skanda Purāṇa.
In the Kūrma Purāṇa.
Whether one is a Vaiṣṇava, a Śaiva, a Śākta, or even a Saura,
whoever performs worship without the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) goes to a downward state.
In the Śivadharmottara: "One should apply the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) on the forehead with white ashes;
being liberated from all sins, one is glorified in the world of Śiva."
The mention of "ashes" is an illustration; the *tripuṇḍra* may also be made with other substances.
"Everyone should always apply the *tripuṇḍra* with the ashes of a sacrifice;
in their absence, with sandalwood paste, or with clay, or even with water," according to this statement from the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa*.
Whatever action one performs without the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) of ash,
all of it becomes utterly fruitless, like union with a barren woman.
That twice-born man of beastly intellect who applies the triple mark with gaps [is likewise lost].
"In matters of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa, a flaw arises for him.

This is the censure of wearing the *tripuṇḍra* with flaws. Now, it may be argued that based on the collection of statements cited, the application of the *tripuṇḍra* to the *ūrdhvapuṇḍra* is prohibited.

If it is argued that the aforementioned statement from the *Kūrmapurāṇa* indicates that there is scriptural evidence of fault for Vaiṣṇavas and others performing worship without the *tripuṇḍra*, and thus— as in the case of the god Lambodara kissing his beloved’s face at the time of dalliance— one thing intended to be joined causes another to fall away, this is not so.
Understand that the prohibition against making a hole in the *ūrdhvapuṇḍra* and the *tripuṇḍra* refers to those other than the Vedic rite;

for in all cases, a prohibition pertains to what is distinct from the Vedic injunction, just as the censure of the *viśikha* (the shaven-headed) refers to those who have not undergone the penance and so forth.

For this very reason, Rāghavabhaṭṭa maintains that Śaivas must apply the *tripuṇḍra* with ashes immediately after applying the *ūrdhvapuṇḍra*, because for the twice-born, the *ūrdhvapuṇḍra* is mandatory.
Now, the Śakti-tilaka.
In the Gautamīya as cited in the Śāktānandataraṅgiṇī.
O beloved! One should draw the weapon-mantra of the Goddess on the forehead with red sandalwood paste or saffron;
then, one should place the seed-syllable of Tārā in the heart, situated within the Śakti—this is known as the Śakti-tilaka.

In accordance with the previously stated principle that "the weapon [mantra] of one's own deity [is used] for the *tilaka*," the "weapon of the Goddess" refers to the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of one's chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*).
In the fifth chapter of the *Annadākalpa*.
Having washed his hands and feet, and then having put on a pair of red garments,
he should apply a tilaka mark resembling a half-moon with a central dot,
using either well-red sandalwood paste or saffron.
Having meditated upon the dust of the lotus-feet of the Goddess— marked with a dot of vermilion and adorned with three lines— the practitioner, by means of the root mantra,
becomes entitled to the worship of Durgā, just like the Moon-crested Lord Śiva himself.
This is also maintained in the *Mālinīvijaya* [Tantra], which is the moonlight of the worship of Kṛṣṇa.

On the forehead, one should contemplate three crescent lines resembling the moon, possessing the playful luster of lightning; below that, in the space between them, a dot (bindu) resembling reddish rays;
in the center of the heart, a lotus-form as white as the moon; in the pair of arms, the luster of vīraṇa grass; and in other locations, [the appropriate forms].
He who applies the drops and the forehead mark is indeed the very form of the Lord of the Universe.
The grammatical construction is: "one forms a red-colored dot in the middle, within the space between the two eyebrows.
This means that in the center of the heart, it has the form of a white lotus.
"In the pair of arms" means in both arms.
"Resembling vīraṇa grass" means having the appearance of vīraṇa leaves.
Regarding the phrase "in other places previously mentioned," the use of the word *etad* (this) denotes the meaning of the word *tad* (that).
And it has been stated in the commentary on the *Sarvanāman-sūtra*: "The pronouns *tyad* and *tad*, when referring to a single object, denote the object already specified."

The other three [types of *pratyakṣa*] are with gesture (*sābhinaya*). Kulacandra states that "with gesture" refers to the movement of the hands and so forth. Otherwise, if the *vimarga* were elided, there would be a metrical fault (*cchandobhaṅga*) due to the phrase "satītyanena. That word, which expresses what has been introduced, does not require a correlative *yad*-word.
And it is said in the *Kāvyaprakāśa*:

In this way, even the word *tad* (that), when referring to an object that has been introduced, is well-established, or has been previously experienced, does not require the employment of the word *yad* (which). However,
those who follow the straightforward path (*ṛjavaḥ*) read "so hi" (for that), because in this system (*tantra*) there is a prohibition against considering corrupt words (*apaśabda*).
p. 351) If the twilight rites (*sandhyā*) and so forth are performed in water, then one should go to the sacrificial pavilion (*yāgamaṇḍapa*), sit down, and apply the sectarian mark (*tilaka*).
Because it is stated thus in the *Annadākalpa*.
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Description of the Branches Beginning with Bathing and Ending with the Tilaka," in the third section (Arthakāṇḍa) of the Śrī Prāṇatoṣiṇī.
Now, the twilight [ritual].
After the Vedic Sandhyā, the Tantric Sandhyā should be performed.
And so it is stated in the first chapter of the *Puraścaraṇarasollāsa*:
"O lady of tremulous glances! Having performed the morning bath and having worshipped the most difficult-to-attain Sandhyā, one should thereafter mutter the Gāyatrī."
Then, having performed the Tantric twilight prayers (sandhyā) and likewise the Tantric Gāyatrī,
and having offered the water libation (arghya) to the Sun, one should enter the house for the purpose of worship.
Also in the first chapter of the Vṛhannīlatantra:
Having first performed the Vedic *sandhyā* as approved by the Āgamas,
and having then performed the *sandhyā*, the hero shall deliver ten million members of his lineage.
Likewise:
This is the salutation performed during the three junctions of day and night.
In the Gandharva Tantra, in the sixth chapter.
I shall now relate another [practice] here that destroys all sins:
having sat in a pure place, one should perform the ritual rinsing (ācamana) three times with the three principles (tritattva);
having performed three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma), one should [perform it] threefold according to the three seed-syllables (bīja).
Taking water in the left hand, the practitioner should perform a sevenfold sprinkling upon his head with the dripping drops of water while recollecting the mantra; then,
taking the remaining water in the right hand, the practitioner [should proceed].
Then, having drawn water through the nostrils, one should perform the *aghamarṣaṇa* rite;
by drawing [the water] into the interior of the body through the *iḍā* [left nostril], the accumulated masses of sin are washed away,
and that water, now black in color, is expelled through the *piṅgalā* [right nostril].
The practitioner of the mantra, having visualized that [sin] in the form of a mass of evil in his right hand,
should cast it onto a vajra-stone in front of him while reciting the Astra-mantra.
Having thus performed the *aghamarṣaṇa*, he should likewise perform the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*) once more.
Then, the supreme practitioner should consecrate [the disciple] on the head according to the ritual:
"Oṃ! We purify the divine waters, the essence, the nectar, the pure Brahman.
He should offer three handfuls of water upon the ground to Mārtaṇḍabhairava.
Then, with arms raised, the practitioner should take refuge in Mārttaṇḍa [the Sun], reciting:
"Oṃ, the banners bear up the god Jātavedas, Sūrya, so that all may behold him.
O Goddess of the gods! At the conclusion of the Mārttaṇḍa mantra, one should utter the word "Bhairava."
However, such a *sandhyā* does not exist in its current form in the Gauḍa country.
As for the Gauḍa tradition, it is found in the third chapter of the *Toḍalatantra*.
One should perform the ritual sipping (ācamana) with the principles of the Self, Knowledge, and Śiva, as well as with water.
The mantras beginning with the Praṇava (Oṃ) and accompanied by the wife of Agni (Svāhā) are to be understood [in this context].
O Goddess! One should perform the invocation of the sacred ford (tīrthāvāhana) with the mantra beginning with "Gaṅge ca" and so forth.
The wise practitioner, having thrice sprinkled the ground with water while reciting the root mantra,
should perform his own ablution (abhiṣeka) over himself seven times with that same water.
Then, O Goddess of the Gods, he should perform the ritual placement of the limbs (aṅganyāsa) upon his left hand.

One should perform the recitation three times of the seed-syllable of space (haṃ), the seed-syllable of wind (yaṃ), the syllable of Varuṇa (vaṃ), the seed-syllable of earth (laṃ), and the seed-syllable of fire (raṃ) joined with the nasal drop (bindu).
O Goddess! by means of this mantra, that water is consecrated.

Having recited the root mantra seven times with the *tattvamudrā*, by the mere act of self-consecration (*ātmābhiṣeka*), one is liberated from all sins. O Maheśānī! One should then take the remaining water into the right hand.
One should fill [the body] with water through the *iḍā* and wash that which resides within the body;
then, O Goddess, one should expel that water through the *piṅgalā*. One should contemplate that water as being black in color and the very form of sin.
In front, one should cast [the stone] upon a vajra-stone with the syllable *phaṭ*;
having washed the hands and performed the ritual sipping (*ācamana*), one should offer the *arghya* oblation to the Sun.
Thereafter, one should offer the *arghya* to the deity and then recite the Gāyatrī, the supreme syllable.

Then the wise one should recite [the mantra] three times and sprinkle water; thereafter, O Supreme Goddess, having performed the ritual placement on the limbs (aṅganyāsa) and sipped water (ācamana), he should mutter the Great Mantra, the Gāyatrī of supreme syllables.

O Great Goddess! having meditated upon one's chosen deity within the solar orb and performed breath control (prāṇāyāma) and other preliminaries, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times.
In the *Lakṣmīkulārṇava*, as cited in the third section (*kāṇḍa*) of the commentary on the *Kalpasūtra*.
He who is devoid of the twilight ritual (sandhyā) shall not obtain the fruit of initiation;
therefore, the twilight ritual preceded by the mantra-sandhyā must be performed, as it is stated in the Navaratneśvara.
The Vedic and Tantric twilight devotions (sandhyā) are performed according to their sequential application.
Also in the fifth chapter of the Mahānirvāṇatantra:

The practitioner of mantras should perform the twilight rite; listen, O Śivā, as it is described according to the Tantra. Having sipped water (ācamana) as before, one should invoke the sacred waters (tīrthas) into the water with the mantra beginning with "O Gaṅgā," and by means of the gesture known as the goad (aṅkuśa-mudrā).

Having invoked the sacred water (tīrtha) into the water, one should recite the root mantra twelve times. Then, using the combination of the thumb and the ring finger while preceded by the utterance of the root mantra, one should sprinkle three drops of that water upon the ground.
Having sprinkled one's own head seven times with that water,
one should then take it in the left hand and cover it with the right hand;
[this consists of] the five seed-syllables of Īśāna, Vāyu, Varuṇa, Vahni, and Indra.
Having consecrated the water with mantras, the knower of the Vedas should bring it into his right hand;
having visualized it as consisting of radiant energy and meditated upon it, the practitioner,
drawing it in through the *iḍā*, should expel the impurities within the body through that which is called *piṅgalā*.

Having drawn [the earth] out and reciting the Vajra-mantra, the practitioner should strike it three times upon a diamond-stone (vajraśilā) placed in front; thereafter, he should wash his hands. Having performed the ritual rinsing (ācamana) with the prescribed mantra, he should offer water for honor (arghya) to the Sun.
Having uttered "Tāra-māyā-haṃsa" (Om Hrim Hamsa), followed by "Ghṛṇi-sūrya," and then saying, "This arghya is for you, Svāhā," one should offer it; thereafter,
one should meditate upon the Great Goddess Gāyatrī, the Supreme Deity.
In the morning, at midday, and in the evening, she has three forms according to the distinction of the qualities (guṇas).
In the morning, she is the Fire-goddess, red in color, with two arms, and a maiden;
she holds a water-pot filled with sacred water and a rosary of beads.
Wearing a black antelope skin as her garment, mounted upon a swan, and possessing a pure smile. || 1 ||
O Maheśvarī! [I meditate upon] Vaiṣṇavī, who is dark-complexioned, four-armed, holding a conch,
a discus, a mace, and a lotus, seated upon Garuḍa, with full and lofty breasts,
and adorned with a forest garland.
One should constantly meditate upon the young woman in the center of the orb of the sun.
In the evening, the ascetic should meditate upon the boon-granting Goddess Gāyatrī—
