white-complexioned, clad in white garments, seated upon the bull, three-eyed,
and holding a boon-granting gesture, a noose, a trident, and a human skull.
She was supporting with her lotus-like hands an elderly woman whose youth had faded away.

Having meditated thus, one should offer three handfuls of water to Mahādevī and then recite the Gāyatrī ten or even a hundred times. By reciting this at the three junctions of the day, one shall obtain the fruit of the Sandhyā rite.
Then, O Goddess, one should offer libations to the gods, sages, ancestors, and deities.
The mantra consists of the *praṇava*, the word "second," followed by "I offer libations" (*tarpayāmi*) and the word "obeisance" (*namaḥ*).
However, if one has the capacity, one should say *praṇava*, *māyā*, and "obeisance" in place of the word "second," ending with the *dviṭha* (the syllable *phaṭ*).
Then, having offered the *arghya* to the Great Goddess, the wise practitioner should mutter the root mantra.
Having performed the recitation according to his capacity, he should offer it into the left hand of the Goddess.
Having prostrated and taken water for the purpose of worshipping the Goddess, the practitioner—
Having bathed at a sacred ford and recited the hymn while intent on meditation upon the deity,
he should return to the sacrificial pavilion and purify his hands and feet.
In the first chapter of the Vṛhannīlatantra.

"O Dear One! One should perform the evening *sandhyā* even on the twelfth lunar day (*dvādaśī*) and other such occasions; for by not performing it, one goes to hell, since this is a daily scriptural duty. This statement is made without understanding the following citation from the *Tantrasāra*: "The Vedic and Tantric *sandhyās* [should be performed] according to their respective sequential order."
Due to the natural sequence of the words, where the Vedic *saṃdhyā* is not present, there the Tantric *saṃdhyā* should also not be performed.

Therefore, as for the claim made by some that the Tantric *saṃdhyā* should not be performed on the twelfth lunar day (*dvādaśī*) and so forth, or during periods of ritual impurity (*aśauca*), that is incorrect.
Because impurity pertains to the domain of Vedic ritual.
And so it is stated in the second chapter of the Viśvasāra Tantra:
"In the event of the death of a great guru or similar calamities, there is no optionality regarding worship;
whether out of delusion or by fate, one must never fail to worship.
Otherwise, there will be the destruction of everything for that person—so it has been declared by the Sadāśivas."
"One should worship" is an elliptical expression for the daily tantric ritual (*tantrika-nityakarman*),
as stated in the ninth chapter of the *Kāmadatantre*.

Those lay devotees who are devoted to Śrī Kālī are indeed always pure; neither the impurity arising from birth or death, nor any other form of impurity, ever obstructs them anywhere, O devotee of Kālikā.

O Goddess of the Gods, how can there be impurity for one who is ever pure like the Gaṅgā? With reference to Kālī, worship, japa, and homa are not to be abandoned during times of impurity; therefore, everything must indeed always be performed by a Śākta.

O Maheśvarī! One should never abandon acts such as giving gifts directed toward Kālī during a period of impurity; for the Śākta alone is always supremely pure. Here, because the term "Śākta" is used in a general sense, the phrase "toward Kālī" in the preceding statement is an illustration (upalakṣaṇa) for all [deities] who possess Śakti.
Now, the twilight [ritual] for yogins, in the third section of the *Kalpasūtra-ṭīkā*.
The Kuṇḍalinī-śakti, who is the form of the Guru, who dwells within the fiber of the lotus-stalk, who is self-luminous,
and who is to be meditated upon within the practice through the state of the essential identity (samarasa) of Kula and Akula;
likewise, at the time of midday, she whose limbs are youthful and exceedingly radiant, having the form of Kāmarāja.
One should meditate [on her] from the root-center up to the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), and from the aperture of Brahmā down to the root-center.
Likewise, at the time of evening, one should contemplate her as white in color, having the nature of the seed-syllable of Śakti, resembling a lotus fiber, by means of the yoga of Kula and Akula.

At midnight, one should meditate on her in the form of the *parāpara-kuṇḍalinī*, the color of a ruby (*padmarāga*), as the form of the *vāgbhava* seed-syllable from the base (*mūlādhāra*) up to the heart; as the form of the *kāma* seed-syllable from the heart up to the space between the eyebrows;
and as the form of the *śakti* seed-syllable from the space between the eyebrows up to the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*).
This has been stated in the Udayākarapaddhati:
The first [power] has the luster of a lotus fiber; the middle one is yellow, while the red one is the internal power (*śakti*). The twilight (*sandhyā*) possesses both forms.
As for the libation (*tarpaṇa*), [one offers it] from the *mūlādhāra* to her who embodies the moon, sun, and fire.
Having raised Kuṇḍalinī and pierced the supreme point (parabindu), one should satisfy one’s chosen deity with the nectar arising therefrom.
This has been stated in the *Navacakreśvara*:
From the union of the moon, sun, and fire, that supreme nectar which flows forth—
by means of that divine nectar, one should satisfy the supreme Sundarī.
Now, the worship of the Sun.

Having raised the Kulakuṇḍalinī from the Mūlādhāra and led her to the solar orb of the heart, one should sprinkle [the deity] with a stream of nectar situated within its pericarp while recollecting the root mantra; this is the internal sacrifice (antaryāga) of the yogins.
Now, the twilight ritual of the Kaulas is described in the sixth chapter of the Gandharva Tantra.
One who is devoted to meditation should always properly meditate upon the Self.
O Beloved! This mental *sandhyā* is supreme because of its distinction from [external] deities.
At whatever time the union of Śiva and Śakti occurs, [that is this *sandhyā*].
That twilight is perceived by those established in samādhi who are devoted to the Kula,
as stated in the first chapter of the Bhūtaśuddhi-tantra.
O Maheśānī! O Pārvatī! Listen attentively to the inner twilight (antaḥ-sandhyā).
At whatever time the union of Śiva and Śakti occurs, that is the twilight perceived by the Kulins established in samādhi.
The ritual procedures for the Vedic *sandhyā* and other rites, however, should be sought in works such as the *Brāhmaṇasarvasva*.
Only the specific procedure for *mārjana* (sprinkling) is given in the third chapter of the *Nirvaṇatantra* as follows:
"Listen attentively to the method for the water used in the *mārjana* mantra."

O Goddess, Queen of the Gods! In the Yajurveda, this [is taught] as being on the earth, on the head, and in space; in space, on the head of the earth; and likewise on the head, on the earth, and in space. O Daughter of the Mountain! Listen now to how it is presented in the Sāmaveda, the Atharvaveda, and the Ṛgveda.

One should perform the ritual sprinkling with water while reciting the mantra "Āpo hi ṣṭhā" according to the sequence of its eight syllables, [touching] the empty head and the sky, likewise the empty ground and the head, and likewise the empty ground and the crown of the head.
The ritual sprinkling (*mārjana*) performed according to that very sequence destroys all sins;

however, O lady of beautiful limbs, if it is performed out of order, one incurs the sin of killing a Brahmin at every step. One should place three *varatha* [grains] upon the head; those who do so are said to be liberated in the sky.
They know that one should not offer [the oblation] on the ground with the three [mantras]; thus they understand the method of sweeping.
For this very reason, out of affection for you, I have revealed the entire sequence.
O Goddess! Having recited the hymn of praise and the armor-mantra (kavaca), the wise man should prostrate.
Now, the Gāyatrī.
In the *Nirvāṇatantra*, in the third chapter on the Brāhmaṇas.
O lady of beautiful limbs, listen to the Gāyatrī, which is worshipped by the four Vedas,
renowned as the Mother of the Vedas, and the bestower of the fruits of the three goals of life;
she is to be known as Gāyatrī beginning with the words "Having extracted the Hālāhala poison," and so forth.
Having recited this, O Maheśānī, one becomes liberated; it is not otherwise.
He who recites "ya" in place of the final two letters, "ya" and "ka," is known as a Caṇḍāla and incurs the sin of Brahmin-slaughter day after day.

Therefore, O Great Goddess! out of affection for you, this supreme Sāvitrī-vidyā, which is very difficult to obtain in the three worlds, has been revealed. Merely by its acquisition, one becomes Brahmā; of this there is no doubt.
As for that which is stated in the first Brāhmaṇa-paṭala of the Gāyatrī-tantra:
The conjunction of three *praṇavas* is proclaimed for Brāhmaṇas;
O Supreme Goddess! the conjunction of two *praṇavas* is recommended at the beginning of a sacred field (*kṣetra*) and so forth.
Also in the second Brāhmaṇa-paṭala:
"Whoever recites the Gāyatrī conjoined with the three *praṇavas* obtains the fruit of the Gāyatrī; otherwise, it is like weeping in the wilderness.
This is the exposition on the Gāyatrī conjoined with the three *praṇavas*.
This is with the intention that [the world] is encapsulated by that in this powerful Kali age; and thus it is stated in that very same [text]:
Whether it be a primary science (vidyā) or a secondary science (upavidyā), by reciting it encased within *praṇavas* in the Kali age, one attains perfection; without that, it would be fruitless.
This is its meaning, as recorded by Rāghavabhaṭṭa.
In this context, Brahman is expressed by the syllable *praṇava*, and it is likewise expressed by the *vyāhṛtis*.
By the etymology "it brings forth (*bhāvayati*) and illuminates everything," *bhūḥ* denotes pure existence (*sanmātra*),
while *bhuvaḥ* denotes the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*).
It is *svar* because it impels all; it is *maha* because its nature is splendor (*tejas*) and because it is worthy of worship;
it is *jana* because it generates all beings;
and it is *tapa* because its essence is knowledge or because it consumes everything.

Because it is supreme, because it is the self of all, and because its knowledge is infinite, the Supreme Brahman alone is denoted by the seven vyāhṛtis together with the praṇava; the internal relationship between them is as follows:
either the seven vyāhṛtis are the seven mātrās of the praṇava beginning with 'a', or they are the seven worlds beginning with Bhūḥ.
The meaning is that these [beings] have as their essence Brahman, which is denoted by the syllable *praṇava*, and there is nothing whatsoever apart from that.
By the word "that" (*tat*), Brahman is expressed, according to the statement: "The designation of Brahman is considered to be threefold: *Oṃ*, *Tat*, and *Sat*."
He is called *Savitṛ* because he is born from the verbal root *su*, meaning "to bring forth," and because he teaches all phenomenal manifestation (*prapañca*).
He is *Vareṇya* because his nature is unsurpassed bliss and because he is to be chosen by all as the most desirable.
He is *Bharga* because he strikes down evil and grants fearlessness through the path of devotion.

Because the Lord is the illuminator of all things, the use of the genitive case in the phrase "of the divine Savitṛ" (devasya savituḥ) is figurative, like the expression "the head of Rāhu. We meditate upon— that is, we contemplate— the Brahman, which shall impel— that is, inspire— our thoughts, that is, our intellects.
In this context, the change of gender in the word *yaḥ* (masculine for neuter) is due to Vedic usage (*chāndasatvāt*).
By this, the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), the illuminator of all internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and the witness of all (*sarvasākṣī*), is denoted.
He is called *āpaḥ* because he pervades (*vyāpnoti*); he is *jyotiḥ* because he is the illuminator of all; and he is short (*hrasva*) because he transcends everything.
Alternatively,
"water, light, and essence" refers to the splendor of Soma and Agni,
for the universe is composed of that.
Because it is imperishable, it is *amṛta* (the immortal); because it is vast and nourishing, it is *brahma*, characterized by truth, knowledge, and bliss.
It is that which is denoted by the words *bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ*, and it is that which is denoted by the phrase "I am That" (*so'ham*).
Thus, the Gāyatrī mantra is the indicator of Brahman as the Self of all.
The term "beginning with *praṇava*" is connected with the word "vyāhṛtis";
the phrase "beginning with the word *tat*" is connected with what follows.
Herein are the seven vyāhṛtis.
Oṃ bhūḥ, Oṃ bhuvaḥ, Oṃ svaḥ, Oṃ mahaḥ, Oṃ janaḥ, Oṃ tapaḥ, Oṃ satyam.
Following this, [recite] the Ṛgvedic verse beginning with "tat savituḥ," and at its conclusion, [recite]: "Oṃ āpo jyotī raso 'mṛtaṃ brahma bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ oṃ idaṃ śivam."
Regarding this, the seed-syllable (*bīja*) and other components as stated in another tantra are as follows: "The syllable *re* shall be the seed; the letter *ya* is called the power (*śakti*);
and *nī* is declared to be the peg (*kīlaka*) for the three-footed Gāyatrī."
Regarding the phrase "at the joints of the feet": there are four syllables at the four joints of the two feet; thus it is said, "the four joints of the two feet.
Likewise, there are four syllables at the four joints of the two arms. Elsewhere, there is one syllable each. In this manner, twenty-four syllables are to be placed.
By [the word] "nīya" being separate from that, the meditation on the seer (ṛṣi), meter (chandas), and deity (devatā) for each of the twenty-four syllables is stated;
and for all the syllables, Prajāpati is the seer.
The application (*viniyoga*) is in the arrangement of the limbs; the *gāyatrī* is said to be the meter.
Now, the deities of all the syllables shall be stated in sequence:
Agni, Vāyu, Sūrya, Vidyut, Yamā, and Varuṇa.
Bṛhaspati, Parjanya, Indra, and Gandharva;
Pūṣan, Śiva, Tvaṣṭṛ, Vāsava, and Marut;
Soma, Aṅgiras, the Viśvedevas, the two Aśvins, and Prajāpati.
(358) Sarva, Rudra, Brahmā, and Viṣṇu are the deities who should be meditated upon at the time of recitation; one shall attain union (sāyujya) with them.
Their seed-syllable is yellow like a campaka flower, consisting of the essence of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva.
One should meditate upon [the deity] seated on a hundred-petaled lotus throne, established in a firm posture;
one should thus contemplate the syllable *Sa*, resembling the Atasī flower,
situated in the center of the lotus, gentle, and the destroyer of minor sins (*upapātaka*).

The phrase "having the luster of an atasī flower" refers to the *teuḍī* plant; it does not refer to the *atasī* (linseed) itself, because in the verse cited from the Gāyatrītantra to be mentioned later, a dark color is observed.
The best of the twice-born, being tranquil, should meditate upon the eternal Kapila, who abides on the lotus-seat and destroys great sins;
the wise man should contemplate the syllable *tu*, which possesses a luster like that of a sapphire.
The wise one should contemplate the syllable *vaṃ*, radiant with the glow of fire, which burns away all evils arising from planetary afflictions and diseases;
even the sin committed by the killing of a fetus perishes at that very moment.
One should meditate on the syllable *re*, pure and resembling clear crystal;
by that, the sin arising from approaching those who should not be approached is swiftly destroyed.
The yogi should contemplate the syllable *ṇī*, resembling clear crystal.
The sin of eating forbidden food perishes at that very moment.
One should meditate upon the syllable *ya*, the color of the stars, adorned with the crescent moon,
the bestower of boons upon yogis, which destroys even the murder of a Brahmin.
Having meditated upon the syllable *bha*, which is black in color and possesses a luster like a dark cloud,
the twice-born man destroys his sins, beginning with [the thought] "I am a person" (*puruṣa*).
Then, [he meditates on] the syllable *rgo*, which is red in color and seated upon a lotus throne.

By meditating upon it, the sin committed through the killing of a cow and other such acts perishes in that very instant. The yogi should constantly contemplate the syllable *De*, which resembles blood in color and is seated upon a lotus throne; it is the supreme burner of the sin of killing a woman.
One should contemplate the letter *va* as pure, with a radiance like the *jātī* flower;
by meditating thus, the sin committed by killing a guru perishes in that very instant.
Likewise, one should contemplate the letter *sy* as yellow, with a radiance like gold.
The sin conceived in the mind, having meditated upon it, the sinless one dispels;
he should contemplate the syllable *dhīḥ*, white and radiant like a kunda flower.
He is liberated from the sin of killing father or mother—of this there is no doubt.
One should meditate upon the syllable *ma* as having the luster of a ruby and blazing with splendor;
the sins accumulated in previous births perish at that very moment.
One should meditate upon the syllable *hi* as being the color of a conch shell and possessing a radiance equal to the full moon.
The wise man should constantly meditate on the burner of all sins without exception.
He should meditate upon the Pāṇḍava [form] seated upon a lotus;
by mere remembrance, the sin committed through accepting gifts is destroyed.

Having meditated upon the syllable *yo*, which is red in color and possesses a luster like that of the *indragopa* insect, the best of sages shall burn away the sin of killing living beings. Furthermore, the second syllable mentioned is the syllable *yo*, resembling blood in color.

It burns away all sins, and one is not defiled by other evils. O best of the twice-born, having meditated even once upon the syllable *na*— which is at the beginning of the word *namas* and resembles the rising sun— one shall go to the supreme state.
Having meditated even once upon the syllable *pra*, which has the dark luster of a blue lotus petal and belongs to the southern course (*dakṣiṇāyana*),
that best of the twice-born shall go to the state of Īśvara.
[Likewise,] the syllable *ca* is gentle, yellow as cow’s gallstone, and four-faced.

Having meditated even once upon the syllable *da*, which is white in color, resembling the moon, and facing the west, that best of the twice-born shall indeed go to the station of Viṣṇu. Having meditated even once upon it, that best of the twice-born shall go to the station of Brahmā.
Since that which is called Śiva is said to possess the splendor of four faces,
the Smṛti states that he is the bestower of manifest results as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra.
Having meditated upon him thus, the wise person who performs recitation (japa) and fire-offerings (homa) [attains success].
For him there shall be no birth-impurity (sūtaka) nor is death-impurity (mṛtaka) found;
but for one who does not know Gāyatrī in such a manner,
O sinless one, I have declared both birth-impurity and death-impurity to exist for him.
Neither the fruit of his charity, nor the fruit of his sacrifice,
nor even the fruit of visiting sacred fords is said to accrue to him while the period of birth-impurity (sūtaka) persists.
Now follows the ritual of colors (varṇakalpa).
Thus it is stated in the Gāyatrītantra:
One should contemplate the syllable *takāra* as yellow as a campaka flower, consisting of the nature of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva; the syllable *tsakāra* as dark blue; likewise, *vikāra* as tawny;
*tukāra* with the luster of a sapphire; and *rvakāra* resembling fire.
The syllable *re* resembles fire; the syllable *ṇi* is red in color;
the syllable *yaṃ* resembles smoke; the syllable *bha* is black;
the syllable *rgo* is red in color; and the syllable *de* is likewise dark blue.
The syllable *va* is white in appearance; the syllable *sya* is adorned with blue;
the syllable *dhī* has the luster of a kunda flower; the syllable *ma* is indeed white;
the syllable *hi* resembles the moon; and the syllable *dhi* is yellow.
The syllable *yo* has the form of lightning, and the syllable *yo* is smoke-colored;
just as the seed-syllable of wind does, it dries up every sin.
The syllable *na* is said to be the mouth, possessing the luster of molten gold.
Near the letter *na*, there are specifically two dots (*bindu*);
the upper dot is proclaimed to be red in color, while the lower one is dark blue.
The syllable *pra* is dark like the petal of a blue lotus and faces south.
The syllable *ca* is gentle, yellow like cow-urine pigment, and faces west;
the syllable *da* has the appearance of a white conch shell and faces four directions;
the syllable *yā* is to be known as being at the crown of the head, facing upward, and is the abode of Brahmā.

Wherever there is a specific variation in the colors mentioned in the previously described meditation on the syllables of the Gāyatrī, it should be understood according to the particular Vedic tradition (Āmnāya). Now follows the Gāyatrī Yantra.
First, having inscribed a triangle, one should place a hexagon outside of it;
then a circle, and outside that, an eight-petaled lotus,
followed by a square provided with four doors— this is declared to be the Sāvitrī Yantra.
In the Śāradā [Tantra].
Having prepared the mandala, the wise one [should make] it with a radiant triangular pericarp;
"mandala" here refers to the Sarvatobhadra mandala.
Regarding the phrase "blazing with a triangle," one should draw a triangle within its pericarp.
Now follows the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the seer (ṛṣi) and other elements of the Gāyatrī mantra.
In the twenty-first chapter of the Śāradātilaka.

These sages and others of the *praṇava* have been proclaimed by the seers. They know Jamadagni, Bharadvāja, Bhṛgu, Gautama, Kāśyapa, Viśvāmitra, and the one named Vasiṣṭha to be the sages of the *vyāhṛtis*.
Furthermore, the Gāyatrī, Uṣṇih, Anuṣṭubh, Bṛhatī, Paṅkti, Triṣṭubh,
and Jagatī are the meters (chandas) declared by the wise.
The deities are Saptārcis, Balin, Sūrya, Vākpati, Varuṇa, and Vṛṣan.
The Viśvedevas are proclaimed as the deities of these [verses] in sequence.
For the Gāyatrī, the sage is said to be the highly resplendent Viśvāmitra;
its meter is stated to be Gāyatrī, and its deity is remembered as Savitṛ.
The sage of this [mantra] is Brahmā; the meters and deities are traditionally taught as beginning with the Goddess.
Gāyatrī is said by the wise to be the supreme self (paramātman) as its deity.
The seven vyāhṛtis preceded by the syllable Om (tārā) are assigned to the heart, face, shoulders, and pair of thighs.
Having placed [the syllables] in the belly, the knower of mantras should place the syllables of the Gāyatrī on the body:
in the joints of the feet, the genitals, the navel, the heart, the throat, and the joints of the arms;
and again in the mouth, nose, cheeks, eyes, ears, eyebrows, and the head.
The practitioner who knows the mantra should place ten steps upon these locations: on the western, northern, southern, and eastern faces, as well as above;
and [he should also place them] on the head, between the eyebrows, the heart, the face, the throat, the heart, the navel, and the private parts.
One should place that head upon the pair of knees and feet, and [the other] head upon the head.
(p. 361) Now follows the ritual placement of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa).
In the Nirvāṇatantra:

O Priyaṃvadā, listen to that mantra for the six-limbed placement (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa)! A wise person should place two *praṇavas* in the heart-lotus, the syllable *bhūḥ* in the region of the head, *bhuvaḥ* at the crest-lock (*śikhā*), and the syllable *svaḥ* in the armor (*kavaca*).
One should assign *bhūḥ*, *bhuvaḥ*, and *svaḥ* to the three eyes; *svāhā* to the pair of hands; and then assign *namaḥ*, *svāhā*, *vaṣaṭ*, *kūrca*, *vauṣaṭ*, and *phaṭ* in their respective order.
But in the case of Śāradā, however.
The heart is declared for Brahmā; the head is said to be for Viṣṇu; the tuft (śikhā) is proclaimed for Rudra; the armor (kavaca) is said to be for Īśvara;
the eye is spoken of as being for Sadāśiva; and the weapon (astra) is remembered as belonging to the Soul of All.
Thus the six limbs have been described; one should place them accordingly in their proper locations.
Now, meditation.
In the Nirvāṇa Tantra:
Listen, O lady of excellent limbs, to the method of meditation, by which a person, having meditated, should perform the recitation (japa):
She is described as white in color, likewise clad in silk garments,
and adorned with white unguents, flowers, and ornaments.
The Goddess resides within the solar disc or has gone to the world of Brahmā;
she holds a rosary and is likewise seated upon a lotus throne.
"Oṃ! You are splendor, you are semen, you are nectar, you are the name of the abode, the beloved of the gods, the unassailable."
Thou art the place of sacrifice for the gods.

Thou art the Gāyatrī: one-footed, two-footed, three-footed, four-footed; thou art footless, for thou art not to be stepped upon. Homage to thy fourth, visible, supreme state, beyond the dust of the world!
The meditation as taught by Śāradā is as follows:
One should visualize her possessing three eyes with complexions like pearl, coral, gold, sapphire, and white, wearing a jeweled crown bound with the moon,
and whose nature consists of the syllables of the ocean of reality.
I worship Gāyatrī, who holds in her hands the boon-granting gesture, the gesture of fearlessness, a goad, a radiant skull, a rosary, a conch, a discus, and a pair of lotuses.
In the first chapter of the Brāhmaṇa of the Gāyatrī Tantra.
Four-armed, adorned with a digit of the moon and a mass of matted hair,
she is the mistress of the Ṛg, Sāma, and Yajur Vedas, her eyes like blossoming lotuses;
her chest is illuminated by a garland strung with the fifty letters of the alphabet.
Adorned at the neck with ornaments fashioned from many jewels,
her limbs anointed with divine perfumes, she is arrayed in white garments;
seated upon a white lotus, she wears a white upper robe.

Having thus meditated upon Her—who is praised by the hosts of deities beginning with Brahmā and who is eternally fresh—one should recite the supreme meter and perform the placement of the syllables (*varṇanyāsa*).
For this Gāyatrī whose face is Agni, the Supreme Brahman is the Seer (*ṛṣi*); the *Ṛg*, *Yajus*, *Sāman*, and *Atharvan* are the meters (*chandas*); and Savitṛ is the Deity (*devatā*).
The application (*viniyoga*) is for the placement (*nyāsa*) upon the Supreme Brahman-Mother. (p.
362) A person of vast intellect should perform the placement from the feet to the top of the head.
For one who recites the *Gāyatrī* without performing the placement, it becomes fruitless.
The installation performed by one who lacks the mudrās becomes fruitless;
an ascetic should diligently perform the installation with the five mudrās,
and a householder should diligently perform it at the three junctions of the day using the Tattva-mudrā.
The little finger, the ring finger, and the thumb;

the thumb and the forefinger; the thumb and the middle finger; and likewise the thumb and the ring finger—through the joining of the little finger and the thumb, these are proclaimed as the five mudrās.
The wise one should place *bhūr*, *bhuvaḥ*, and *svar* from the feet to the head;
the learned yogi should perform the sevenfold placement of the Gāyatrī according to the sequential method,
and he should place the syllable *takāra* on the big toe, contemplating it as supreme.
One should place the syllable *tsa* between the two ankles, *vi* likewise on the two calves,
*tu* in the middle of the two knees, *rva* in the middle of the two thighs,
*re* in the region of the private parts, and *ṇi* on the testicles.
One should place the syllable *yaṃ* at the region of the waist and the syllable *bha* in the circle of the navel;
one should place the syllable *rgo* in the stomach and the syllable *de* on the breasts;
one should place the syllable *va* in the middle of the heart and the syllable *sya* from the throat downward.
O auspicious lady, one should place the syllable *dhī* in the mouth and the syllable *ma* on the palate;
the syllable *hi* at the tip of the nose and the syllable *dhī* in the two eyes;
and first, the yogi should place the syllable *yo* between the eyebrows.
And the second [syllable] should be known as being on the forehead, without a doubt;
the syllable *na* should be known in the mouth, and the syllable *pra* on the right face.
Likewise, the syllable *co* is on the west, and similarly, the syllable *da* is on the north.
The syllable YĀT should be known as being at the crown of the head, always remaining pervading everything.
In the tenth Brahmana chapter of the Gāyatrī Tantra.
Now, O beloved, I shall fully describe the worship of Gāyatrī;
just as the worship of a mantra that has been practiced is prescribed,
even so, O auspicious lady, I shall tell you the worship of Gāyatrī.

O auspicious lady, whatever worship there may be— be it the worship of Śiva, the worship of Śakti, or the worship of Viṣṇu— all such worship is in vain without the worship of Gāyatrī. Having entered the pavilion of worship, one should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) for Gāyatrī.
The wise practitioner should place the first seed-syllable of the Gāyatrī at the site of worship;
having sat upon a seat of Kuśa grass, he should perform breath control (prāṇāyāma).
The retention of the vital breath of the Gāyatrī should be performed according to the sequence of inhalation (pūraka) and the others.
Then one should perform the general *arghya* offering according to the path of the previously mentioned sequence.
Having recited the *gāyatrī* once, one should pour water into a copper vessel;
having invoked the sacred waters (*tīrtha*) with effort, one should then mutter the *gāyatrī*.
Then, having rendered the cow immortal with the first eight-syllable [mantra],
and having gazed at the water for the sake of pacification with the second eight-syllable [mantra],
O Goddess, one should perform the purification of oneself with the waters using the third eight-syllable [mantra].

O Supreme Goddess! Worship consisting of creation, maintenance, and dissolution, performed according to this very procedure, bestows fruit at that very moment. The ritual placement (nyāsa) of the yantra, meditation (dhyāna), and so forth, have already been written about previously.
There, one should worship the solar seat (saura-pīṭha) with the nine powers beginning with Dīptā;
these [powers] such as Dīptā and others are described in the fourteenth chapter within the Sarvatobhadra maṇḍala.
For example:
Dīptā, Sūkṣmā, Jayā, Bhadrā, Vibhūti, Vimalā, Aghorā, Vidyutā, and Sarvatomukhī are the Pīṭha-śaktis. The Saura-pīṭha is to be understood from the section on the Sun (Sūrya-prakaraṇa).
One should worship the Goddess in the form fashioned with the root mantra.
In the Nirvāṇa Tantra.

Having performed the placement of the vital breaths (jīvanyāsa) and other rites, one should worship her, the bestower of the three aims of life. O Supreme Goddess! Having uttered the entire mantra beginning with "Hālāhala," one should then say "pādyaṃ" followed by the Sāvitrī mantra joined with the suffix "-ṅe."

Thereafter, one should worship the mantra whose essence is renunciation with great effort and extensive displays of wealth; otherwise, one is considered a Brāhmaṇa [in name only]. Thus it is stated in the Śāradā-tantra.
In the three corners, the powers (śaktis) beginning with Brāhmī are to be worshipped externally;
thereafter, the deities beginning with Āditya, together with Ūṣā and the others, are to be worshipped in sequence.
The deities beginning with Āditya and those beginning with Ūṣā are to be understood as described in the section on Sūrya.
Then one should worship the six limbs according to the rule upon the filaments;
thereafter, one should worship Prahlādinī, Prabhā, Nityā, and Viśvaṃbharā, and again Vilāsinī, Prabhāvatī, Ūṣā, and Śāntā.
Then one should recite Kānti, Durgā, and Sarasvatī, who are the forms of knowledge; thereafter,
one should recite Īśā together with Viśālā, as well as Vyāpinī, Vimalā, Tamo’pahāriṇī, Sūkṣmā, Viśvayoni, and Jayāvahā.
Then one should worship Padmālayā, who possesses supreme splendor and has the form of a lotus.
One should worship Brāhmī and the others, characterized as previously described, together with Aruṇa on the exterior.
Then one should worship the planets on the exterior, along with Indra and the other gods, together with their weapons.
In this manner, one should worship the Goddess with these ten veils;
thus, O best of the twice-born, he shall become an enjoyer of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa.
In the Nirvāṇa Tantra.

O lady of excellent limbs! In the absence of ritual substances, having worshipped with water-based offerings such as *pādya* and the rest, one should recite the Gāyatrī, the supreme syllable, for the Goddess. (p.
364) By this [it is shown that] even when worship must be performed with water and so forth due to the lack of materials—
For this very reason, the Smṛti states that one should say, "This is the water for the feet," and so forth;
furthermore, if a performer of sacrifice should use oil as a substitute for ghee for the sake of the sacrifice,
he should then recite the verse beginning with "ghṛtavatī" (endowed with ghee) by its very original nature, because of that underlying cause.
Therefore, the statement "this water is for the purpose of *pādya*" (water for washing the feet) contradicts the authoritative injunctions.
The fruit of the recitation (*japa*) is also mentioned in that very same place.
The Gāyatrī destroys the sin produced in ten lifetimes by [one hundred recitations], that committed in a previous life by one hundred, and that born of three lifetimes by one thousand;
a specific rule regarding the recitation is stated in the Gāyatrī-tantra.
Having encased the desired mantra within the Gāyatrī, one should recite it a hundred times;
having encased the Gāyatrī within the desired mantra, one should likewise recite it a hundred times.
O Maheśānī! This recitation is the supreme relationship between the support and the supported.
O Maheśānī! Without a substratum, and likewise without that which is supported,
the substratum is not established, O auspicious lady, nor is that which is supported established—
this applies to all Viṣṇu-mantras as well as those of the Sun and Gaṇapati.

O lady with beautiful hands, the relationship of container and contained exists everywhere; yet, he who might enter a house suddenly through its windows and doors would not see anything situated within the interior of that house with his eyes.

O auspicious lady, when a twice-born person thus establishes the substratum and the superstratum, a sprout is born from a hundred thousand recitations; of this there is no doubt. Furthermore, Gāyatrī, whose form is Brahman, is not distinct from the individual soul (jīva) and the Self (ātman).

The Gāyatrī would not be distinct from the individual soul (jīvātman), for she is its very essence; there is always oneness between the two, like water within a coconut. Indeed, it is said that a twice-born one becomes a Brāhmaṇa only through his divine nature.
Just as even copper becomes gold through contact with the touchstone,
so too is the self, when accompanied by the Gāyatrī, declared to be the essence of the twice-born.
In the Gayatrī Tantra.
A Brahmin should recite [the mantra] facing the sun; there is no restriction regarding direction whatsoever.
One should daily recite the Gāyatrī at the three junctions of the day—of this there is no doubt.
However, O Maheśānī, during a period of impurity, one should remember the Gāyatrī mentally.
The Gāyatrī is multiform; meditation itself is the three junctions of the day.
In that very same [text].

"Oṃ! Born from the mouth of Maheśvara, residing in the heart of Viṣṇu, permitted by Brahmā—go, O Goddess, according to your will! Having recited this mantra over the left hand of the Goddess, the wise one [should proceed].
One should then offer the fruit of the recitation and thereafter recite hymns and other such prayers.
Now, the Gāyatrī-kavaca.
The Goddess said:
O God of gods! O Mahādeva! O Savior from the ocean of saṃsāra!
O Lord, out of compassion, please tell me the Gāyatrī-kavaca.
The illustrious God of Gods said:
In the root-supports (mūlādhāra), she who is eternal is Kuṇḍalinī, whose nature is the ultimate reality;
she is subtler than the subtlest, supreme, and has the form of a lotus fiber;
she resembles a mass of lightning and possesses a coiled shape.
She is the supreme Brahman’s housewife, possessing a form of fifty letters;
she is Śiva’s eternal dancer, worshipped by the Supreme Brahman.
She alone is the Gāyatrī of Brahmā, whose nature is existence, consciousness, and bliss.
This wind of the whirlpool of delusion, whose nature is the vital breath (prāṇa), is eternally new;
may Kuṇḍalinī remain forever in bliss within the body of worldly existence.
This is a great merit, most secret, and endowed with the essence of thirty million sacred pilgrimage sites.
O Goddess! Consisting of all sacrifices, always consisting of all gifts, O Goddess!
always consisting of all knowledge and the Supreme Brahman—O Pārvatī, beloved of my life! I shall now recite this armor (kavaca).

Oṃ oṃ bhūḥ oṃ oṃ oṃ oṃ bhuvaḥ oṃ oṃ oṃ oṃ svaḥ oṃ oṃ oṃ oṃ tat oṃ oṃ tsat oṃ oṃ vi oṃ oṃ tu oṃ oṃ rva oṃ oṃ re oṃ oṃ ṇi oṃ oṃ yaṃ oṃ oṃ bha oṃ oṃ rgo oṃ oṃ de oṃ oṃ va oṃ oṃ sya oṃ oṃ dhī oṃ oṃ ma oṃ.
Oṃ hi oṃ oṃ dhi oṃ oṃ yo oṃ oṃ yo oṃ oṃ naḥ oṃ oṃ pra oṃ oṃ co oṃ oṃ da oṃ oṃ yāt oṃ oṃ oṃ oṃ | Oṃ bhūḥ oṃ; may it protect my root, which is endowed with four petals.
Oṃ Bhuvaḥ! Oṃ, may it protect my *liṅga*, endowed with six petals. Oṃ Svaḥ! Oṃ, may it protect my throat, together with space, possessing sixteen petals.
Oṃ Ta! Oṃ, may it protect my form—the supreme Brahman, which is without cause.

Oṃ tsa oṃ: may my face, together with the tongue, be protected. Oṃ vi oṃ: may my sense of smell, ever associated with the body, be protected. Oṃ tu oṃ: may my sense of touch, which is the cause of the body, be protected.
Oṃ rva oṃ: may it protect my sense of hearing, the cause of the manifestation of sound.
Oṃ re oṃ: may it protect my skin, the constant guardian of the body. Oṃ ṇi oṃ: may it protect my eye, the sole cause of all principles of reality.

Oṃ yaṃ oṃ: may it protect my hearing and the cause of hearing. Oṃ bha oṃ: may it protect my nose and the cause of perceiving fragrance. Oṃ rgo oṃ: may it protect my speech in the assembly, which takes the form of sound.
Oṃ de oṃ: May [the syllable] protect my pair of arms, the cause of Brahman. Oṃ va oṃ: May [the syllable] protect my pair of feet, the cause of Brahman.
Oṃ sya oṃ: May [the syllable] protect my *liṅga*, which is joined with water and the six petals.
Oṃ dhī oṃ: May [the syllable] protect my primordial nature (prakṛti), the cause of sound, eternally. Oṃ ma oṃ: May [the syllable] protect my mind, which has the form of Brahman, eternally.
Oṃ hi oṃ: May [the syllable] always protect my intellect, which consists of the Supreme Brahman.

Oṃ dhi oṃ! May [the syllable] protect my ego (ahaṅkāra) always, in whatever manner it may be. Oṃ yo oṃ! May [the syllable] protect my earthly body (pārthiva-vapuḥ) and the earth (pṛthivī) always. Oṃ yo oṃ! May [the syllable] protect the water everywhere and at all times.

Oṃ naḥ Oṃ! May the mass of splendor protect me eternally, in every way. Oṃ pra Oṃ! May the wind, the cause of the body, protect me eternally. Oṃ co Oṃ! May space, which resembles the moon, protect me eternally.
Oṃ da oṃ: may it protect my tongue, the instrument of the sacrifice of recitation (japayajña). Oṃ yāt oṃ: may it always protect my mind, which consists of the knowledge of Śiva.
Oṃ: may Gāyatrī, the supreme deity, eternally protect my principles of reality (tattvas).
Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ! May Brahmāṇī protect my belly from hunger eternally;
may Tvaṣṭṛ, as Brahmāṇī, bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ, protect me constantly.
Of this Śrī Gāyatrī, the Supreme Brahman is the Seer (ṛṣi); the Ṛg, Yajus, Sāman, and Atharvan are the Metres (chandas).
The deity is the Śrīgāyatrī-Brāhmaṇa; the application is for the sake of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa.
Then one should recite the Gāyatrī.
Through its mere remembrance, all things such as desire and anger attain a state of equanimity.
If one should mutter the Gāyatrī without knowing this armor (kavaca), [it yields no fruit].
O beloved! Success does not arise merely by reciting [the mantra] ten million times;
rather, through the recitation of the Gāyatrī, the entire Smaraṇa is certainly accomplished.
Having recited the Kavaca, a Brāhmaṇa should utter the Gāyatrī once.

The twice-born one shall be liberated from all sins and become liberated while living. O Goddess! If anyone recites another armor-mantra without knowing this armor-mantra, everything of his—including the *Trailokyamaṅgala* and other such texts—is in vain.

He who always possesses the Gāyatrī-kavaca upon his tongue has a tongue that is pure and nectar-like for recitation and worship. If one should recite the Brahma-vidyā without knowing this armor (kavaca), [it is fruitless].
O lady of beautiful limbs! That recitation becomes as futile as weeping in the forest.
Yet, even the great sins—killing a Brahmin, drinking liquor, theft, and violating the teacher's wife—shall go to destruction through mere remembrance of it.
That which is composed of skin, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow, and semen,
and is joined with wind, bile, and phlegm, is called the gross body (sthūla-deha). The subtle body (sūkṣma-deha), consisting of light and composed of the five elements, is what the wise know [to be].
Abiding within the Great Lotus Grove and complete with all limbs,
through the relationship of container and contained, Gāyatrī herself is the Brāhmaṇa;
for this very reason, she is called the Supreme Brahman, possessing a dual nature.
The living self (jīvātman) of the Brāhmaṇa alone is a body conjoined with Gāyatrī;
it resides within the lotus of the heart like the flame of a lamp,
resembling a smokeless light produced by the union of oil, fire, and a wick.

That light is the supreme Brahman; he alone is the supreme Śiva. Having performed the placement of the Gāyatrī armor (gāyatrī-kavaca-nyāsa) upon the locations and joints of the Mātṛkā, that best of Brāhmaṇas may then perform any other ritual placement.
The ritual placement (nyāsa) must be performed in this specific manner; otherwise, it is like weeping in the wilderness.
By the mere performance of the Gāyatrī-nyāsa, the twice-born becomes composed of the Supreme Brahman.
He who practices celibacy without knowing this armor (kavaca) [is ineffective].
The practice of celibacy (brahmacarya) would be in vain without the Gāyatrī-kavaca. By the grace of this armor, a Brāhmaṇa becomes like a blazing fire.
O Supreme Goddess! This armor is the very essence of creation, sustenance, and dissolution.
Indeed, by the grace of this armor, Brahmā performs creation;
Viṣṇu maintains it, and I, Rudra, am the cause of its dissolution.
O Goddess, there is indeed another armor which exists apart from creation, maintenance, and dissolution.
This very armor named Brāhmaṇa, consisting of Brahman and comprising creation, maintenance, and dissolution— whosoever, having risen at dawn,
recites it and remembers the Gāyatrī even once, shall obtain the fruit of a hundred thousand recitations.
Having recited the Gāyatrī ten times, one obtains the fruit of a hundred lakhs [of recitations].
If one recites the Gāyatrī in this sequence a hundred times,
having attained the fruit of a hundred lakhs, one may roam upon the earth like a god.
During an eclipse of the moon or sun, if a learned twice-born man, having recited the armor (kavaca),
should chant the supreme syllable Gāyatrī even once,
he would become perfected at that very moment and attain union with Brahman.

If one recites the Gāyatrī without knowing this armor (kavaca), that recitation alone shall be devoid of luster and not grant success. O Goddess! He who constantly recites the armor in the presence of Śiva—
In the presence of Lord Viṣṇu and in the presence of Śakti,
a Brāhmaṇa certainly becomes a mass of splendor at that very moment.
Thus ends the Gāyatrī-kavaca within the *Āgama-saṃdarbha*, in the *Jñānadarpaṇa*, the *Gāyatrī-brāhmaṇa-sarvasva*, in the dialogue between the God and the Goddess.
(p. 368) Now follows its preliminary ritual practice (*puraścaraṇa*).
In the Śāradā [Tantra].
Eating only alms-food, with senses subdued, one who knows the reality should perform one hundred thousand oblations according to the prescribed rite.
For the sake of attaining mantra-perfection, one should offer three thousand oblations each of milk-rice, sesame seeds, dūrvā grass, and the excellent fuel-sticks of milky trees.
By the phrase "one hundred thousand [recitations] according to the prescribed rule," the preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*) of twenty-four hundred thousand recitations is stated.
"According to the rule" means according to the procedure prescribed for the preliminary practice.
"Milk-rice" (*kṣīraudana*) refers to rice cooked with milk.
The four substances are sesame seeds and *dūrvā* grass;
the "milk-tree" group consists of the four substances: the *aśvattha*, *udumbara*, *plakṣa*, and *vaṭa*.
By the phrase "three thousand each," a homa of twenty-four thousand oblations is indicated.
But in the Nirvāṇatantra, however:
The preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) is declared to consist of one hundred thousand recitations according to the prescribed rule;

thereafter, for the sake of accomplishing the preliminary rite, one should perform a fire-oblation (homa) consisting of one-tenth of that number. Furthermore, the ritual libation (tarpaṇa) is said to be one-tenth of the number of oblations.
After that, one should perform the consecration (abhiṣeka) with a tenth part of the libation (tarpaṇa).
Then, one should provide a meal for Brahmins with a tenth part of the consecration.
Thereafter, O Goddess, one becomes perfected (siddha), achieving the fruits of the three aims of life (trivarga).
And the majesty of this mantra has been proclaimed by the Caturveda.
Now, regarding the rites for specific desires as stated in the Śāradā-tilaka:
"A knower of mantras should offer oblations with sesame seeds numbering one thousand times the number of principles (tattvas).
Liberated from all sins, he attains a long life."

For the sake of long life, one should offer three thousand oblations with the mantra using only clarified butter as the sacrificial offering, or with *dūrvā* grass, the three [medicinal herbs], and sesame seeds. Thereafter,
one should offer ten thousand oblations with red lotuses smeared with the three sweets (*trimadhu*).
Great fortune shall be his within six months; of this there is no doubt.
For the sake of Brahmanic glory, one should offer oblations with flowers born of the Brahma-tree (palāśa).
What is the use of saying more here? When performed properly and well-accomplished, [it yields the desired result].
This knowledge is considered by the twice-born to be a cow that yields the milk of all desired perfections.
Now, the Tantric Gāyatrī is found in the fifth chapter of the *Annadākalpa*.
She is the liberator from all sins, the dryer up of all calamities,
the constant subduer of poverty, and the bestower of happiness and liberation.
By a single utterance, she destroys every sin, including the mortal transgression of killing a Brahmin.
It certainly brings about the destruction of [sins] arising from another birth;
ten [recitations] destroy those born of ten births, a hundred those born of a hundred births,
and a thousand those born of a thousand births— thus it is the destroyer of sins.
This eternal digit of consciousness (citkalā), which is the essence of all the scriptures along with their auxiliary branches,
is proclaimed here with a thousand introductory verses.
Thus ends the preliminary practice (puraścaraṇa).
The seer is Brahmā, the meter is proclaimed to be Gāyatrī,
and the goddess is celebrated as the deity who bestows food and grants the fourfold aims of human existence.
The term "Ānanda-pradā" (Bestower of Bliss) is an epithet for one's own chosen deity (iṣṭadevatā).
The seed-syllable is *māyā* (hrīṃ), *namaḥ* is the power (*śakti*), and *pracodayāt* shall be the pin (*kīlaka*).
One should meditate upon the Goddess during the three periods of the day according to the distinction of the three qualities (*guṇa*):
in the morning, she is Brāhmī, red in color, two-armed, and a young maiden.
Carrying a water-pot filled with sacred water and a rosary of beads,
clad in a black antelope skin, mounted upon a swan, and possessing a pure smile;
at midday, she is dark-complexioned, belonging to Viṣṇu, and four-armed.
Holding a conch, a discus, a mace, and a lotus, seated upon Garuḍa,
with a pair of full and elevated breasts, adorned with a forest garland, and youthful,
she should always be meditated upon in the center of the orb of the sun.
In the evening, she takes the form of Sarasvatī, with the crescent moon as her crest-jewel;
while the sun is half-set, she who is eternally youthful should be meditated upon.
Furthermore, according to the *Tantrasāra*, Gāyatrī is generally to be regarded as the deity of all deities.
In the *Annadākalpa*.
Having brought water for the purpose of worship and having bowed to the sacred ford (tīrtha) according to the prescribed rite,
one should enter the sacrificial pavilion while meditating on the Goddess and reciting her hymn of praise.
And in the fifteenth chapter of the Matsyasūkta:
"The preceptor, having bathed according to the rules and performed his morning rites,
should go, adorned and empowered by mantra, to the sacrificial pavilion for the sake of the sacrifice."
Also in the second chapter of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa of the Rudrajāmala:
Having arrived at the pavilion for worship (pūjā-maṇḍapa), one should then wash one's feet and hands;
having sprinkled the door with the Astra-mantra, one should worship the left and right doorposts while uttering "Salutation to Gaṅgā" and "Salutation to Yamunā."
Then, [one should offer] obeisance to Śrī at the upper door and to Adhodehalī at the lower threshold.

In the phrase "the sacrificial pavilion" (yāgamaṇḍapa), by means of metaphorical indication (lakṣaṇā), "in the vicinity of the sacrificial pavilion" is obtained; otherwise, it would not be consistent with [the rule]: "contracting his limbs, he should enter within with his right foot."
In the Matsya-sūkta:
Having sipped water according to the rules and having offered the *arghya* to the Sun there,
one should approach the western door and enter with the right foot.
Having sprinkled the doors with water empowered by the weapon-mantra (*astra-mantra*), one should perform the worship of the door-deities (*dvārapūjā*).
In the sequence from top to bottom, one should worship Gaṇeśa, the destroyer of obstacles;
Mahālakṣmī, Mahāmāyā, and likewise the goddess Sarasvatī;
as well as Kṣetreśa, Gaṅgā, and Yamunā, with flowers and water.
O Goddess of gods! One should worship the threshold with the Astra-mantra.
The meaning is that one should sprinkle the door after reciting the weapon-mantra, namely the mantra "astrāya phaṭ."
In the Śāradā [Tantra].
On the upper part of the Udumbara post, one should worship Vighna, Mahālakṣmī, and Sarasvatī;
then on the southern branch, Vighna, and Kṣetreśa elsewhere.

The essential meaning is that one should worship Vighna at the threshold of the upper door (ūrdhvoḍumbaraka), Sarasvatī at the two corners of the threshold of the southern door of the house, and Mahālakṣmī in the middle.
The sense is that one should worship Vighna on the right jamb and Kṣetreśa on the other, the left jamb.
On the two sides [of the door], one should worship Gaṅgā and Yamunā with flowers and water;
at the threshold, one should worship the Weapon-mantra (astra) at each door in this sequence.
"Two sides" (tayoḥ pārśvau) means on the two sides of the lords of the field of obstacles (vighnakṣetreśa).
The worship of Durgā is also mentioned in the passage cited by Rāghavabhaṭṭa.
In the corners, one should worship Vighna, Durgā, Vāṇī, and Kṣetreśa.
The mantra for these, however, is as follows:
The syllable *tāra* (om) with the nasal bindu, followed by the name in the dative case ending and joined with *namaḥ*.
This has been stated in the Uḍḍāmareśvara:
The syllable Oṃ joined with the Bindu, followed by the first letter of the name;
for all [deities], the name is joined with the suffix -ī (ṅe) and accompanied by "namas," O Goddess, [to form the mantra].
In the Vaiṣṇava tradition, the worship of the door has been described by Rāghavabhaṭṭa as follows:
One should worship the door-keepers according to their various divisions, such as those of Viṣṇu and others,
with two on each side at every door, following this sequence:
Nanda, Sunanda, Caṇḍa, Pracaṇḍa, and Caṇḍanāyaka.
Prabala, Bhadra by name, and Subhadra are considered Vaiṣṇavas.
Now, as for the door-keepers of Śiva:
Then Nandi and Mahākāla, Gaṇeśa and the Bull; then Bhṛṅgiriṭi, Skanda, and Pārvatīśa as the seventh;
and Caṇḍeśvara as the eighth—these are the Śaiva door-keepers in their respective order.
But [the mantra] of Gaṇeśa, however...
Vakratuṇḍa, Ekadaṃṣṭra, Mahodara, Gajānana,
the one named Lambodara, Kaṭha, and Vighnarāja as the seventh,
and Dhūmrarāja as the eighth— these are to be known as the Gaṇapatyas in their respective order.
The Mothers, beginning with Brāhmī, have been declared; the door-keepers belong to the Śakti group.
In the Śāradā [Tantra].

Immediately thereafter, the supreme practitioner, by beholding with divine vision, should dispel the celestial obstacles; those moving in the intermediate space, he should drive away with the [divine] weapons;
and the terrestrial obstacles, he should ward off with three blows of the heel.
Touching slightly with his left hand the branch [of the doorframe], he should then step over the threshold;
contracting his body, he should enter within with his right foot.
This is also stated in the *Matsyasūkta*:
Having surveyed with divine vision, he should then dispel the obstacles;
having struck the ground three times and given three claps of the hands,
the best of practitioners should enter within while contracting his limbs.
Now, regarding the seat:
[it is described] in the Gaurījāmala as cited in the Śāktānandataraṅgiṇī.
If one should perform the worship of the deities while in water,
even then, one should act while seated upon a seat and not while standing;
having prepared a seat mentally, one should perform the worship in the water.
Seated upon his seat, he should recite the mantra with his mind fully absorbed in the meaning of the mantra.
In the Sammohanatantra.
Seated upon a red seat, situated in a house of lac and agallochum, or else clothed in red as prescribed by the ritual manual, the practitioner, firm in his posture,
[should use] cotton, woolen blankets, garments, or the skins of lions, tigers, and deer.
The wise one should prepare a seat that increases good fortune and wisdom;
it may be made of silk, or of leather, or even of oil-cloth,
or of reed-palm leaves, or of palm-leaf, or of woolen blanket, or of wooden material.
Success in knowledge is attained on a black antelope skin, and liberation is attained on a tiger skin.
Householders have no entitlement whatsoever to the black antelope skin;
a householder who has not been initiated must never sit upon a black antelope skin.
A renunciant, a forest-dweller, a celibate student, and a mendicant may sit upon a cloth seat;
it destroys disease, while a woolen blanket (kambala) brings liberation from suffering. Indeed, a cloth seat causes the loss of mantra-recitation, meditation, and austerity.

In this context, the prohibition of clothing refers specifically to wearing only a single garment, for otherwise a contradiction would arise. Longevity is attained on a seat of *kuśa* grass; liberation is attained on a tiger skin; one obtains sons on a deerskin (*ajina*); and supreme accomplishment (*siddhi*) is attained on a woolen blanket (*kambala*).
For rites of pacification (*śāntika*), a white [woolen] blanket is prescribed; for all purposes, a multicolored blanket is used.
For rites of nourishment (*pauṣṭika*), however, a silk blanket brings liberation from suffering.
O Goddess! A red blanket is highly recommended for the worship of Tripurā.
This [image] should not be longer than two cubits, nor wider than one and a half cubits;
for the rite of worship, it should be collected [in size] such that its height does not exceed three finger-breadths.
Then, one should prepare a seat that is neither too low nor too high.
In the Gandharva Tantra.
On the ground, there arises suffering; on a seat made of wood, misfortune.
A seat made of mango, nimba, or kadamba wood brings about the destruction of one's lineage.
On seats made of vakula, kiṃśuka, or jackfruit wood, one's prosperity is destroyed.
A practitioner of mantra should avoid a seat made of bamboo, bricks, the earth, grass, or twigs, as it bestows poverty, disease, and suffering.
The further result of these has been stated.
If one sits on the bare ground, suffering arises; on a wooden seat, there is misfortune;
on a bamboo seat, one becomes poor; and on a stone seat, there is affliction by disease.
On a seat of grass, there is loss of fame; on a seat of sprouts, mental confusion;
on a seat of cloth, the loss of recitation, meditation, and austerity is ordained.
When the practitioner of mantra sits upon a soft seat covered with silk, wool, or kuśa grass, [the practice is successful].
"A householder who has not received initiation should never sit upon a black antelope skin;
however, an ascetic, a forest-dweller, a student, and a mendicant may do so.
Thus it has been said.
The Gandharva Tantra specifies [the requirements for] a wooden seat.
O Dear One, a wooden seat made of gambhārī wood is praised, or one made of various auspicious woods;
it should be twenty-four finger-breadths in length,
sixteen finger-breadths in width, and four finger-breadths in height.
O Goddess, O lady of excellent complexion! For the worship of Mahāmāyā, a seat made of wool, leather, or stone is declared to be praiseworthy.
In the third chapter of the Muṇḍamālā Tantra.
A tiger skin is for the attainment of all perfections; a deer skin is for the attainment of knowledge.
A cloth seat removes disease, while one made of cane increases affection. Silk is said to grant nourishment, and a woolen blanket bestows all perfections.
Whether it be white or black, or especially a red woolen blanket;
the seat for the Northern Tradition (Uttarāmnāya) is indeed in that very place.

Indeed, a seat made of a monkey fallen in battle, or one killed by a creature, or even a dead monkey; or the skin of a woman who has miscarried, or the skin produced from the female organ— these, when spread out soft and supple, [are suitable].

O Goddess! It bestows all accomplishments and grants supreme prosperity in every respect. One should prepare a *vīrāsana* from the skin of those in the prime of youth, or an auspicious seat made of wood carved from the timber of a cremation ground.
A householder who has not received initiation should never enter upon a black antelope skin;
remaining like one indifferent toward those who are *snātaka* or celibate students,
he should [occupy] a square space on all sides, provided with *kuśa* grass, an antelope skin, and a garment.
One should construct a square measuring either one cubit or two cubits;
however, the specific types of seats for particular rites are described in the second chapter of the *Samayācāra-tantra*.
A ram-skin is for the purpose of subjugation, while tiger-skin is for attraction;
deer-skin is recommended for pacification, and tiger-skin for the sake of liberation; O Goddess! cow-hide is for paralyzing, and horse-hide for causing birth.
For the rite of eradication (*uccāṭana*), one should use the skin of a camel; for inciting enmity (*vidveṣa*), the skin of a dog;
and for killing (*māraṇa*), the skin of a buffalo—one should perform the prescribed ritual according to the specific task.
O Goddess! Likewise, a seat made of cloth or silk grants all desires and goals.
A seat made of wool or a blanket is honored in all rites;
a seat made of wood or stone causes suffering and poverty,
O Goddess, while one made of gold or other gems increases great good fortune.

Listen, O Goddess! specifically to the seat (āsana) of the Northern Tradition (Uttarāmnāya), by which one quickly attains the merit and the fruit of the God that is difficult to obtain. O fortunate one! it is the corpse-seat (śavāsana) as well as the skull-seat of the dead (mṛta-muṇḍāsana).

O Goddess! The cremation ground is a seat, as is the sight of the vulva; likewise, the seat of beholding the vulva, the seat of sexual union, and even the state of having performed sexual union grant the fruits of one's desired objects.
In the fifteenth [chapter] of the Mātsya [Purāṇa].
O noble lady! A deer skin is recommended for one desiring prosperity; a tiger skin for one seeking both worldly splendor and liberation;
and for one seeking power, the skin of a black tiger is praised.
One may also use a spread of grass, a stone slab, or garments that are red or yellow.
Success is swiftly attained on a woolen blanket and likewise on one made of *bhadradāru* wood. Furthermore,
one should enter the *yogāsana* and the *kūrma* posture while recollecting the earth.
In the second chapter of the *Yogasāra*.
A woolen blanket, one that is soft, one made of silk, and likewise one made of darbha grass—
these are declared to be suitable seats, as is a seat of animal hide. However, if one sits upon the hair [of the hide], then everything is destroyed.
Merely by the sight of hair, the loss of accomplishment arises.
For the sake of desired objects, a blanket is prescribed; the best is a red blanket.
On black antelope skin there is the accomplishment of knowledge; on tiger skin, prosperity and liberation.
Success in mantra comes on a seat of kusha grass; no deliberation is required in this matter.
In the *Samayācāra-tantra*:

O beautiful one, for the mantra of Pṛthivī, Merupṛṣṭha is declared to be the seer (ṛṣi), Sutala the meter (chanda), and Kūrma the deity. Its application (viniyoga) is in the seat; one should enter [the practice] while seated in the bound lotus posture (baddhapadmāsana).
"Having assumed the lotus posture" is an elliptical expression (upalakṣaṇa).

"One should perform recitation, worship, and so forth while seated in a single posture, such as the lotus, the svastika, or the vīrāsana; otherwise, it shall be fruitless," according to the words of Rāghavabhaṭṭa.
The posture for ascetics is tortoise-shaped, while for others it is quadrangular,
as recorded by Rāghavabhaṭṭa.
One should have a smooth seat for ascetics made in the shape of a tortoise;
for others, however, one should have it made four-legged and square.
Likewise.
One should not perform giving, sipping water for purification, fire-offerings, eating, worship of the deities, Vedic study, or libations while the feet are crossed over one another.
The definition of *prauḍhapāda* is also given in that same [text]:
"One who has placed his feet upon a seat, or upon the knees, or upon the shanks,
with the hem of his garment tucked in, is called *prauḍhapāda*."
Thus ends the description of the mature foot-marks sustained by Rāghava.
In the Gorakṣasaṃhitā:
"There are as many postures (āsanas) as there are living beings;
Maheśvara alone knows all their varieties."
Each one of the eighty-four lakhs has been proclaimed;
likewise, Śiva created one hundred and sixteen seats (pīṭhas). Regarding all these seats, this pair has been declared.
One is declared to be Siddhāsana and the second Kamalāsana.
Having firmly placed the feet so that the base of one foot is joined to the root of the yoni, and having made the body even with the heart centered, one should place the other foot upon the penis.
Standing like a pillar with the senses restrained, gazing at the space between the eyebrows with an unwavering vision—
this is called Siddhāsana, which effects the breaking open of the door to liberation.
Thus ends the Siddhāsana. || 1 ||
Having firmly placed the right foot upon the left thigh and likewise the left foot upon the right thigh according to the prescribed method, and holding [the body] steady with both hands,
one should place the thumbs at the heart and gaze at the tip of the nose; this destroys the afflictions of disease and physical disorders.
This is declared to be the lotus posture (padmāsana).
There is something else here as well.
Having placed the right foot upon the left thigh and likewise the left foot upon the other thigh,
holding them firmly with both hands,
and placing the two big toes at the heart, one should gaze at the tip of the nose; this [posture] brings about the destruction of disease for those who practice self-restraint.
This is declared to be the lotus posture (padmāsana). || 2 ||
Thus is the lotus posture (padmāsana).
These and other such postures are useful only for yoga;
they have no purpose in ritual worship.
In the Matsya-sūkta:
Having purified the pavilion and the sacrificial ground with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya),
one should perform the sprinkling with an arrow and the inspection with the root mantra.
There, one should scatter the ritual offerings (vikirān) over which the sevenfold recitation of the arrow-mantra has been performed.
Thereafter, one should likewise fumigate the interior with sandalwood and agallochum.
Likewise.
One should place the articles of worship on one's right side;
on the left, a well-scented jar filled with water from a sacred bathing place (tīrtha), filtered through a cloth; thereafter, one should avoid using water collected at night.
In the Śāradā [Tantra].
After washing the hands, one should place the vessel behind;
then, one should set up auspicious lamps, brightly blazing with ghee, all around.

One should also set out the vessels for the water for the feet (pādya), the respectful offering (arghya), the water for sipping (ācamana), the honey-mixture (madhuparka), and the subsequent water for sipping (ācamana) at this very moment.
In the Devīpurāṇa:

One should prepare vessels made of gold, silver, copper, clay, stone, or wood— possessing auspicious lines and excellent craftsmanship— for the purpose of offering the *arghya*, food offerings (*naivedya*), worship, and the presentation of oblations (*balidāna*).
In the Śivarahaśya, in the Śeṣārdha.
May all my vessels be made of gold;
by offering the *arghya* with silver, one obtains long life, sovereignty, and sons;
through a copper vessel, good fortune; and when it is made of clay, righteousness.
But if nothing else is available, it may be made of clay (māheya), provided it is fashioned by one's own hand;
"māheya" means earthen.
Then one should place the seat and the arghya-vessel;

in all cases, these should be made of gold, copper, or at least another [metal], provided it is of superior quality. One must show great care regarding the vessels, for the vessels themselves are the primary object of reverence.
Indeed, for the purpose of performing the bali-homa rite, success is achieved even without a ritual seat (pīṭha).
A vessel of thirty-six finger-breadths (aṅgulas) is proclaimed as the best;
the middle-sized is three parts less than that, and the smallest is twelve finger-breadths.

In some readings, it is stated that "the medium [size] is twenty-four finger-breadths and the smallest is twelve finger-breadths. Another reading states: "A wise person should not have a vessel made that is deficient by eight finger-breadths."
In the absence of all [suitable vessels], one should discard that vessel from which water leaks;
that from which water does not leak is fit for ritual action, as it is perceived to be capable of performing its function.
Furthermore, the forms of the apertures of the navel are shaped like lotuses (*puṇḍarīka*).
One should prepare vessels made from conch shells, mother-of-pearl, or wood.
Now, the characteristics of the vessel for water for the feet (*pādya*),
according to the *Vaikhānasa* treatise.
The vessel for receiving the water used for washing the feet is marvelous;
it may be made of iron, or born from a lotus, or of gold, silver, or even copper,
provided it has a stand for the sake of Vāyu— so say the virtuous.
In the Siddhāntaśekhara.
One should make the width six finger-breadths and the height four finger-breadths;
the lip should be one finger-breadth, and the nose four finger-breadths.
At the back, it should be joined with a foot [of the base] and measure four finger-breadths in length.
This is known as the vessel for foot-water (pādyapātra), used in the worship of all the gods.
Thus ends the description of the characteristics of the vessel for water for the feet.
Now follows the description of the vessel for pouring the water for the feet (pādya).
In that very same [text].
One should fashion a vessel in the shape of a shallow bowl with a height of eight finger-breadths, a width of sixteen finger-breadths,
and a rim of one finger-breadth;
for both vessels, one should make the rounded rims at the edges equal.
On its back, it is joined with a foot, well-expanded by six finger-breadths;
the height of the foot is four mātrās; this is proclaimed as the characteristic of the vessel for pouring the *pādya* (water for the feet).
Thus ends the description of the vessel for the offering of *pādya*.
Now follows the definition of the vessel for the arghya offering.
In the Siddhāntaśekhara.

I shall describe the characteristics of the *arghya* offering according to the distinctions of substances such as *pala* and so forth: the general *arghya*, the *tirodhāmya* [concealing], and the *viśeṣārghya* [special] which is turned away from the face. There are four *arghya* vessels, along with gold, *dūrvā* grass, and unbroken grains (*akṣata*).
Silver [vessels] should be known as inferior; those made from copper, mother-of-pearl, stone, wood, metal, or clay are even lower than that.
An excellent [vessel] is made with twenty palas, while a middling one is made with ten palas.
One should prepare five palas as the minimum for the water for rinsing the mouth (ācamana) and the water for washing the feet (pādya).
These [grains] should have four joints, or eight joints protruding;
they should be marked with auspicious signs on their backs, or otherwise fashioned into specific shapes.
One should fashion four square vessels for the *arghya* offering.
One should deposit camphor, saffron, *dūrvā* grass, white mustard seeds, bilva leaves, barley, *darbha*, and *kuśa* grass into the general *arghya*.
One should cast these seven substances— sesame flowers, white mustard, *darbha* grass, *dūrvā* grass, barley, and unbroken rice— having first concealed them;
likewise, sesame, rice, white mustard, *dūrvā* grass, mung beans, and barley as well.
And when offering the *arghya* with one's face turned away, one should perform the purification of the materials.
Thus ends the description of the characteristics of the arghya vessel.
Now, the characteristics of the vessel for sipping water (ācamana) are described in the Vaikhānasa text.
Having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), one should prepare an excellent vessel for holding water, made of iron,
shaped like the pericarp of a lotus, and wonderful to behold.
It should be made of gold, thick, or else made of silver, which is purifying.
*Kārttasvara* means gold.
The same applies even to the finest iron.
Since all that is metallic is iron by its very nature, it refers to silver or copper.
In the Siddhāntaśekhara.
The middle of the belly should be twelve finger-breadths in width and circular;
one should make the edge of its petals six finger-breadths, and likewise the lip one finger-breadth.

Its height should be three *mātrās*, and on its sides the width should be four finger-breadths (*aṅgulas*). The opening at the front should be equal to the little finger, while below it it should be double that size.
At the back, one should make it a quarter [of the front], and its thickness should then be two finger-breadths.
The vessel for the purpose of sipping water should have a width of six finger-breadths.
Thus ends the description of the characteristics of the vessel for sipping water (ācamana).
Now, the characteristics of the incense bowl.
In the *Siddhāntaśekhara*.
"The vessel for the fragrance (gandhapātra) shall be like the vessel for the respectful offering (arghyapātra).
Here, by the phrase "like the arghya-vessel," there is an extension of the characteristics of a complete arghya-vessel.
The meaning is that the fragrance-vessel must be prepared in exactly the same manner as the arghya-vessel is made.
Thus ends the description of the characteristics of the incense bowl.
Now, the characteristics of the incense burner are described in the Vaikhānasa treatise.
The incense burner, fashioned from gold or other precious materials, should be lotus-shaped;
its height above the base should be four finger-breadths,
and its lid should have many perforations and be symmetrical to it.
Hollow means a cavity.
*Pidhāna* means covering;
[as stated] in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*.

I shall describe the procedure for the incense burner (*dhūpapātra*); the materials, such as the *pala* weight, are as before. The width of the vessel should be [measured] in finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) by four, five, six, or seven;
"six" refers to the *rasas*, and "seven" refers to the *aśvas*.
The length [of the bowl] should be equal to its height; the lip is considered to extend to half [the height].
The bowl should be shaped like a lotus all around, and the lower neck (gala) should be two finger-breadths [in width].
The base (pāda) should have a height of one finger-breadth and a width of two finger-breadths.
It should have six joints and a long navel, rising two finger-breadths high;
it is considered to be joined with the height of the previous part, circular like a wheel or a bow,
and its lid should be two finger-breadths high and provided with various apertures.
One should fashion it with a single aperture and the shape of a water-pot at the top.
Thus ends the description of the characteristics of the incense burner.
In the Vaikhānasa treatise:
That lamp-vessel has a stalk in its center, radiant like a white water-lily (kumuda),
and is provided with a hundred wicks, or eight, or twenty-one,
or eight, or two, or ten.
Or, the best of those who possess the marks [of initiation] should arrange five [offerings] according to his capacity,
as stated in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*.

I shall describe the procedure for the lamp-vessel; the substances, such as the *pala* measure and so forth, are like those for the *arghya*. It is said that it should be made with a base of *nāgala* and so on, just like the incense-vessel. It may have one petal, four petals, six petals, or eight petals.
In that [mandala], there should be a single petal in the center, shaped like a hollowed-out leaf of the *aśvattha* tree;
in the four directions, there should be four petals with a hollow pericarp in the middle. Likewise, the six-petaled [lotus] is remembered as being provided with secondary petals.
Thus ends the description of the characteristics of the lamp-vessel.
Now follows the description of the circle of lamps.
In the Siddhāntaśekhara.
A garland of lamps made of wood, iron, or copper is considered inferior;
those made of gold or silver are respectively middling and superior.
One should fashion it with a handle like a door-frame, having the shape of a flame upon the back of the *liṅga*.
In another place, away from the door, one should arrange a very beautiful row of lamps.
Having made the shoulder [of the frame] four finger-breadths long and one finger-breadth wide, one should thus fashion it and fix it in the middle of the staff as a single division.
One should make the distance between one pillar and the next equal to the size of a *bhūtamātra*;
this is called a "garland of lamps" (*dīpamālā*) for the worship of all the gods and others.
Thus ends the description of the characteristics of the garland of lamps.
Now follows the characteristics of the lamp-stand.
In the Siddhāntaśekhara.
One should construct the superior and other types [of lamp-stands] from copper, brass, and so forth;
beginning at twelve finger-breadths and increasing by two finger-breadths each time,
the height of the lamp-stand base is declared to be eighteen finger-breadths.
At the base of the oil-vessel, a swelling (unnāha) equal in length [to the vessel] is prescribed;
the oil-vessel itself is also equal to that, being one-third of the measure of the foot-boat (pādanāva).
Above that, one should fashion a bud-like ornament (mukula), provided with a spout (prādika) and other features.
Adorned with various ornaments and garlands made of various vessels,
it is called a lamp-stand (*dīpādhāra*). Those lamps, made of metal, should be of various colors, beautiful, and four cubits in measure.
[One should prepare] vessels made of copper or silver, measuring three cubits, one cubit, or two cubits according to one's strength,
using pairs of those [vessels] as oil-drippers.
Thus ends the description of the characteristics of the lamp-stand.
In the Vaikhānasa scripture.
The vessel for the rite of lustration (nīrājana) is fashioned from gold, shaped like Mount Meru,
spacious, filled with ghee at its center, and enchanting.
In the *Siddhāntaśekhara*.
Indeed, [the vessel] made of gold, silver, copper, and so forth is classified as superior and so on;
it is best when thirty-six finger-breadths in width, middling at thirty finger-breadths,
and inferior at twenty-four finger-breadths, respectively.
One should fashion the pericarp (karṇikā) in the center using one part out of the eleven parts [of the lotus];
its height should be equal to the measurement of the pericarp.
One should construct a pedestal (pīṭhikā) all around, extending by two barley-corns in width.
Here, one should fashion eight petals around it, equal in height to that [central part],
and likewise an eightfold set of directions (spokes) with half that measurement all around.
One should make the lip one finger-breadth wide, while the pericarp is raised in height.
It is similar to the full moon in its radiance, and the lamp-stand is like a water-pot.
With four measures of height and two finger-breadths in width,
one should fashion two apertures there, centered within the pericarp and level with it.
Thus ends the description of the characteristics of the vessel for the lustration rite (nīrājana).
Now, the characteristics of the bell.
In the Vaikhānasa text:
"The bell, consisting of the Word-Brahman (Śabdabrahman), should be one cubit in height;
it should have the form of the cosmic egg (Brahmāṇḍa) and be considered as having the nature of the gods and other beings."
Then, [the structure] should have a height and width of one tāla with its face turned downwards;
furthermore, four bells of various kinds are placed in each direction.
That bell is proclaimed to be marked with a wheel or marked with a lotus.
The bell should be of this kind, or according to one's own preference;
thus it is stated in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*.
The bell should be five finger-breadths in height and likewise endowed with that same width;
the circumference of the bell is declared to be half its width.
The handle should be one finger-breadth in length, and it is considered to be equal in circumference to its length.
