One should have a bull, a trident, or a lotus fashioned at the top of the staff;
it should be made of pure bell-metal, as the characteristics of the bell have been described.
Thus ends the description of the characteristics of the bell.
Now, the characteristics of the vessel for the food offering (naivedya).
In the Vīramitrodaya.
I shall describe the vessel for the food offering for the great-souled Keśava:
it may be made of gold, silver, copper, bell-metal, or even clay;
a vessel of palāśa wood is middling, while a vessel of plakṣa wood is exceedingly dear to Viṣṇu.
One should prepare vessels according to the measurements of the sacrificial materials.
In the Siddhāntaśekhara.
One should prepare the vessel for the deity’s food offering (naivedya) from gold, silver, or copper— starting with the most excellent quality— or from pure bell-metal;
beginning with a single vessel and proceeding in order up to seven.
One should prepare offering vessels for those occasions where the offerings are of inferior quality and the like.
A vessel weighing one hundred palas is considered excellent; half of that is regarded as middling;
and half of that again is known as the lowest—the number of vessels is thus proclaimed.
The vessel should be made ninefold, with dimensions of thirty-six finger-breadths;
the bases, measuring half a finger-breadth each, increase sequentially by eight finger-breadths.
Thus, the width of the nine vessels has been described in order.
The three superior [vessels] should be at the front, the three intermediate ones in the middle,
and again the three inferior ones at the bottom, according to the sequence of the sthālikās.
Thus ends the description of the characteristics of the vessel for the food offering (naivedya).
Now follows the characteristics of the water-vessel.
In the Vaiśvānara-saṃhitā.

The water vessel should be made of gold, silver, or even copper; it may be as long as a tree branch, perfectly circular, or simply elongated. It should be auspicious, with an internal capacity sufficient to hold a *prastha* measure of water.
Thus ends the description of the characteristics of a water vessel.
Now follows the characteristics of the betel-box.
In the Vaikhānasa treatise:
One should fashion a creeper of passion (*rāgalatikā*) complete with stalks and leaves;
it should be made one *aratni* in width, or as large as possible according to one's means.
Thus ends the description of the characteristics of the betel-box (*tāmbūlapātra*).

Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Sprouts," within the third section on Ritual Matters (*arthakāṇḍa*) of the *Prāṇatoṣiṇī*, concerning the placement of vessels for perfumes and other offerings.
(p. 380) [As stated] in the *Śāradā*.
Having joined his palms in reverence and bowed to the Guru and Gaṇeśāna on his left and right sides, he should then perform the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi).
Having performed the purification of the hands, the preceptor should then perform three claps with the hand;
then, with the Astra-mantra, he should perform the binding of the directions (digbandha) from top to bottom.
By that means, he should provide protection on all sides with the blazing splendor.
In the fourth chapter.
One should unite the self with the Supreme Self by means of the path of the *suṣumṇā*,
being composed through the method joined with yoga and the *cin-mantra*.
One should [unite] the self residing in the heart-lotus, together with the *kuṇḍalinī*, by means of the path of the *suṣumṇā* according to the method joined with yoga.
The syntactical connection is that one should unite [the self] with the Supreme Self by means of the *cinmantra*, that is, the mantra *haṃsa*. She whose path is the *suṣumnā* is [described] as such;
however, the Self resides in the heart-lotus.

This is to be understood from the statement cited by Rāghavabhaṭṭa: "The soul should be meditated upon by the wise as being at the tip of the *tāra* (the syllable Om), within the heart-lotus produced at the *brahmarandhra*, which has knowledge for its stalk.
This is the meaning of the phrase "by the method joined with yoga."
Having raised the Kuṇḍalinī by means of the syllable *Haṃ* according to the path taught by the Guru, and having visualized her as having reached the heart-lotus,
one should then grasp the life-force (*jīva*) at its mouth and visualize it as having reached the thousand-petalled lotus.
By means of that *Vyohaṃsa* mantra, [one reaches] the Supreme, which resides beyond the twelve-syllabled [mantra].
By virtue of this statement being syntactically unified with the preceding, the *cinmantra* is "haṃsa," as stated in the *Śāradā*.

One should also contemplate the principles (tattvas) of all beings as being dissolved by way of their seed-state within the Supreme Self, the cause of all beings; the meaning is that one should contemplate the principles dissolved in the form of seeds within the Supreme Self, the cause of all beings, in reverse order.
"From the transposition" means with respect to the order of emanation (*sṛṣṭikrama*).
By the word "also," it is meant that the phonemes (*varṇa*) are also [included].
This has been stated in the *Piṅgalāmata*:
Having thus formed the mental resolve, one should then withdraw the phonemes from their positions of placement in reverse order: the *kṣa* and *la* into the *ha*;
the *ha*, *la*, and *ya* into the *sa*; and the *sa*, *la*, and *ya* into the *ya*.
Having thus diligently produced an infinite dissolution in this sequence,
one should join the letter 'A' to the Sahasrāra at the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra).
In the *Śāradā*: (p. 381)
Then, one should dry up the body with the wind through the wind-seed (the letter *ya*);
with that very fire-seed (*ra*), one should burn the entire body;
and with the wind-seed *ya*, by means of the wind arising from it.

By means of the fire-seed *repha* (the letter *ra*), and by the fire arising from that very fire-seed, one should burn "all"— meaning the entire body together with the personification of sin (*pāpapuruṣa*).
Because this is a rule containing a qualification (*saviśeṣaṇavidhi*), it does not imply the destruction of the current physical body.
The reason for this is the maxim: "When injunctions and prohibitions pertain to a qualified subject, they apply to the qualification provided there is sublation of the qualified subject";
sublation, moreover, is the impossibility of logical connection (*anvayānupapatti*).
When there is an impossibility of syntactic connection (anvayānupapatti) regarding the meaning that constitutes the intended purport (tātparya),
injunctions and prohibitions apply to the qualified [meaning] where the purport lies in the qualified, and not to the qualificand alone;
as Bhartṛhari has stated:
In common worldly usage as well, when one says "make a blue cloth," two things are observed:
in some cases it is an injunction regarding the qualified [cloth] possessing the quality of blueness, and in other cases it is an injunction regarding the quality of blueness alone.
Therefore, in the Guptasādhanatantra, in the sixth chapter:

"O Mahādeva! If one should destroy the body during the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi), in what place would creation reside, and where would one accumulate the nectar?"—this is the answer to the Goddess's question of doubt.
Mahādeva said:
The personification of sin (pāpapuruṣa), with the luster of lampblack, resides in the left side of the belly;
for the purpose of destroying him, O Maheśānī,
this great Liṅga-body has been manifested— of this there is no doubt.
The sinful body shall be burnt away, yet it shall not destroy one's own true self.
Thus spoke Śiva.
The meditation on the personification of sin (pāpapuruṣa), however, is maintained by Rāghavabhaṭṭa.
It has the murder of a Brahmin as its head, the theft of gold as its two arms,
the drinking of liquor joined with its heart, and the violation of the Guru’s bed as its two hips;
it has association with such sinners as its pair of feet, and all manner of minor sins as its limbs and sub-limbs.

One should visualize the Sin, black in color and facing downwards, upon the left side of the belly; it has hair like that of a goat, red beard and eyes, carries a sword and a shield, and is the size of a thumb.
In the Śāradā [Tantra].
Then, separating the impurities with the nectar of the water of immortality,
one should cause it to flood the body from the soles of the feet to the crown of the head.
Alternatively, the separation of the impurities— which are of the nature of the sinful person— into ashes is also accomplished by means of the *vāyu* seed-syllable (*yaṃ*).
And likewise, in the Gaṇeśavimarṣiṇī:
Then, having scattered that entire heap of ashes with the wind produced from the seed-syllable *vāyu* (yaṃ),
one should subsequently flood one's own body with the nectar-seed-syllable (*amṛtabīja*).
By "with nectar" is meant by this nectar-seed-syllable, namely *vam*.

The syntactical connection is as follows: having caused the body, from the soles of the feet to the crown of the head, to be reached by the nectar arising from that [ambrosia], one should flood it with the ambrosial water.
In the Śāradā [Tantra]:
Then, one should cause the principles (tattvas) dissolved within the self to reach their own respective places;
one should bring the self to the lotus of the heart of the Supreme Self.
Thereafter, one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) and other rites with the mantra of the Lord Haṃsa.
The syntactical connection is as follows: from the presence of the Supreme Self, one should bring the self into the lotus of the heart by means of the mantra of the deity Haṃsa.
The Supreme Self is the deity of the *haṃsa* seed-syllable because it is the object of worship; this is done by means of its mantra, "so 'ham" (that am I).
This has been stated in the *Vasiṣṭhasaṃhitā*:

The mantra-practitioner, having thus meditated with the mantra upon her who has been realized as the perfection at the end of the *nāda*, should place the life-force (*jīva*) from the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*) into the heart.
In this regard, the procedure is written down according to the teacher’s instruction:

having made the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*) beginning with "Oṃ, today... and so forth, "I shall perform the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) and other rites for the sake of attaining the qualification for the worship of the Śrīdevī," one [visualizes] [the energy] rising from the *mūlādhāra*, brilliant with the luster of a thousand flashes of lightning, in the form of a lotus fiber, along the path of the *suṣumṇā*.

Having visualized Kuṇḍalinī situated in the heart-lotus, one should take the individual soul (jīva) from the heart-lotus in the form of a lamp-flame and place it at the mouth; then, having visualized the twelve-syllabled lotus located within the thousand-petaled lotus, one should unite the individual soul with the Supreme Self there by means of the Haṃsa-mantra.
Then, having visualized the square earth-maṇḍala from the feet up to the knees,

and having recollected therein the action of walking with the feet, the destination, the smelling of odors, the earth, the Brahmā principle, and the *samāna* breath, one should recite this mantra: *oṃ hlīṃ brahmaṇe pṛthivyadhipataye nivṛttikalātmane huṃ phaṭ svāhā*.
One should dissolve those [elements] into the waters through the door of Kuṇḍalinī; thus, one should withdraw them into the locus of water.

Having meditated upon the white water-maṇḍala, shaped like a half-moon, extending from the knees up to the navel, one should establish Viṣṇu—the tongue that tastes the rasa to be grasped by the hand—therein, with the mantra for the wind: *oṃ hlīṃ viṣṇave jalādhipataye*.

Having uttered this mantra, "Pratiṣṭhā-kalātmane hūṃ phaṭ svāhā," one should dissolve all those [elements] into the fire through the door of Kuṇḍalinī, thinking, "I dissolve them in the fire," and thus withdraw them into the locus of the fire.
Then, having visualized the triangular fire-maṇḍala, red in color, extending from the navel to the heart, therein—

Having recollected the anus as the Visarga-form, the eyes as fire, Rudra as knowledge (vidyā), and Vyāna as wind, one should recite this mantra: "Oṃ huṃ, to Rudra, lord of fire, whose essence is the kalā of knowledge, huṃ phaṭ svāhā.
Then, thinking, "I dissolve all of these into the wind through the door of Kuṇḍalinī," one should withdraw them into the locus of the wind.
Then, having visualized from the heart up to the eyebrows a black circular wind-maṇḍala marked with six dots,

and having recollected therein the locus of water, its object, touch, the tangible, the quality of air, tranquility, and the downward breath (*apāna*), [one recites] this: *oṃ hauṃ īśānāya vāyvadhipataye śāntikalātmane huṃ phaṭ svāhā*.
Having recited the mantra, one should dissolve all those [elements] into the space through the door of Kuṇḍalinī, thinking "I dissolve them," and thus withdraw them into the locus of space.
Then, one should visualize the sphere of space as a white circle extending from the middle of the eyebrows up to the Brahma-randhra.

There, having recollected speech, face, the unspeakable, sound, the ear, space, Sadāśiva, Śāntyatīta, and the vital breath (prāṇa), one should recite this mantra: "Oṃ hauṃ, to Sadāśiva, the lord of space, whose self is the Śāntyatīta kalā, huṃ phaṭ svāhā. Then, thinking "I dissolve all these into the ego (ahaṅkāra) through the door of the Kulakuṇḍalinī," [one dissolves them] into the ego.

Having dissolved the principle of Mahat (mahattattva) into Prakṛti— which is experienced as the Hṛllekhā and whose nature is the Śabdabrahman known as Mātṛkā— one should dissolve that [Prakṛti] into the Supreme Brahman, whose essential nature is eternally pure, thinking, "I dissolve [it]. One should thus perform the dissolution.
This has been stated in the *Mantratantraprakāśa*:
One should dissolve the earth, which is conjoined with smell and the other [objects] as well as the nose, into water;
one should dissolve water, together with taste and the other [objects] as well as the tongue, into fire;
one should dissolve fire, together with form and the other [objects] as well as the eye, into air.
The wise man should dissolve the wind, which possesses touch and other qualities, into the Lord (Īśvara);
he should dissolve the ether, together with sound, into the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra);
and he should dissolve that great principle into the Unmanifest (avyakta), the supreme cause of all powers.
That which is the supreme state of Viṣṇu, whose nature is existence, consciousness, and bliss.

One should contemplate that everything, beginning with the earth, is dissolved therein in due order. Then, the internal controller of the body is the seer (ṛṣi), Truth is the deity, Nature-and-Spirit (prakṛti-puruṣa) is the meter, and purification is the application (viniyoga).

Having said this, one should contemplate the personified sin (pāpapuruṣa) in its released form within the left side of the abdomen. [One should recite: "The seer of the seed-syllable *yaṃ* (the wind-seed) is Kiṣkindha; the deity is Vāyu; the meter is Jagatī; its application is for the purification of the body and the personified sin.
Having said this, one should contemplate *yaṃ* at the base of the navel within a mandala marked by two dots (*bindu*).

Having meditated upon that seed-syllable of wind (*vāyubīja*) as smoky-colored, joined with a flickering banner, accompanied by the sound "dhūṃ dhūṃ," the dryer of all things, and having Haṃsa as its presiding deity, one should recite that seed-syllable sixteen times through the practice of inhalation (*pūraka*),
and visualize the Person of Sin (*pāpapuruṣa*) residing within one's own body as being purified by the wind arising from that seed-syllable.

Then, having stated: "The seed-syllable *ram* has Kaśyapa as its seer (*ṛṣi*), Agni as its deity (*devatā*), Triṣṭubh as its meter (*chandaḥ*), and its application (*viniyoga*) is for burning"— and having meditated upon a red triangular fire-mandala in the heart, conjoined with the *vidyā-kalā* and having Rudra as its presiding deity—
one should repeat that seed-syllable sixty-four times through the ritual practice and contemplate it as being reduced to ashes by the fire arising from that seed-syllable.

Then, by means of the exhalation (*recaka*) consisting of thirty-two measures (*mātrā*), one should rotate the previously mentioned wind-seed-syllable (*vāyu-bīja*) and exhale the ashes of the personification of sin (*pāpapuruṣa*).

Then, for the Varuṇa-seed-syllable *vaṃ*: Hiraṇyagarbha is the seer (*ṛṣi*), Haṃsa is the deity (*devatā*), Triṣṭubh is the meter (*chandaḥ*), and its application (*viniyoga*) is in the act of flooding (*plāvana*).
Having said this:
"The Varuna mandala on the head is white, resembling the crescent moon;
it has two white lotuses and bestows the gesture of fearlessness, with Varuna as its presiding deity."
Having meditated thus, one should visualize the ashes of that body becoming a solid mass through the nectar flowing from the seed-syllable produced therefrom.
Then, having recited: "The seer of the earth-seed *laṃ* is Brahmā, the deity is Indra, the meter is Gāyatrī; its application is for the purpose of solidification."

In the foundational mandala, one should meditate as before in the mind upon the earth mandala, marked with a vajra, four-cornered, firm, yellow in color, presided over by Indra, and joined with the seed-syllable *laṃ*.
Having meditated thus, one should contemplate the body as firm through the solidity arising from that seed-syllable.

Then, having stated: "For the seed-syllable *haṃ* of space, Brahmā is the seer (*ṛṣi*), space is the deity (*devatā*), the Paṅkti meter is the meter (*chandas*), and its application (*viniyoga*) is in the act of expansion."
The sphere of space is circular and non-flaming at the end of the twelve;
it is joined with the *kalā* beyond tranquility (*śāntyatītā*). Having meditated thus upon the deity of space, one should contemplate space by means of the space arisen from that [meditation].
In the same way, the transformation into air occurs by means of the seed-syllable *haṃ*.
Having thus contemplated one's own body, one should cause the principles (*tattvas*) to reach their respective locations through the process of emanation from the Supreme Self.
Thereafter, by means of the mantra "So 'ham," one should bring the individual soul (jīva) from the presence of the Supreme Self into the heart-lotus; this is the summary.
And this purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) is essential.
A worship performed by one devoid of the five purities is like a malevolent spell;
it yields a contrary result, just as worship offered without devotion does. Indeed, Nirṛti destroys the fruit of rituals that are deficient in their prescribed procedure.
And by the command of Śaṅkara, he exercises sovereignty over the night-stalkers.
Thus it is stated in the Śaiva Āgamas; and elsewhere as well:
"The purification of the elements which constitute the cause of the body..."
This purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) is considered to be a constituent part [of the ritual] due to its connection with Brahman.
Without the purification of the elements, all rites— such as recitation, fire-offerings, and worship—
will be fruitless, even if performed in every possible manner.
Thus, in the fifteenth chapter of the Matsyasūkta.
Having bowed to the Guru and Gaṇeśāna, one should perform the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi).
O Goddess, having grasped the syllable *yaṃ* with both hands through the union of the index finger and the thumb, and having smelled it while reciting "O *yaṃ*, forgive me!", one should cast it away.
And in the fifth chapter of the Mahānirvāṇatantra.
Placing his two hands palms-upward upon his own lap,
the best of practitioners should fix his mind on the root *huṃ* syllable;
then, having raised the Śaiva Kuṇḍalinī together with the Earth element by means of the *haṃsa* mantra, he should proceed.
Having brought [the self] into its own foundation (svādhiṣṭhāna), one should then unite it with the principle (tattva).
One should dissolve the earth element, which is conjoined with the sense of smell and the other [objects of smell], into water;
and the water, together with taste and the tongue, one should cause to melt into fire.
Having dissolved form and the other [objects] along with the eye into fire, and that [fire] into wind;
one should dissolve touch and the others, together with the skin, into wind, and that [wind] into space.
One should cause space, along with sound, to pass into the ego-principle (ahaṅkāra), and that [ego-principle] into the Great Principle (mahat) as well.

One should dissolve the principle of Mahat into Prakṛti, and that Prakṛti into Brahman. Having thus dissolved them, the wise man should contemplate within his left side a Puruṣa who is black in color, with red beard and eyes.
One should visualize [the being] holding a sword and shield, wrathful, the size of a thumb,
the very embodiment of all sins, and always remaining with its face turned downwards.
Then, one should contemplate the seed-syllable *yaṃ*, smoke-colored, within the left nostril.
Having reflected thus, he should fill the breath with sixteen *mātrās*;
by that, the foremost of practitioners should purify the body consisting of sin.
Having meditated on the syllable *raṃ*, red in color, at the navel, [he should burn it] with the fire born from it.
One should burn the sinful body with sixty-four *kumbhakas*,
having meditated upon the white-colored seed-syllable of Varuṇa at the forehead;
then, with thirty-two *recakas*, one should flood it with the water of nectar.
Having bathed [the body] from the feet up to the head,
one should thereafter contemplate the newly arisen body as consisting of the deity.
While contemplating the yellow-colored seed-syllable of earth (laṃ) at the *mūlādhāra*, [one should perform the purification].
With that divine vision, one should stabilize one's own body.
Placing the hand upon the heart while uttering *āṃ hrīṃ kroṃ haṃ saḥ*,
one should establish the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) of the Goddess within that body by means of the mantra *so'ham*.
Having thus performed the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi), one should be solely intent on the state of being the Goddess.
Also in the fourth chapter of the Nīlatantra:
O sinless one, listen attentively as I shall now describe the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi).
Having caused the apāna wind to move upward and having filled [the body] with divine principles,
one should, by means of the Haṃsa-mantra, [awaken] the supreme Kuṇḍalinī power from the foundation (ādhāra).

Having sequentially pierced through the cakras, one should then lead the individual soul (jīvātman) from the lotus to the thousand-spoked [cakra] and unite it with the Supreme Brahman. One should likewise [dissolve] the ten senses, the one [mind], the great principles (mahattattva), and their qualities.
One purifies the mind and the principles that constitute the body of primordial nature (*prakṛti*).
One should then join the twenty-four principles in the form of seeds.
Thereafter, one should contemplate them within the empty body on the left side.

Then, one should meditate within the intermediate space upon the Self, which is stainless, devoid of qualities, pure, and identical with Tāriṇī; from the syllable ĀḤ, a red lotus [should arise], and further above that,
one should meditate on a white lotus from the syllable ṬĀṂ.

Furthermore, one should meditate upon the syllable *huṃ*, resembling the color of a dark blue sapphire, above that. Then, within the seed-syllable *huṃ*, one should meditate upon a knife adorned with the seed-syllable,
and visualize oneself as being enveloped by that knife and consisting of the essence of Tāriṇī.
Likewise:
for subjugation and the like, one should visualize him as red in color; for attraction, as having a yellow form;
for killing and expulsion, as smoky or black, according to the specific requirement of each case.
One should meditate upon one's own self as being thus constituted and identical with Tāriṇī.
In the second chapter of the Viśvasāra-tantra.
One should fill [the breath] with the sixteenth vowel *yaṃ*, which is the seed-syllable of Vāyu;
and with that same syllable repeated sixty-four times, one should purify the body of sins.
Then, according to the prescribed method, one should exhale through the Piṅgalā channel using that same seed-syllable.
One should slowly draw in the ash through the path of the breath for thirty-two measures;
having done this three times, it is known as the purification of the elements.
Then the preceptor should fill [the body] in reverse order with the seed-syllable of fire (RAṂ).
With sixteen [breaths] and sixty-four [repetitions], one should perform the filling (kumbhaka) and then the exhaling (recaka).
Burning (dahana) is proclaimed to consist of thirty-two measures (mātrās).
Then, having performed the recitation fourfold, one should recite that [specific] syllable in sequence.
Drying, burning, and floating have been proclaimed [as the functions of the elements].
Kiṣkindha, Kaśyapa, and thereafter Hiraṇyagarbha—these are declared to be the sages of the seeds; listen, O lotus-eyed one!
Then the best of teachers should perform breath control (prāṇāyāma) in due order;
he should contemplate his chosen deity within the great thousand-petaled lotus,
according to the meditation and the path of the guru as it has been described.
Then, having withdrawn the elements— along with their presiding deities, qualities, and ritual prescriptions,

as well as all the powers— according to the sequence of the phonemes in reverse order, [one should dissolve them] together with the constituent principles (tattvas) and the bodily constituents (dhātus).
Having meditated upon the Mūlādhāra and the Sahasrāra through the sequential yoga of the six cakras,
and then having meditated upon them in reverse order up to the Sahasrāra,
one should move the seed-syllable within the Oṃ-mantra according to the sequential yoga of the six cakras.
Having contemplated oneness in that place, one should practice the single mantra.
Having uttered the "So 'ham" mantra, one should meditate upon the subtle Brahman.
At that very moment, the body becomes stainless, free from dualities, and devoid of possessions.
There, one should contemplate non-duality with the mind through the application of fire,

following the sequence of the garland of letters from *a* to *kṣa*. One should contemplate by means of breath control— through inhalation (*pūraka*), retention (*kumbhaka*), and exhalation (*recaka*).
Having reflected thus upon those syllables, one should then meditate upon the Moon-mantra (candramantra):
the letter ending in *ṭ* (ṭa), joined with the nasal drop (*bindu*) and adorned with the half-moon (*ardhacandra*).
The wise practitioner should mentally recite this mantra four times while employing the vital air (*vāyu*).
O Goddess! One should then recite the seed-syllable of Indra (the letter *I*), followed by the seed-syllable of reality (*Tattva-bīja*).
Having removed [the previous state] according to the ritual procedure, one should again sustain it with a stream of nectar.
Thereafter, O Goddess! one should contemplate that which was previously described, consisting of the Mātṛkās.
Then, one should contemplate the body in its forward order (anuloma) as being conjoined with all that is beginningless, accompanied by its own power,
endowed with the fifty letters, and possessed of the great elements,
consisting of the nature of the five elements.

Antaryāmī is the seer (ṛṣi) of that breath-control (prāṇāyāma), and its deity is [the same]. Placing his right hand upon his chest, the best of practitioners [should perform it] with the previously mentioned Prāṇa-mantra, accompanied by its seer and meter.
The invocation of that vital breath (prāṇa) is declared to be performed with the *haṃsa* mantra.

One should extract this mantra, ending with the wife of Fire (*svāhā*), as follows: "May [the elements], together with the constituents (*dhātu*) and the principles (*tattva*), come here and remain for a long time in happiness."
Having mentally contemplated the body as being composed of the fifty letters from 'a' to 'kṣa', a person then becomes a god.
Having performed three rounds of breath control (prāṇāyāma), one should project strength into the vital breaths (prāṇas).

Having meditated upon the sequence from the letter *a* to the letter *kṣa* through the processes of inhalation (*pūraka*), retention (*kumbhaka*), and exhalation (*recaka*), both in reverse and direct order, and having thus drawn in the vital breath (*prāṇa*),
the practitioner of mantra becomes instantly stainless and is directly Sadāśiva himself.
One should project the seed-syllable into the body using the Nṛsiṃha mantra itself.
Then, having reached the *mūlādhāra*, one should contemplate the individual soul (*jīvātman*),
which has arisen in the form of *kuṇḍalinī* and possesses a radiance equal to lightning and fire.
Stainless, abiding in the changeless state, and endowed with all perfections—
one should place the Mātṛkā in the form of phonemes within the body at its conclusion;
having meditated upon her with this mantra, one should place her throughout the entire body.
Now, the regulation of breath (prāṇāyāma).
In the seventh chapter of the Dakṣiṇāmūrtti-tantra.

O Goddess of Gods! Having filled the abdomen with the left [nostril] using the root mantra, one should exhale through the right [nostril] after three repetitions by means of retention (kumbhaka). The holding of the nostrils is performed with the little finger, the ring finger, and the thumb.
That should be known as *prāṇāyāma*, excluding the index finger and the middle finger.
The specific details regarding breath control (prāṇāyāma) will be explained later.
Then, one should perform the ritual placements (nyāsa) and other rites as described in the *Dīkṣāpaddhati* and as stated in various *Kalpas* cited in the *Tantrasāra*.
Now follows the determination of the substratum of worship,
as stated in the twelfth chapter of the *Mātṛkābhedatantra*.
In the Śālagrāma stone, in a gem, in a yantra, in an image, in a water-pot, in water, in a book, in the Gaṅgā, in a Śiva-liṅga, and in a flower— therein,
according to the difference in the substratum, there is a specific distinction in the fruit [of worship].

In a Śālagrāma stone one obtains a hundredfold fruit; in a gem, one obtains a fruit equal to that. In a yantra the merit is a hundred-thousandfold, and in an image, O fair-eyed one, it is a hundred-thousandfold.
In a water-pot the merit is single-fold, and in water, O beloved, it is likewise single-fold.
In a manuscript, the fruit is indeed equal to that of a thousand [offerings] at the Gaṅgā;
in a Śiva-liṅga, it is infinite—except for the earthen liṅga (pārthivaliṅga).
O Maheśānī! By worshipping in a flower-mechanism (puṣpayantra), one becomes a possessor of all perfections.
There is even a prohibition against drawing a yantra in the vicinity of a Śālagrāma stone and the like:
"One should not draw an excellent yantra during the worship of a Śālagrāma;
O Maheśānī, while the jewel [the Śālagrāma] is present, one should not draw an excellent yantra."
Having carefully placed a water-pot before the image,
O Supreme Goddess, one should worship the retinue there in that pot;
and one should worship the presiding deities of the yantra at the mouth of the pot.
One should contemplate the jar as the embodiment of all deities;
for this jar, O Supreme Goddess, is indeed the very nature of the celestial tree (Kalpavṛkṣa).
The prohibition against making a mechanical image near a *pratimā* (idol) is also stated in that same source:

"If a practitioner should construct a great mechanical device (*mahāyantra*) at his place of birth, he should not make an image there; however, if he should have a mechanical device made, [he may do so]."
But if, out of delusion, one should perform it, O beloved, one should worship twice; there the worship is twofold, the offering of the bali is twofold,
one should mutter the mantra twofold, and one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) twofold.
Otherwise, worship is fruitless and the offering of bali is fruitless;
since everything indeed becomes fruitless, one should not perform the yantra.
(From the *Guptasādhanatantra*, Chapter Eight).
O Goddess! Worship performed in ordinary water is for the sake of pacifying faults and other evils;
likewise, one should not perform rites such as the worship of the Goddess upon an earthen linga.
O Goddess! From worshipping [the Linga] made of earth, the loss of spiritual perfection (siddhi) arises.
O Maheśānī! If, by chance, there should be a slipping of the clay, one dwells for that many thousands of years in hell amidst pus and blood.
In the most terrible Kumbhīpāka hell, one is cooked together with one's ancestors;
for this very reason, O Maheśānī, one should certainly not worship [the deity] upon an earthen image.
Having carefully brought crystal and other such materials, one should fashion a liṅga with great effort.
Indeed, by worshipping there at that linga, one shall become endowed with all accomplishments.
In another tantra:
Whoever worships Kālikā, Tāriṇī, Tripurā, and Bhuvaneśvarī upon an earthen liṅga attains the supreme goal.
O Supreme Goddess, [this applies] to Tāriṇī, Kālikā, and Sundarī as well.
"O Goddess! By worshipping the earthen [liṅga], one obtains the fruit of the four aims of life.

And thus, the statement spoken in the *Guptasādhana* refers to [the worship of] Kālī and other specific deities, rather than others, according to the maxim of the general and the particular (*sāmānya-viśeṣa-nyāya*).
Although meditation and the like are impossible because the deity is formless, nevertheless, [it is performed] by way of having a form (*sākāratayā*).
Meditation is entirely appropriate for her; however, the reason for its having a formal aspect (sākāratva) has been stated in the seventh chapter of the Muṇḍamālā Tantra.
Śiva said:
Nature is truly devoid of attributes, and I alone am likewise devoid of attributes.
Indeed, when you possess attributes, I am Sadāśiva with attributes.
Truly, the Goddess possesses attributes; truly, Śiva is devoid of attributes.
For the sake of the accomplishment of the lay followers, he is considered to possess qualities as well as to be devoid of qualities.
In the fifth chapter of the Mahānirvāṇatantra.
Meditation is said to be of two kinds, distinguished by the categories of with-form (sārūpa) and formless (arūpa).
That meditation of yours which is formless transcends the reach of speech and mind;
it is unmanifest, all-pervading, and devoid of such qualifications as "this" or "thus."
Accessible to yogis through all their various meditative absorptions, yet difficult for others to reach,
I shall first set forth subtle meditation and then explain gross meditation to you, for the purpose of concentrating the mind and for the swift attainment of one's desired goal.
In the thirteenth chapter (ullāsa).
The Goddess said:
How can the form of Mahākālī— the supreme power of the Great Lord, possessed of great luster,
and who has become subtler than the subtlest— be described?
"Form (rūpa) is the direct [manifestation] of the primordial nature (prakṛti) and its effects, yet it is higher than the highest. O Lord! You ought to sever this doubt of mine specifically."
Thus, immediately after the Goddess’s question, the venerable Sadāśiva spoke.
O beloved! For the sake of the lay devotees, it was previously stated that the form of the Goddess was fashioned according to their qualities and actions.
Thus it has been said.

Just as colors such as white and yellow dissolve into black, so do all beings enter into Kālī, O Daughter of the Mountain! Now, of that power of Time (Kāla-śakti), which is devoid of qualities and formless—
The color of Hitā, who has assumed a form, is described as black;
she is eternal, the very form of time, formless, and of the nature of Śiva.
Because of her immortality, the mark of the moon is depicted upon her forehead.
Since Kālikā perceives the entire world with eyes that are the moon, the sun, and fire,
she is therefore conceived as having three eyes;
and because she devours all beings and chews them with the staff of Time (Kāladaṇḍa).
The entire universe is illumined by her in the form of red garments.
O Śivā! At every moment, she provides protection from calamities for living beings, impels them toward their respective duties, and bestows the boon of fearlessness.
Having pervaded and supported all the worlds produced from *rajas*, He remains established therein;
therefore, O auspicious lady, She is said to be seated upon a seat of red lotuses.
Also in the sixth chapter of the fifth section of the Kulārṇava.
For the benefit of practitioners, a conceptualization of the form of Brahman— which is composed of consciousness, immeasurable, partless, and bodiless— is devised;
[this occurs] upon a linga, a sacrificial mound, fire, water, a yantra, a wall, or a cloth.

O Goddess of the Gods! Men devoted to the ritualistic section (karmakāṇḍa) worship the supreme Śivā—who is formless yet made manifest in form—in these ten locations: the mandala, the sacrificial board, the head, or the heart.
Just as milk produced from all the limbs of a cow flows forth from the openings of her udders,
so does the omnipresent Lord manifest within images and other forms.
This is due both to the aesthetic excellence of the image and, in particular, to the specific nature of the worship offered.
And through the faith of the practitioner, the presence of the deity occurs;
as stated in the second chapter of the *Nāradapañcarātra*.
Nārada said:
Devotion and knowledge for devotees, and the yoga of knowledge for yogis—of these, which path is most excellent? You should tell me that.
The illustrious Mahādeva said:
All yogins meditate upon the eternal form of light;
yet those yogins do not consider it to have a body.
(p. 391) That entire primordial body is devoid of qualities and transcends primordial nature (*prakṛti*).
"How could there be a body born of qualities for that which is devoid of qualities?
Thus has the entire Yoga-śāstra been proclaimed by the knowers of Yoga.
O twice-born one, we Vaiṣṇavas, including Kumāra and others, do not accept that.
All Vaiṣṇavas indeed say that there is no splendor apart from the splendor of the resplendent ones;
Kṛṣṇa is the eternal embodied one, for his splendor truly exists. They declare that the eternal form of Kṛṣṇa is situated within that very splendor.
All yogis meditate upon that splendor preceded by devotion;
through mature devotion and longing, that yogi indeed becomes Vaiṣṇava.
Yogis always meditate on the form within that splendor.
O Nārada, how can there be servitude for servants without a body?
O Nārada, the doctrine of the Vaiṣṇavas is praised above all others;
indeed, there is no knower of wisdom higher than a Vaiṣṇava within the cosmic eggs of the Brahmas.

Thus, the deity’s possession of form being established, one should perform the meditation on the deity as prescribed for one's own specific kalpa or as stated in the *Tantrasāra* and other such works;

having performed mental worship, one should carry out the ritual actions described in the *Tantrasāra*, beginning with the installation of the conch (*śaṅkha-sthāpana*) and ending with the worship of the enclosures (*āvaraṇa-pūjā*).
I shall explain the mental worship (mānasapūjā) hereafter; for now, the specific procedure for the consecration of life-force (prāṇapratiṣṭhā) is being written.
In the twenty-third chapter of the Śāradātilaka.
The ritual procedure for the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* (consecration of the vital breath) mantra is now described,
by which the previously mentioned mantras become endowed with life.
Although there is no need for the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* of mantras because they possess inherent efficacy, nevertheless:

The statement that those [objects] inscribed on diagrams and the like become possessed of life through the rite of *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* means that by means of *prāṇapratiṣṭhā*, everything— including diagrams, prescribed ritual applications, and effigies— is rendered possessed of established life-force (*pratiṣṭhitaprāṇa*).
The noose (pāśa) consists of the syllable *śa* with the hands joined in the gesture of the noose (*puṭā*). Śakti is the syllable *va*. Vāṇī is the syllable *la*, adorned with the bindu.

The seven letters beginning with *ya* possess the kalās. Vyoman is the syllable *ha*, conjoined with the half-moon (*ardhendu*). First is the seed-syllable of the noose, then the seed-syllable of Śakti, then the seed-syllable of the goad (*aṅkuśa*), and by the phrase "Vāṇīyaḥ, adorned with the bindu," [the syllable *la* is indicated].
Regarding the phrase "yaṃ yādyā," by restating the extracted letter *ya*, the seventh [seed-syllable] is "tadyam," which is a distinct seed-syllable (*bīja*).
The previous separate extraction of all seven was for the purpose of indicating that they all possess the nasal bindu (*sabindutā*).
And so it is stated in the passage cited by Rāghavabhaṭṭa:
If, after pronouncing the *śakti* (the letter *s*) following the *manas* (the letter *m*), one recites "the eight-fold quality" (*vasu-varṇa-guṇam*) along with the *haṃsa* (the letter *h*),

then the void (*vyoma*) is the letter *ha* joined with the half-moon (*ardhendu*), making *haṃ*. In some places, however, there is a reading "joined with the moon" (*sa-indu-saṃyutam*), in which case it is *hoṃ*.
At the end of that, there should be the *haṃsa* mantra; then one should utter the word "of such-and-such" (*amuṣya*).

After that, one should say "the vital breaths" (*prāṇāḥ*), and thereafter "here the vital breaths" (*iha prāṇāḥ*). Following that, one should utter the word "of such-and-such," saying "the life-force (*jīva*) of such-and-such is stationed here."

"May all the senses of this person—speech, mind, sight, hearing, and smell—along with the vital breaths, come here and remain happily for a long time; may the wife of Agni [Sarasvatī] likewise remain at the end. This is declared to be the *prāṇa-mantra*.
First, one should employ the word *pratyamuṣya*, followed by the fetters (*pāśa*) and so forth.
This mantra consists of sixty-six syllables;
it is proclaimed by the wise as the *prāṇamantra* for ritual applications.
This is to be applied everywhere else except for the purpose of mere recitation (*japa*).

Therefore, whether it be in oneself or in a doll (*puttalikā*) and so forth, at the time of the installation of the vital breath (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*), one should utter the mantra after joining the word "of such-and-such" (*amuṣya*) with the fetters (*pāśa*) and other elements, and substituting the name of the person to be acted upon (*sādhya*) in the genitive case in place of the word "of such-and-such. Thus one should recite the mantra.
It should be known.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva are declared by those learned in the Tantras to be the sages;
they are spoken of as the Ṛg, Yajus, and Sāman by those proficient in the meters of the Vedas.
My life-breaths, whose nature is consciousness, are said to be the power of the deities.
The heart is said to consist of the letter *ha* preceded by the sky (*viyat*) and the guttural class (*kavarga*), along with the element earth (*bhūta*).
Immediately thereafter, Śiva is said to be represented by the letters at the beginning of the classes and their conjunctions.
That which consists of the letters at the beginning of the eight classes, pertaining to the organs of knowledge (*jñānendriya*), is proclaimed as the crest-lock (*śikhā*).

The armor (*kavaca*) is proclaimed by means of the organs of action (*karmendriya*), beginning with the *ta*-group; the eye (*vilocana*) is declared by means of speech and the rest, beginning with the *pa*-group;
and the placement of the weapon (*astra*) is taught by means of the intellect (*buddhi*) and the rest, conjoined with the *ya*-group.
The limb-mantras, together with their respective classes, are declared to end in the dative case for one's own self.
The formal application is as follows:
Ṅaṃ kaṃ khaṃ ghaṃ gaṃ, salutation to the heart, whose essence is space, wind, fire, water, and earth.

Ñaṃ caṃ chaṃ jhaṃ jaṃ, svāhā to the head, whose essence is sound, touch, form, taste, and smell. Ṇaṃ ṭaṃ ṭhaṃ ḍhaṃ ḍaṃ, vaṣaṭ to the crest-lock (śikhā), whose essence is the ear, skin, eye, tongue, and nose.
Naṃ taṃ thaṃ dhaṃ daṃ, to the Self of speech, hands, feet, anus, and genitals; to the armor, *huṃ*.
Maṃ paṃ phaṃ bhaṃ baṃ, to the Self of speaking, grasping, moving, excreting, and procreating; to the three eyes, *vauṣaṭ*.
Haṃ yaṃ raṃ vaṃ laṃ kṣaṃ śaṃ ṣaṃ laṃ saṃ.
To the weapon whose essence is intellect, mind, ego, consciousness, and knowledge—phaṭ!
One should place the seed-syllable of the noose (pāśabīja) from the navel down to the feet;
then, the seed-syllable of power (śaktibīja) from the heart down to the navel;
and thereafter, one should place the goad (aṅkuśa) from the head down to the heart.
One should place [the syllables], intensely radiant, in sequence within the heart and the elements;
then, one should separately place the two syllables of the color of the *haṃsa* in the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and the individual soul (*jīva*).
The placement (nyāsa) of both the vital breath (prāṇa) and the individual soul (jīva) is also in the heart alone;
"separately" means for each one individually.
The knower of the ritual procedure should perform this entire pervasive rite by means of this [mantra].
The meaning is: "by means of the entire root."
Then one should meditate upon the Goddess, who is the life-force of all beings and identical with the universe—
red in hue, seated upon a lotus as crimson as a boat in a sea of blood, holding in her lotus-hands a noose, a goad, a spear, a skull-cup, a sugarcane bow, and arrows; I bow to the three-eyed Goddess.
Having meditated thus upon the Mother of the Universe, one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times.
One should perform oblations with sacrificial porridge mixed with clarified butter amounting to a tenth part of that number.
One should worship according to this rite upon the seat of Śakti, which is enriched by the noose.
One should worship Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Īśvara in the six corners, followed by Gaṇī, Lakṣmī, and Umā; thereafter, one should worship the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga).
This is the sequence of worship.
In the southeast, west, and north, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Īśa are to be worshipped; in the east, southwest, and northwest, Vāṇī, Lakṣmī, and Umā are to be worshipped;
the measurements, however, are as previously stated.
On the petals the Mothers are to be worshipped, and outside of those, the Leaders of the World.
In this manner one should worship the Goddess with fragrant flowers and other offerings.
Thus, when the mantra has been mastered, it shall grant the fruits of the six rites.
The preceptor should establish the vital breaths everywhere with this mantra;
at the end of the seed-syllable, he should employ the female messengers (dūtīs) at the beginning of the words "of this one" (amuṣya).

By this, the method for the installation and consecration of the vital breath (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*) in all rites everywhere, such as in effigies (*puttalī*) and so forth, has been shown. [The phrase] "at the end of the seed-syllable" means at the end of the *pāśa* and *haṃsa* mantras.
"[At the beginning] of the words 'amuṣya'" means at the beginning of the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*).
As it has been stated by Rāghavabhaṭṭa:
"Having gone [to the victim] and bound him with the *pāśa* seed-syllable, and having seized the object of practice (*sādhya*) with the *śakti* seed-syllable,

then drawing out his vital breaths (*prāṇa*) with the *aṅkuśa* [seed-syllable], and having addressed the messenger-goddesses (*dūtī*) beginning with the letter *ya*, the mantra-practitioner [should utter] the name of the object of practice."
Mṛtavaivasvatā, Bhūyojīvahā, Prāṇahā, Ākṛṣyāgrahaṇā, and thereafter Pramadā, Visphuliṅginī,
Kṣetrajñā, and Pratihā— these nine are remembered as the messengers of breath (prāṇadūtīs).
One should quickly perform [the rite] for one whose movements are bound by a noose, whose mind is seized by power (śakti),
and who has been drawn forth by a goad along with the waters;
having fashioned an effigy of the target person measuring twelve finger-breadths.
At that time, when the object of the rite (sādhya) is asleep at midnight, one should place the life-force mantra along with the insect within the heart-lotus;
thereafter, [one should place] Vāyu, Agni, Indra, and Varuṇa upon its petals.
Within the pericarp [of the lotus], one should contemplate the letters beginning with *ya*, joined with swans and having the form of bees, belonging to Īśa, Rakṣasa, Śītāṃśu, and Yama; these,
whose forms are connected by threads, have arisen from the *bindu* of Śiva.

Thus, in the lotus of one's own heart, the practitioner who knows the ritual procedure should, in the form of a bee, bring each individual lotus of the person to be acted upon (sādhya) along with its path, and place each individual bee within the effigy or within his own consciousness.

Here, as in the first case, for each of the second and subsequent names of those to be accomplished (*sādhya*), one should first utter the seed-syllables beginning with *pāśa* and ending with the *haṃsa-mantra*, followed by the name of the first messenger (*dūtī*) in the vocative case; thus, this is applied first in four places.
The same applies to the other messengers as well.
There is a repetition of the mantra nine times, according to the statement cited by Rāghavabhaṭṭa: "This mantra is recited in this manner precisely according to the number of the planets."
In this regard, it should be understood that for each individual cycle (*āvṛtti*), there is the bringing of one *bhṛṅga* at a time.

When the first female messengers (*dūtī*) are not employed, there is the bringing of the first *bhṛṅga*; when the second female messengers are not employed, there is the bringing of the second *bhṛṅga*. This sequence continues until the end of the ninth.
Endowed with the fire-seed (raṃ), one should perform the severing of the threads;
having drawn forth the bees from the heart of the target, O Bhavānī, one should then cause them to whirl.
In this manner, one should perform eleven repetitions in all ritual acts.
The wise practitioner should visualize the Varuṇas as yellow for the rites of subjugation and attraction;
as smoky for delusion and hatred; as black for the rite of killing;
and as yellow for paralyzing, while one skilled in the rite of drawing in the vital breaths should meditate upon them accordingly.
One should establish the vital breaths (prāṇas) drawn from the heart of the target (sādhya) within one's own heart;
for cruel rites, their establishment is said to be in an effigy (puttalī).
One should [visualize] the vital breaths of the target as frogs and one's own self as serpents.
An expert should always remember [this] in cruel rites:

the *prāṇātma* yantra, situated on the earth, surrounded by letters, containing the syllables from *ya* onwards written with Vāyu, Agni, Śakra, Varuṇa, Īśvara, Rākṣasendra, Indu, and Pretendra, ending with the *bindu*, joined with the *haṃsa* and the name of the person to be acted upon (*sādhya*), and enclosed by the letters.
Thus, skilled in the application of this mantra,
the knower of mantras shall bring all the gods under his control, let alone ordinary human beings.
The mudrās for invocation and so forth were maintained by the author of the *Tantrasāra*, but they are not required here.
Now, regarding the seat, it is stated in the fifth chapter of the *Mātṛkābhedatantra*:
"A span [caturaṅgula] in width," and so forth.
Now, the water for washing the feet.
In the *Prapañcasāra*, in the sixth chapter.
The water for washing the feet (pādya) is said to consist of *śyāmāka* grain, *dūrvā* grass, lotus, and *viṣṇukrāntā*; thus is the *pādya*.
Now, the arghya offering.
Fragrance, flowers, unbroken rice, barley, tips of kuśa grass, sesame seeds, mustard seeds,
and dūrvā grass— these are declared to be the eight substances for the arghya offering in their respective order.
The specific details regarding the Śākta arghya are found in the seventh chapter of the Yoginītantra.
That which is produced from curved grains, as well as that produced from fine grains—
one should offer that unhusked rice, numbering seven, eight, or nine,
together with sprouts of *dūrvā* grass, to the Blessed Lady.
On the eighth or the ninth [lunar day], he shall obtain the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice.
Thus is the *arghya*.
Now follows the water for sipping.
The water for sipping (ācamanīyaka) is prepared with nutmeg, cloves, and kakkola.
Thus ends the water for sipping. Now follows the honey-mixture (madhuparka).
And the wise have declared that the madhuparka consists of curd mixed with honey.
In the Śāradā [Tantra].
Clarified butter mixed with curd and honey—this, as stated by the wise, is called madhuparka.
Now, furthermore, this is the Ācamanīya [water].
The water for sipping (ācamanīyaka) has been prepared with pure water once again.
Thus again is the water for sipping. Now, the fragrance.
As for the etymological derivation of the word *gandha*, it is found in the Kulārṇava, in the seventeenth chapter of the fifth section.
Because it causes the destruction of profound, boundless misfortune and affliction,
and because it bestows the knowledge of the Dharma, it is called "fragrance."
In the Prapañcasāra.
The paste of sandalwood, agallochum, and camphor is here called "fragrance."
The fruit of that gift, however, is stated in the Yoginītantra:
Having offered fragrant unguents, one obtains the fruit of the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice;
having anointed the Noble One with saffron, one obtains the fruit of giving a thousand cows.
[One should worship] with sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, white flowers, and saffron.
One should worship Durgā when she has been anointed with these; one shall obtain the fruit of the Vahniṣṭoma sacrifice.
Now, the eight fragrances (gandhāṣṭaka).
In the fourth chapter of the Merutantra.
Now, the eightfold incense (gandhāṣṭaka) for each respective deity is proclaimed.
Sandalwood, agallochum, camphor,
yellow pigment (rocanā), saffron, musk, red sandalwood, and jasmine— this is declared as the "Gāṇapatya" eightfold incense, belonging to Gaṇeśa.
Hrīvera, candana, kuṣṭha, aguru, candana, murā, sevyaka,
and jaṭāmāṃsī— this is declared to be the Vaiṣṇava group, known as the eight fragrances of Viṣṇu.
Sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, water, saffron, gorocana, jaṭāmāṃsī, and kapi—these they know as the eight-fold fragrance of Śakti; thus is the eight-fold fragrance of Śakti.

With *jalaja*, *kāśmīra*, and *kuṣṭha*, along with red sandalwood (*raktacandana*) and sandalwood (*candana*), as well as *uśīra*, *aguru*, and camphor (*karpūra*), they know this as the "eightfold fragrance of the Sun" (*saura-gandhāṣṭaka*). (p. 396)
One should always [apply] gorocanā, kuṣṭha, camphor, aguru, saffron, sandalwood, and the leaf [inscribed with] the Varada mantra upon the face.
In the Śāradā [Tantra].
Sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, tamāla, water, saffron, kuśīta, and kuṣṭha—these combined are known as the eight-fold fragrance of Śiva; thus is the *śaivagandhāṣṭaka*.
Now, the flower.
The etymological derivation of the word *puṣpa* (flower) is found in the *Kulārṇava*.
Because it increases merit, because it wards off the flood of sins,
and because it bestows abundant wealth, it is called "puṣpa" (flower).
In the Prapañcasāra.

The two types of *tulasī*, the two types of lotus (*paṅkaja*), the two types of *jāti*, the two types of *ketakī*, the two types of *karavīra*, as well as red lotuses (*raktotpala*), blue lotuses (*utpala*), white water-lilies (*kahlāra*), and night-blooming lilies (*kumuda*)— these ten flowers are recommended.
In the second chapter of the Viśvasāra-tantra, at the end of the verses, the reading is "bahūni kusumāni" (many flowers).
Mālatī, kunda, mandāra, nandyāvarta and others; palāśa, pāṭala, pārtha, parantya, and āvartaka; campakas along with nāgas, and red mandārakas.
And those originating from the Aśoka, the Bilva, and the Karṇikāra trees.
In the Viśvasāra-tantra, a specific teaching regarding Śakti is stated as follows:
"Now, with the consent of the Goddess, I shall speak of the flowers; listen, O Pārvatī!
Having said this, he spoke of the *tulasī* leaves, the lotuses, and so forth.
Immediately after that: "O beloved! Indeed, there are these other flowers in this Tantra;
they may originate from various countries and may bloom at all times."
One should especially offer *kulapuṣpas* to the Goddess.
Now, O Maheśvarī, I shall describe the flowers for ritual application;
listen with supreme devotion to what was spoken by Brahmā in the past.
The lotus, the oleander, the two types of safflower, the two kinds of *tulasī*, the jasmine, the *aśoka*, the two types of *ketaka*, the *kumārī*, the *campaka*,
the blue lotus, the *kunda*, the *mandāra*, the *punnāga*, the *pāṭala*, the *nāga*, and the *campaka*.
Āragvadha, karṇikāra, pāvantī, navamallikā,
saugandhika, koraṇḍa, palāśa, aśoka,
sarjaka, sindhuvāra, apāmārga, vāpulīka, and kāmajam.
Then follow vyāghracela, damanaka, and maruvaka;
likewise lavaṅga, jalakarpūra, tagara, and javā;
as well as śivapuṣpa, droṇapuṣpa, kāmarāja, and suketa.
Furthermore, there are other forest flowers, both aquatic and terrestrial,
as well as mountain-born and region-specific flowers of various kinds.
Also in the Śāradā [Tantra]: (p. 397)
The *kamala*, the *karavīra*, the two kinds of *kumuda*, the two kinds of *tulasī*, the two kinds of *jātī*, the two kinds of *ketaka*, the *kahlāra*, the *campaka*,
the *utpala*, the *kunda*, the *mandāra*, the *punnāga*, the *pāṭalā*, and the *nāgacampaka*.
Āragvadha, karṇikāra, pāvantī, navamallikā,
saugandhika, koraṇṭa, palāśa, aśoka, mallikā, dhustūra,
sarjaka, bilva, arjuna, and munipuṣpaka.
The wise practitioner should also take other fragrant leaves and flowers that have been prescribed by the teachers for worship.
Also in the seventh chapter of the third part of the Yoginītantra:
Listen, O Goddess! I shall explain the chapter on flowers in brief.
[One should worship] with flowers produced in their proper season—mallikā, jātī, and saffron;
likewise with white and red flowers, as well as blue and pale lotuses.
With *kiṃśuka*, *tagara*, *javā*, *kanaka*, and *campaka* flowers; with *vakula*, *mandāra*, *kunda*, and *kuruṇḍaka*;
together with *dhustūra* and others, as well as those produced from the *bandhūka* and *agastya* trees.
With *madana* flowers, *sindhuvāra* blossoms, and the tender sprouts of *dūrvā* grass,
as well as with clusters of *kuśa* grass and very delicate *bilva* leaves.
Also in the ninth chapter:
One should offer *tulasī*, the two kinds of *mālatī*, *tamāla*, *āmalakī*, *punnāga*, *munipuṣpa*, and *mallikā*.
Those people who worship Janārdana with *karavīra* flowers [attain great merit].
O Goddess of the gods! By the mere sight of him, the fire of hell is extinguished.
Now, the majesty of the *karavīra* and other [plants],
in the tenth chapter of the *Puraścaraṇarasollāsa*.
O Goddess! The Karavīra flower is Javā; it is Kālī herself and not otherwise.
Tārā, Aparā, and Tripurasundarī herself are likewise.

O Daughter of the Mountain! O Goddess! O Beautiful One! If one should give up their life at the root of a Karavīra or a Javā plant near a Tulasī, its greatness cannot be described even by a hundred million mouths and a hundred million tongues.
I am never able to describe his greatness.
Thus, at the root of the *karavīra* and *javā*, the fruit is the relinquishing of life. O Maheśānī! The *karavīra* may be white, black, yellow, green, or red, and likewise for the *javā* flower.
She herself is Kālī! She herself is Mahāmāyā; she herself is Tripurasundarī.
One must not show disrespect toward her, for by doing so, one goes to hell.
In the tenth chapter.
Kṛṣṇāparājitā is directly Bhadrakālī herself; of this there is no doubt.
Karavīra is Bhuvana, and Droṇa is Bhuvanasundarī;
Javā is the Goddess herself, the embodiment of all vidyās.
Those practitioners who worship the Mother of the World, the beloved of Śiva—

O Caṇḍī! With these flowers, that Śiva is indeed worshipped; of this there is no doubt. What need is there for recitations, or for austerities, or for gifts, or for sacrifices, by which the Mother of the World has been worshipped with droṇa, kṛṣṇā, javā, and other [flowers]?

O Caṇḍī! Whatever fruit is produced by the Rājasūya, Aśvamedha, Vājapeya, Agnihotra, and other such sacrifices—all that is obtained from the worship with flowers. [The flowers are] the hibiscus, the droṇa, the black flower, the wood-apple, and the oleander.
One should offer the very essence of Brahman to Mahādevī;
he who gives it with a spirit of devotion, anointed with red sandalwood and joined with white sandalwood, is undoubtedly the Lord of the Universe himself.
Now, regarding the specific flowers for one who has desire, it is as follows in that very same place.
He who offers a thousand *karavīra* flowers in the month of Māgha,
having attained his desired objects, is glorified in the world of the Goddess;
there, with a single *karavīra*, two thousand lotuses [are equal].
In times of great terror, great calamity, and great adversity;
in times of distress, great suffering, great disease, great sorrow, and great fear— one should worship Kālikā, Tārā, Bhuvanā, Ṣoḍaśī, and Śivā.
One should worship Bālā, Chinnā, Vagalā, Dhūmā, Bhīmā,
Karālinī, Kamalā, Annapūrṇā, and Durgā, the destroyer of suffering;
[one should worship] all the vidyās with javā, droṇa, and beautiful karavīra flowers.
O Maheśānī! By worshipping Kṛṣṇā with black leaves of the mālūra tree upon the ground, the best of practitioners becomes liberated; of this there is no doubt.
In the tenth chapter of the Muṇḍamālā.
One should worship the supreme goddess Caṇḍikā with the highest devotion using javā flowers, droṇa flowers, beautiful karavīra flowers, kṛṣṇāparājitā flowers, lotuses, and agasti flowers.
In the Yoginītantra and the Matsyasūkta.
"O Goddess of gods! Mādhava becomes pleased for many cycles of four yugas with those who worship the Lord of Men with white and black karavīra flowers.
By this statement, which is in syntactic agreement with the previously cited words "white and black" (*sitāsitaiḥ*) meaning "white and dark," the word *asita* [is understood].
In the *Yoginīhṛdaya*, red, yellow, and so forth are understood, but not black alone.
One obtains the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice by offering Vakapuṣpa, Jātipuṣpa, and likewise Rudrajaṭa; it is not otherwise. Among all flowers, the blue lotus (nīlotpala) is the most excellent.
O Goddess! Listen to the fruit of merit for him who, according to the prescribed rite, offers a garland of a thousand blue lotuses to Durgā:
for thousands of crores of years and hundreds of crores of years.
Having become an attendant of the Goddess, he is glorified in the world of Rudra;
thus it is said in the Muṇḍamālā.
If this Mother of the World, who has been worshipped with hundreds of thousands of buffaloes, rams, goats, gifts, and auspicious sacrifices, is now honored even with flowers,
then Kṛṣṇā alone knows the full extent of the greatness of Kṛṣṇā.

O Goddess! Half of that belongs to me, half of that always to the Lord of Śrī (Viṣṇu), half of that to the Lotus-born (Brahmā), and half of that to the knower of the Vedas (Śiva). O Śaṅkarī, I shall now speak briefly of the majesty of other flowers.
On the surface of the earth, in heaven, in Vaikuṇṭha, or in the city of Kālikā—what fruit does one obtain through hibiscus, oleander, and other petals?
O Mother of the World! No one knows this except Pārvatī; who else could know it?
He who worships upon the surface of the earth with white and red *karavīra* flowers mixed with red sandalwood will certainly become the Lord of the Universe.
And he who worships the Goddess with *kṛṣṇāparājitā* flowers—

Having obtained the fruit of thousands of horse-sacrifices, he shall go to the auspicious realm of Śiva. He who, in the face of great calamity, gives a javā, a kṛṣṇāparājitā, a droṇa, or a karavīra flower, shall go to the city of Kālikā.
Thus ends the journey to the city of Kāli, even by means of giving the gift of the horse and other offerings as a cause for averting great calamity.
In that very same [text].
Furthermore, what is the use of water for the feet, or musical instruments, or food offerings, or acts of worship?
What is the use of gifts of honey, or the madhuparka offering, or of kumbhaka breath-retentions, or of recaka exhalations,
or of pūraka inhalations, or of meditations, or even of prāṇāyāma exercises?
What is the use of recitations, or what use for austerities, or fish and meat as the fifth?
What use for other mantras, what use for tantras, what use for yantras, and what use for spiritual accomplishments (sādhanas)?
What use for the Vedas, for intoxicants, or for cremation grounds and the practice of mantra-attainment?
What is the use of sacrifices purified by mantras, or the meanings of mantras, or those who live by mantras?
What is the use of the *yonimudrā*, or of sacred pilgrimage sites (*tīrtha*), or of the means for attaining Brahman?
What is the use of the various applications (*nyāsa*) of the *mātṛkās*, or of ear-rings, water-pots, and cloths?
What is the use of the sixfold ritual placements (ṣoḍhānyāsa) like the crow’s beak, or of religious practices,
if the Great Goddess has been worshipped with oleanders (karavīra),
with *javā* flowers, with black *aparājitā* blossoms, and with beautiful oleanders?
For those by whom the Blessed Lady has been worshipped with *droṇa* flowers, *ketakī* blossoms, and leaves of *javā* and *mālūra*, what need have they for the performance of ritual acts?
In the eleventh chapter of the Nityātantra.
One should not worship Kālī with *tulasī*, nor should one worship Viṣṇu with unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*).
By the offering of *aparājitā*, Śivā herself becomes truly pleased.
Karavīra is exceedingly dear to both Kālikā and Tārā.
O Maheśānī! One should offer the Java flower, but one should never wear it.
O Deveśī! One should worship Kālikā even once with a red lotus;
one shall obtain the fruit of a hundred thousand years of worship.
Likewise: "Even *dūrvā* grass, when joined with its seed, brings satisfaction to the Goddess," as stated in the *Puraścaraṇarasollāsa*.
One should offer a cluster of blossoms from the mango tree to Keśava;
likewise, one should offer those of the jambu and tinduka trees to Keśava. One should also offer śephālikā, tagara, and bandhūka flowers.

One should avoid flowers from the *rudrajaṭā*, the *śirīṣa*, the pomegranate (*dāḍima*), the *kāñcana*, the *nīlakaṇṭha*, the peacock (*mayūra*), and those shaped like a vulva (*yonyākāra*) when offering flowers for the sake of desired fruits; this is stated in the *Nityātantra*.
The Lord said:

O Goddess of the Suras! O Great Goddess! For the expiation of sins such as the killing of a Brahmin, one should worship the King of Wheels (Cakrarāja) with red flowers, adorned with camphor powder, according to the sequence of the Kula tradition.
Even ten million great sins committed in previous lives are destroyed within a single month; this is the truth, the truth, there is no doubt.
O Goddess praised by heroes! Prosperity shall remain firmly established in his home.

O Maheśānī! If one worships as before with Java flowers, within a single month even the sins committed over seven lifetimes, such as the killing of a Brahmin, are destroyed; one becomes wealthy and a poet.
O Goddess of gods! if one should worship as before with ketakī flowers or leaves, within a single month, millions of minor sins [are destroyed].
"They perish"—this is to be connected with what was stated previously.
"The practitioner obtains royal fortune; there is no doubt in this.
O Great Goddess! one should worship Śivā with *śatapatra* flowers as before.

O Goddess of the gods! Within just one month, one shall destroy all sins. One should worship the Goddess with *campaka* flowers for one month as previously described. O Supreme Sovereign! Having thus destroyed the sin accumulated over a hundred lifetimes, [one attains liberation].
O Pārvatī, the practitioner of mantra attains good fortune in the three worlds!
O Maheśānī, if one worships for just one month with white lotuses, one shall destroy the sins committed in thirty lifetimes; of this there is no doubt.
O Goddess! One should worship for one month with bandhūka flowers as before;
having destroyed all sins, one shall bring the three worlds under one's control.
[One should also worship] with mālatī, mallikā, jātī, kunda, and white lotuses.

O Goddess! One should worship for one month with the mixed offerings as before. O Supreme Sovereign! [This practice] destroys sins such as the killing of a Brahmin, even those committed over a hundred lifetimes; liberation stands within his grasp.
O Supreme Goddess! One should worship Śivā for one month as before with red lotus, javā, fire (saffron), bandhūka, and agastya flowers;
having destroyed his sin, that man shall become equal to me.
O Goddess! One should worship her who dwells within the Śrīpīṭha with Nāgakeśara, Kahlāra, Vakula, Sindhuvāraka, and Pāṭala flowers. O Goddess!
With a tranquil mind, one should perform this worship for exactly one month, as previously described.
It destroys the sin accumulated over a thousand births; of this there is no doubt.
By the grace of the Goddess, he shall possess incomparable good fortune.
In the Yoginītantra.
One should never offer flowers that grow in the wild without first releasing them;
for even when the gods exert themselves to draw them forth, they are unable to do so,
since ten yakṣas guard each individual flower.
Likewise, there are five yakṣa maidens covered everywhere with flowers;
having gathered flowers from them, one should worship both the gods and the ancestors.
Thus ends the prohibition against giving flowers from trees.
In the Matsyasūkta:
O Goddess, that man who plucks a flower at the time of midday after having bathed shall be reborn in the Raurava hell for the sake of worshipping with those flowers.
Because of the specification "at midday," there is no fault in one who has bathed in the morning gathering flowers.
Now, the Flower Garland.
In the Viśvasāra Tantra:
O Goddess! Listen to the meritorious fruit for him who offers a garland made of a thousand blue lotuses to Durgā according to the prescribed rites:
for thousands of crores of years and hundreds of crores of years.
Having become an attendant of the Goddess, he is glorified in the world of Rudra.
In the ninth chapter of the Yoginītantra.
"By him who has worshipped Viṣṇu with a garland of *mālatī* flowers during the month of Kārtika,
the garland of sinful syllables is destroyed by Viṣṇu;
it is wiped away on the solar tablet"— this is the reading in the fourteenth chapter, at the end of the section, in the *Matsyasūkta*.
Likewise.
O Maheśānī! Even Devendra joins his palms in reverence when Mādhava offers him a garland made of karavīra flowers.
Now, regarding the fruit of giving the *dhātrī* fruit and other gifts on specific months, it is stated in that very same [text]:
O beloved! He who worships me with a dhātrī fruit or leaf when the sun is in Aries obtains the fruit of ten horse-sacrifices.
One should offer a cluster of mango blossoms to Keśava.
Likewise, indeed, [the fruits] of the jambū and tinduka trees, as well as those of the keśava tree.
In the Matsya-sūkta:
O Maheśānī! Even the Lord of the Devas joins his palms in reverence to one who offers a garland made of *karavīra* flowers to Mādhava.
By the use of the word "ca" (and), it is also for another deity.
In that very same [text].
One should not break the sacrificial thread, nor should one break the rosary;
specifically, this applies to a garland of jasmine and likewise to a tiger skin.
In the second chapter of the Vṛhannīlatantra.
The kokanada, the bandhūka, and the two types of karṇikāra are recommended;
as are the red vakula, mandāra, and karavīra flowers. The three kinds of mallikā, the jātī, the kṣauma flower, and the jayantī are also praised.
The bilva leaf, the kuruvaka, the munipuṣpa, and the keśara; the vasantī, the fragrant saugandha, the charming kālapuṣpa;
the āmalaka, the kādamba, the vakula, and likewise the yūthikā.
One should offer all auspicious flowers— such as bilva, maruvaka, and others, excluding tulasī—
and especially oḍra and vajra flowers,
with a mind endowed with devotion.
O Maheśānī! One should especially offer the javā flower to the Goddess;
the lotus is most dear to the Goddess, as are the śephālī and the vakula. O Deveśī! One should worship the supreme Śivā with the red lotus.
One shall obtain the fruit of a hundred thousand years of worship.
Śirīṣa is supremely pleasing to the Goddess, as is tagara;
sthalapadma is even more excellent, according to the sequence of a hundred thousand [offerings].
O Maheśānī! O Sureśvarī! if one should offer [this], all perfections (siddhis) will be attained;
at that very moment, there shall be success in mantra—of this there is no doubt to be made.
[One should offer] a beautiful, distinct Tulasī, which is supremely pleasing to Him.
O Maheśānī! One endowed with devotion should offer every kind of flower—whether golden, red-colored, or that which is most beloved from the beginning—even in great abundance.
In the Vṛhannīlatantra.

He who worships Hari with one hundred thousand mālatī flowers during the Cāturmāsya period destroys, in that very instant, the sins committed throughout a hundred lifetimes. Those who worship with karavīra blossoms on the day of Hari [attain the same].
O Goddess of the gods! By the mere sight of him, the fire of hell is extinguished.
Now, the flowers to be avoided.
One should not worship with *jhiṇṭī* flowers, nor with yellow *tagara*,
nor with white *uḍra*, nor with black *vijaya*.
In the sixth chapter of the *Prapañcasāra*.
One should not worship with garlands that have fallen on the ground, or those that are withered, defiled by insects, smelled, touched to the body, or stale.
In the Śāradā [Tantra].
The Guru should discard food that is dirty, touched by the ground, defiled by worms, hair, and the like, touched by the body, smelled, or stale.
In the fourteenth chapter of the Matsyasūkta.

(403) The *śephālikā* and the *kahlāra* are praised during the autumn season; at other times, O Goddess, one should not touch them, for there is an expiation required for worshipping with them. One should likewise not worship with flowers that are red or black, nor with those of pungent fragrance.
O Goddess, the blood of the Karavīra, the Māghya, the Bandhūjīva,
the Keśara, and the Vajra is indeed highly praised.
In the Yoginītantra.
One should offer bilva leaves, śamī leaves, tamāla,
and āmalakī leaves, as well as apāṅga, bhṛṅga leaves, kuśa grass, and likewise dūrvā grass.
In the absence of flowers, one may also present fruits.
But in the absence of fruits as well, one should worship Hari with their leaves.
Thus, in the absence of flowers and other offerings, worship may be performed even with leaves.
And the flower for secret worship is also right there.
O Śaṅkarī! [There are] Siṃhāsya, Māsūra, and the fourfold Dhustūra, as well as the two Rudrajaṭas and Guhyapuṣpa.

O Goddess! The lotus, the blue water-lily, the *vaka*, the *mandāraka*, the golden flower, the two kinds of *mādhavī*, and the *tamāla*—these are the secret flowers for the worship of the Exalted One.
The worship according to the distinction between day and night, and by means of specific flowers, is taught in that very same [text].
O Śaṅkarī! Golden flowers that are fragrant should be offered at night;
other flowers should be offered during the day, and the mallikā may be offered both by day and by night.
He who worships the deity with a flower from a temple shall also incur blindness for fifteen years.
Regarding the avoidance of specific flowers for specific deities, that is also mentioned in that very same [text].
One should avoid the *kunda* flower for Śiva; for Maheśvara, the *māghya* is praised.
For Gaṇeśa, one should avoid the *māghya*, as well as the *aśoka* and the *tagara*.
For Sūrya, the *māghya*, the *mandāra*, and likewise the *kanaka* should be avoided.
And for Mahālakṣmī, one should offer *tulasī*, *jhiṇṭikā*, and likewise *kāñcana*;
here, the exclusion of *jhiṇṭikā* is for the purpose of indicating a greater fault [in its omission].
One should cause the *bandhūjīva* and the *droṇa* to be offered to Sarasvatī;
likewise, one should offer *bilva* leaves to the planets and *śamī* leaves as well.
For Brahmā, one should avoid *kāśa*, saffron-dyed cloth, and *śamī* flowers.

One should not offer the *dhātrī* flower, the *kuruṇṭa*, nor likewise water-born flowers to Durgā; likewise, one should not offer the *soma* flower to her. To Tripurā, one should not offer the *kāñcana*, the *kanaka*, or the *vāsaka*.
Kiṃśuka, kṛṣṇakāntā, indrākṣī, and likewise varccanā.
In the Yoginītantra.
The bilva leaf, the māghya, the tamāla,
the āmalakī leaf, the kahlāra, the tulasī, the lotus, and the munipuṣpa— these do not become stale; nor does any other flower that consists of buds.
O Śaṅkarī, one should not be repelled by flowers that are cut, broken, or born on trees;
as for the etymological derivation of the word "dhūpa," it is found in the Kulārṇava.
Because it has the power to remove the foul odor of all great defects and because it generates supreme bliss, it is called "dhūpa" (incense).
In the Prapañcasāra.
The mantra-practitioner should fumigate the pedestal with guggulu, aguru, uśīra, white sugar, clarified butter, honey, and sandalwood, which have been cast into the embers of heartwood.
In the Yoginītantra.
O Maheśvarī! That man who gives black agallochum, camphor, sandalwood, and likewise storax to the Blessed Lady,
attains his desire in this world and is glorified in the realm of Durgā.
Thus is the incense offering.
The derivation of the word *dīpa*, however, is found in the *Kulārṇava*.
Because it pacifies the darkness of delusion, prevents the birth of further existence,
bestows a divine form, and illuminates the supreme reality,
it is known as the "Lamp of Liberation," the sole means for achieving the path to liberation.
In the Prapañcasāra.
With cow’s ghee or oil, and a wick of light substance,
one should kindle fragrant milk and cause the lamp to burn brightly.
Thus ends the section on the lamp.
The gift of clothing is described in the fourth chapter of the Varadā Tantra.
O Goddess of gods, when wealth is available, one should never offer a cloth that is less than thirty-six finger-breadths in length for any ritual action performed for specific desires.
The ornament, however, is in that very same place.
Whatever is not suitable for an eight-year-old girl, one should not give her ornaments; one must avoid stinginess regarding wealth.
But as for the fruits of all the ritual services, they belong to the inferior and the superior [practitioners] in that very same way.
O Goddess! In an inferior [rite], one obtains an inferior fruit; in a superior [rite], one obtains a superior fruit.
The etymological derivation of the word *naivedya* is found in the *Kulārṇava*.
O Mistress of the Family, that fourfold substance endowed with six flavors which brings satisfaction through its offering is declared to be *naivedya*.
In the *Prapañcasāra*.
