One should offer as the food offering (naivedya) well-cooled, perfectly pure milk-rice (pāyasa) with ghee, along with white rice, plantains, curd, and other such items. Thus ends the food offering.
Regarding betel-leaf, it is stated in the twenty-sixth chapter of the Matsyasūkta:
Then, having performed the recitation of the *vāstuguvāka* and provided it with *parṇasa*,
one should offer it smeared with the powder of conch and *śambūka*. Likewise:
O Goddess! One should offer that which is scented with camphor, blended with musk, and prepared with dhanvayavāsa, madhūka, and other ingredients;
likewise, mouth-perfume made with cardamom, campaka, musta, and so forth, is highly recommended.
The forbidden powders and leaves are also mentioned in that very same place.
O Śaṅkarī! O Goddess! One should avoid the powder of the *kapardaka*, the *vṛkṣa*, and the *palāśa* trees; one should not cause the leaves of these trees to be offered.
One should not offer a leaf from a tree of the Kali age, nor one situated on a *panasa* tree.
One should always avoid staying in a grove of *aśoka* or *śālmali* trees.
The *kalivṛkṣa* tree, known as the *vayaḍā* in Gauḍa, is the abode of spirits;
it is recommended for use in that very region.
"O my beloved! A leaf from either the mango or the nimba tree is also praised.
Thus [ends the section on] betel.
Then, having performed *prāṇāyāma* and other preliminary rites, having recited the root mantra one thousand and eight or one hundred times,
having offered the recitation (*japa*), and having recited the hymn (*stava*), the armor (*kavaca*), and so forth, one should prostrate.
This is stated in the fifteenth chapter of the *Gandharva-tantra*:
Praising her with various hymns and endowed with a spirit of devotion,
the best of practitioners should prostrate before the Supreme Goddess according to the prescribed rite.
[So too should] gods, humans, gandharvas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, and pannagas.
The Great-souled Ones are pleased on all sides by a single salutation;
through salutation, one obtains the fourfold aim of great prosperity.
For the sake of attaining every accomplishment everywhere, let a single prostration be performed.
Through dance one conquers the worlds; through dance dharma proceeds.
By means of prostration, one obtains long life and unbroken progeny.
A devoted practitioner shall attain the fourfold aims of human existence before long.
Prostration is a great sacrifice that always bestows delight in every respect;
pay homage to the Great Goddess with devotion and circumambulate her.
In the eighth chapter of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa of the Yoginītantra.
One should perform three circumambulations in the form of a lotus and then bow;
O Maheśvarī, having gone from the south to the north of the God!
The phrase "three circumambulations" and so forth should be understood as applying to both the middle and the conclusion.
Likewise, with reference to the worship of the Kumārī, it is stated in the sixth chapter of the Uttarakhanda of the Rudrajāmala:
One should perform three circumambulations— at the beginning, in the middle, and likewise at the end—
and thereafter offer a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) consisting of silver, gold, and pearls. Then, having joined the palms in reverence and performed the waving of lights (bhrāmaṇa), one should bow down.

O Goddess! At each circumambulation, one should prostrate like a staff; if one does not bow after having completed the circumambulation, then an offense occurs. He who offers salutation with his hands joined but not bound [in the añjali gesture] commits a fault.
One is cooked in the hell of the darkness of delusion; of this there is no doubt.
During the interval between breaths, one should bow with the head, yet not touch the ground;
the deities curse such a person, and that [act] is proclaimed to be fruitless.

O beloved! O Maheśānī! Listen to the fruit of the merit of one who performs prostration before the God of gods: as many particles of dust as there are on his body, for as long as he remains, and for as many moments as those particles persist—[such is his reward].
For that many thousands of years, he is honored in the world of Brahmā.
In the Gandharva Tantra.
Salutation is traditionally held to be threefold: physical, vocal, and mental. These salutations are to be understood as superior, inferior, and middling.
The gods are always pleased by physical salutations.

Among all forms of salutation, the physical one is considered the foremost. That salutation which is performed by touching the ground with both knees and touching the earth with the head is called the physical salutation (*kāyika*).
Placing his palms together above his head as a means for accomplishing the purpose of all dharmas,
he then extended his right hand while bowing his own head;
filled with devotion and faith, he showed his right side.
Having performed a single circumambulation in a circular form,
the practitioner should be known as one who has performed the circumambulation that grants satisfaction to all the gods. He who performs one hundred and eight circumambulations of the Goddess—
Having attained all desires, he shall subsequently attain liberation.
The triangular, the hexagonal, the semicircular, the circumambulatory,
the staff-like, the eight-limbed, and the fierce— these are the seven characteristics of prostration.
Having gone from the south toward the northwest, and then turning back from there toward the south,
that prostration which is performed is the "Half-moon" (ardhacandra), which is dear to me.
O Daughter of the Mountain, one should know this to be the natural form of these prostrations.
Having left his own seat and place and gone behind to offer salutation,
prostrating himself upon the ground like a staff— this is called "daṇḍa" by the wise.
Likewise, having prostrated upon the ground like a staff with the heart as well;
With the chin, the face, the nose, the jaw,
the eyes, the two ears, and indeed the aperture of Brahma (brahmarandhra),
that which touches the ground in succession is declared to have eight limbs (aṣṭāṅga).
In the Merutantra:
With the two hands, the two feet, the two knees,
as well as the chest, the head, the gaze, the speech, and the mind— the eight-limbed [prostration] is thus described.
With the hands, knees, head, speech, and intellect— the five-limbed [prostration] is described.
In the Gandharva Tantra.

He whose salutation involves contact with the earth through the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra) should be known as Ugra, who bestows satisfaction upon Viṣṇu. That salutation which is composed by oneself in both prose and verse—
That which is performed with devotion is remembered as the highest verbal [salutation].
Whether performed by those following the Purāṇas, the Vedas, or the Tantras,
that prostration is always considered the middling salutation according to traditional practice.

When a salutation to others is performed through prose or verse, it should be known as the lowest among all forms of verbal salutation. It becomes threefold according to whether the mind is directed toward what is desired, neutral, or undesired. (p. 407)
Bowing is said to be mental, categorized as superior, inferior, or middling;
and among these three types of salutation, the physical is considered the most excellent.

Then, having dismissed the deity and worshipped the respective deities as prescribed in their respective ritual manuals (kalpas) with the remnants of the food offering (naivedya), one should perform the cleaning of the site and other such duties.

Now, regarding the determination of the time for the *nirmālya* (remnants of offerings): the statement from the seventh chapter of the third part of the *Yoginītantra* has already been cited by the author of the *Tantrasāra*, and thus serves no further purpose here.
[The following is] from the sixteenth chapter of the *Matsyasūkta*.
Jewels, pearls, corals, and those things given by the gods,
as well as metallic objects, do not become *nirmālya* for twelve years; likewise,
a cotton mattress remains so for six months, and one made of *avija* grass for five years.
A cloth woven from silk,
cotton cloth, a garment for a year, one for half a year, and one for half of that—
these are the offerings at the conclusion of the great worship, which grant [their fruit] by mere sight.
O Maheśvarī! As long as the food remains warm, it is known as *yajñasūtra*; likewise, rice mixed with sesame and water (*kṛśara*) lasts for half a watch (*yāmārddha*).
O Goddess! So too do garlands of *karavīra*, as well as lotuses and water-lilies.
O Great Goddess! With half a *yāma* [of time], one may likewise [attain the fruit] of one made of *vilva*;

and with a full day and night (*ahorātra*), O beautiful one, the head and blood [are attained]. Furthermore, there are two *tulasī*s, two *mālatī*s, as well as *tamāla*, *āmalakī*, *punnāga*, *muni*-flower, and the three kinds of *mallikā*.
Whoever should offer two *jātī* flowers, two *ketakī*, two blue water-lilies (*kumuda*), and two red lotuses (*padmaka*) to Vāsudeva, his merit shall be infinite.
Now, the substances prescribed or prohibited for offering to the deities.
In the sixth chapter of the Vṛhannīlatantra.
One should present a supreme message to the Goddess, accompanied by ritual substances:
jaggery, milk, honey, grapes, aged sugarcane,
plantain fruit, citron, and likewise coconut.
O Maheśvarī! One should offer coconut fruit mixed with honey;
likewise, even one's worldly dealings should be accompanied by honey and sweetness.
In the eighth chapter of the Yoginītantrōttarakhaṇḍa.
Iṅguda fruits, bilvas, jujubes, and emblic myrobalans;
dates, jackfruit, citron, and honey;
mangoes, udumbara fruits, and likewise palm fruits.
One should diligently offer pomegranate and plantain;
likewise, one should present lakuca, madhuka, and betel nuts,
as well as sweet citron and karkandhu fruits.
Radish greens and various other kinds as well,
mustard greens and likewise lotus greens;
for whatever has a large root, its leaf is its sprout.
O my beloved! The leafy vegetables of the vāstūka and the pālaṅka should be given; likewise, the tamarind fruit, the mountain cucumber (kuṣmāṇḍa), and whatever grows in the forest should be avoided.
One should likewise avoid plantain, citron, vāmaka, piṇḍraka, unseasonal panasa, and any other such [forbidden items].
Thus ends the description of the fruits of prescribed and prohibited acts. O Śaṅkarī! I shall now declare the uses of rice grains;
O Śaṅkarī! listen with a concentrated mind to this method of obtaining them.
Soma-grain, bṛhaddhānya, and red śāli rice;
mahaddhānya, barley, sesame, mung beans, and mudga beans; peas, round grains, white mustard seeds, and saffron.
One should also employ small cumin and sweet flag among these.
The grains to be avoided are also mentioned in that very same place.
O beautiful one, you should avoid black pot-herbs, peas, jīvaka, chickpeas, and kodrava grain for me.
In this context, the *kalāya* (pea) is either triangular or flattened;
since a round shape is prescribed, the meaning is that one should therefore avoid varieties such as *atasī* and *masūra*.
Milk and the milk of a black cow, salt produced from earth,
and salt originating from the eastern sea as well as that arising from the northern sea.
Milk refers to the milk of a black cow and so forth.
O Goddess! I shall now declare [the rules] regarding domestic and wild animals,
by which the milk and ghee of cows,
as well as the meat of deer, goats, śāla deer, and hares, are to be utilized.
With these one should present offerings that are dear to Viṣṇu.
One should avoid the meat of buffaloes; thereafter, [one should offer] milk, curd, and ghee.
I shall now declare which birds are to be employed as food for my sake.
And those which they always consume in the sacrifices to Viṣṇu: the green partridge, the peacock, the quail, the francolin, as well as the tawny partridge,
the blue rock pigeon, and the heads of the crow and the cock.
The wild cock, the śarāri, the pigeon,
the vellaka, the kulika, the red-tailed bird, the ṭiṭṭibha,
and the black fish-eater— among birds, these are distinguished as excellent.
The syntactical connection is as follows: "Whether it be that which is unfit to be eaten, or that which belongs to the five-toed animals (pañcanakha), or whatever else;
if meat is unfit to be eaten, or if it is fit to be eaten, then [the same applies] to the five-toed animals and 'others' (ca)."

One should avoid these divine fish: the *citramatsya*, the *rohita*, the *pāṭhīna*, the *nalamīnaka*, the *mahāśāla*, the *śāla*, the *rājīva*, and the *siṃhatuṇḍaka*; one should also avoid the *vaḍālī*.
The *citramatsya* is known as *ciṭala*;
the *nalamīna* is well-known as *ciṅḍī*;
and the *siṃhatuṇḍa* is well-known as *riṭhā*.
It is well known as the *vaḍālī-bheda*.
One should avoid wild birds, as well as small pigs;
safflower, potherbs, and oil-cakes; and red-footed fowl. One should also avoid dates, jackfruit, grapes, citrons, and śīraka.
One should diligently offer plantains, oranges, as well as rose-apple fruits, lotus roots, and licorice;
one should also offer plantains, citron, and milk-pudding.
Kandupakva, kaśeru, and jambu are dear to the young; likewise, ginger,
salt, cumin, long pepper, nutmeg,
and tinduka are most beloved by the Goddess.
The fruit of what is to be avoided is stated in that very same [text]:
One should not offer to Mahādevī ripe *rāmarambhā* fruit, nor plantain heated by smoke, nor the seed of the blue lotus (*utpala*). A mortal should avoid *śrāvaṇika* grain that has been steamed twice.
One should offer to Mahādevī coconuts that have a golden luster and those known as *rāmaka* coconuts; water from such a coconut is especially recommended.
However, one should avoid using *bhāṇḍīra* coconuts for offerings to the gods or in ancestral rites (*śrāddha*).
One should offer ripe *vakula* fruit as well as lotus fruit to Mahādevī; one shall obtain the fruit of the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance.
He states the prohibition in that very same place:
One should avoid from afar the jujube fruit mixed with sugar, as well as daṇḍa-śāka, and mountain-grown pumpkin (kuṣmāṇḍa).
In the twenty-sixth chapter of the Matsyasūkta.
Listen, O Goddess! I shall speak; understand from me the varieties of meat.
One should not give [as an offering] the bitter tortoise, nor the animal with horns, nor the *gomīna*, the *cakraka*, the *śakula*, the *vaḍāla*, and likewise the *rāghava*.
One should avoid those that are curved, of inferior color, marked with a discus, or moving;
likewise, one should avoid those that are earth-born, or belong to Aniruddha, or originate from the Gaṅgā.
One should also avoid those that are pleasing to the eye, golden, or shaped like a discus.
The goat, the large goat, and likewise the mountain goat;
the sheep, which is of two kinds, and the ena deer, which is of four kinds;
furthermore, in the Kali age, the meat of cows, monitor lizard meat, and hare meat [are forbidden].

O Supreme Goddess! In Nepāla one should eat the buffalo, in Kāmarūpa the boar; the rhinoceros and the four-faced [animal] are to be eaten as food. The gayal, the musk deer, and especially the buffalo are also recommended.
In all places, there is the Kṣudravārāha and likewise the Nīlahaya;
in Malaya, in Saguṇa, and likewise in the Jālandharas,
as well as in all Pīṭhas, fish and meat are not to be eaten, nor is the Vaḍāla.
In this particular region, because the consumption of fish and meat is prohibited, the eating of fish and meat is permitted in other regions such as Gauḍa and Nepāla;
however, the *vaḍālī* is inedible in all regions— this is the meaning.
A practitioner of mantras should always avoid mountain ginger (*śṛṅgavera*) and the mountain *kuṣmāṇḍa* gourd; he should also renounce the golden *rohitaka* tree,
the golden-colored lizard, and the white boar.

One should not eat a tortoise marked with wheel-signs, nor a royal swan; one should likewise avoid eating domestic aquatic animals that are otherwise edible. One should also avoid the pigeon, the cock, the peacock, and the curlew.
One should not eat the vardhana, the vabhrubāla, the dātyūha, nor the kokila; likewise, one should not eat the vulture, the owl, the heron, or the vistārākṣa.
Nor should one eat the bottle-gourd, the eggplant, the partridge, or the mayūra.

If a twice-born man eats the meat of the Bhāradvāja, the Matsya-cakra, or even the Daśāvatāra unintentionally, he becomes pure by means of breath control (prāṇāyāma). He must completely avoid all meat that has been kept for three nights.

O Pārvatī! Regarding the mountain-grown *siṃhatuṇḍa* that has been consumed, it is indeed pure even in sweat and heat; likewise, O Supreme Goddess, its sprout is consecrated by being perfumed with fragrance.

O Goddess, by eating its flesh, there is yet more [merit] found there! O Goddess, he who would renounce meat—especially even a mere morsel of meat—obtains the full fruit of all sacrifices; of this there is no doubt.
In a full year, the merit is tenfold; in six months, it is fourfold.

Even for one who is unable to perform it at the prescribed times of the lunar festivals (parvan), he shall obtain the fruit of the Pitṛmedha sacrifice. This applies with special effort during the time of Viṣṇu’s sleep and during the Cāturmāsya period.

One obtains the supreme fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice; O Goddess, he who is unable [to perform other vows] should avoid fish and meat during Kārttika. In Kārttika, one should especially avoid pork, beef, and fish.
Therefore, with every effort during the month of Kārttika,
one should avoid eating the lāvaka bird, the vartika, as well as the haricitraka;
the cāsa, the citrakapota, the tṛṇākṣa, and the mayūraka.
The wise declare that *kāma*, *kalabha*, and *tolikālaka* are indeed edible foods.
It is also prohibited in that very same [text].
The two types of *bhṛṅgarāja*, the *pika*, the *kadalī*,
the *sāraṅga*, the long-beaked bird, the golden-necked one,
the dancing one, the restless one, the red-throated one, and the red-winged bird.
The *cilla*, the *kīlāla*, and the *gaṅgācilla*—
these alone are declared to be inedible for the twice-born. Likewise, the wild cock with red tail-feathers and the one with a red beak [are forbidden].

One should eat the praised meats of the white-necked crane, the blue-throated peacock, the red-throated one, the hare, the patravāha, the pīḍaka, and the jīvaka, when they are obtained at the proper time.
Regarding that very point, he states what meat is not to be eaten:

One should not eat the flesh of humans, monkeys, bears, tigers, cats, or turtles; nor the flesh of village pigs, śarala deer, or horses; likewise, one should not eat the flesh of dogs. Having eaten [any of these], one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
Having intentionally eaten the meat of a gavaya as well as that of a cow,
or having eaten elephant meat through negligence, one must perform two *cāndrāyaṇa* penances;
likewise for the thick meat of a boar, a rhinoceros, or a deer.
The "gross" [size] is said to be achieved in two, three, four, or six years;
however, that which is called "excessively gross" should never occur.
[This applies to the skins of] the black antelope, the hare, the goat, and the bull.
Likewise, in the Kali Yuga, the meat of the camel, the rhinoceros, the boar, and the buffalo—
meat that is exceedingly thick— is fit for consumption; however, outside the Kali Yuga,
the meat of cows is forbidden, while the meat of pigs is permitted according to local custom.

A twice-born man should not eat the flesh of a dead mouse of two kinds, nor that of a meka, a kṣudrāṭaka, a śambūka, or a crab. If he eats these unintentionally, he becomes pure by means of breath control (prāṇāyāma).
One who eats fish or meat that has not been mentioned [as permissible] becomes pure through bathing.
Having eaten beef out of a desire for meat, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance. Likewise, having eaten the flesh of a jackal, one should perform the Ṛṣicāndrāyaṇa.
Having eaten things that have a foul odor or contain insects, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance;
having eaten things that are harsh or dried out, one is purified by means of breath control (prāṇāyāma);
and one should entirely avoid meat that has been kept for three nights.

O Pārvatī! The pure [silk] from Śalla, Parvatīya, and Siṃhatuṇḍa does not become defiled by the heat; it is likewise purified by fire. O Supreme Goddess! That which is new and consecrated with fragrant substances [is also pure].
"O Goddess! For the consumption of its flesh, no expiation exists.

From this prohibition of eating and the observation of the fault in eating it without first offering it, it follows all the more clearly that the meat is intended as an offering to the deity; furthermore, the fruit of abandoning meat is also found in that very context.
He who completely abstains from meat during the months of Libra, Capricorn,
and Aries shall obtain the very fruit of the horse-sacrifice (*hayamedha*).
Furthermore, by renouncing it for as long as he lives, he shall obtain the fruit of the royal consecration sacrifice (*rājasūya*).
O Goddess! By the avoidance of even one, there is the avoidance of fish and meat.
O Maheśānī! A householder should renounce them, except for the ancestral śrāddha rite;
whether through negligence, ignorance, or by formal resolve, he should observe this vow.
Then, having performed the Cāndrāyaṇa penance, one should perform the Paurṇamāsī rite; thereafter,
having performed the Śrāddha for the ancestors and having abstained from meat,
one should avoid untruth, or else perform the vow for the murder of a father.
O Maheśānī! One should perform the Pitṛmedha sacrifice with even one's entire possessions, for it is superior to all vows and higher than all sacrifices;
yet even more significant than that is the violation of the menstrual period of one's own wife.
When the sixteenth day is complete, the husband who had gone abroad returns;
yet, whether it be on a Hari-vāsara (the eleventh day) or on a Śrāddha day,
she must not let the fertile period pass, for that indeed is her very vow.
O Supreme Goddess! One who destroys the season (ṛtu-hā) should perform the vow for the killing of a Brahmin (brahmahatyā-vrata).
O Queen of Gods! When that vow has failed, an expiation (prāyaścitta) must follow.
Therefore, the gratification of one’s own wife should be known as the most meritorious act.
Now follows the rule concerning what may and may not be eaten, beginning with the sacrificial oblation.
In the second chapter of the Viśvasāra.
Now, O lotus-faced one, listen as I describe the foods to be consumed:
grain, milk, as well as buttermilk, milk-rice, cakes, and soup;
fresh butter, fruits, and indeed molasses mixed with milk-rice.
One who knows the ritual rules [should avoid] all fruits and flowers of various kinds,
as well as roots, leeks, lentils,
garlic, the citron, the breadfruit, bell-metal, bottle-gourd, and sour substances.
Rājamāṣa, as well as māṣa, leafy vegetables, onions, meat, red vegetables and the like, betel-leaf, oil, palm fruit, dates,
stale milk, spoiled food, and so forth.
One who eats sacrificial food (haviṣya) should avoid wearing poor clothing, as well as oil, honey-wine (mādhvī), nails and hair, anointing the body,
and improper conversation. Among the sacrificial foods,
clarified butter (sudhā) is considered foremost, followed by rice grains (vrīhi).
According to the opinion of Śaṅkara, [the offerings should be] free from alkaline salt;
likewise, barley, wheat, mung beans, milk mixed with sugar, and pleasant fruits, roots, and so forth, along with ghee, all being free from alkaline salt.
Likewise, one should avoid red clothing and razors during the consumption of sacrificial offerings (haviṣya).
In the second chapter of the Śāradā[tantra].

Alms-food, sacrificial oblations, vegetables, prescribed fruits, milk, roots, and barley-based preparations— these are the foods permitted for practitioners of mantra. The term "alms-food" (bhaikṣya) refers specifically to the student (brahmacārin) and the ascetic (yati).
The true nature of alms-seeking has been stated in the verse cited by Rāghavabhaṭṭa.

Alms should be sought from the houses of twice-born men who are endowed with Vedic conduct, pure, prosperous, and born of noble lineage; the types of sacrificial food (haviṣya) prescribed in the Smṛtis [are what should be accepted].
Winter rice that has been steamed while cold, grains such as mung beans, sesame, and barley;
peas, *kaṅgu*, and *nīvāra* millet; *vāstūka*, *hilamocikā*, sixty-day rice, black potherb, radish, and *kemuka* (except for the latter).
Kanda, rock salt, sea salt, cow's curd, and cow's clarified butter;
milk from which the cream has not been removed, jackfruit, mango, and chebulic myrobalan;
tamarind, cumin, orange, and long pepper.
Sages declare that plantains, lavalī fruits, emblic myrobalan, agallochum, and molasses— when not fried in oil— constitute *haviṣya* food;
the terms "fruit," "milk," and "root" are understood to follow as prescribed options.
Now, regarding what is not to be eaten, it is stated in the Matsyasūkta:
Coconut water in a bronze vessel, goat’s milk in a glass vessel,
and buffalo milk in a stone vessel are proclaimed to be unfit for consumption.
In the fifteenth chapter.
He who worships Varāha shall not eat boar or tortoise;
he who worships Brahmā shall avoid buffalo, yak, and *caru*;
and the worshiper of Gaṇeśa shall avoid *madhuka*, jackfruit, and *koradūṣaṇa*.
O Goddess of the gods! A devotee of Āditya [should avoid] a peacock;
a sacrificer to Śiva, sesame paste; a worshipper of the Cakra, the tamarind tree;
likewise, a devotee of mine [should avoid] the madgura fish, the śakti-tamarind, and the vaḍālaka.
O Goddess of the Gods! One seeking the goal of Tripura should not eat safflower leaves, garlic, or *śṛṅgiṇa*; likewise, one seeking the goal of Tvaritā should avoid bitter neem and mango;
and one seeking the goal of Gopāla should not consume *pālaṅka* or raw fish.
One seeking the boon of eloquence should avoid the *pārāvata*, *vāmana*, *cakraka*, *śāka*, and *vaḍālaka* plants; one desiring prosperity should avoid the *nimba* and *karañjaka*;
and likewise, one should avoid the *kālāndha*, *kodrava*, and *candramatsya*.
O Śaṅkarī! In all mantras and in all sacrifices, one should avoid the vaḍāla, the white pūtī, the vārttākī, the kuṣmāṇḍa, and that which grows on mountains.
One should diligently avoid ciñcā fruit and food belonging to others. Vaiṣṇavas should likewise avoid leafy vegetables, roots, tubers, sprouts, dried grains, rājīva, vāstūka, and pālaṅkī.

O Goddess, even if a Vaiṣṇava should ever abandon [these] through a prior resolve, he must nevertheless not abandon them; rather, he should perform an expiation. Ghee is to be avoided during the Saura vow, and betel-leaf among the Vaiṣṇavas.
One who abandons cow products is a great sinner; one who abandons honey takes away prosperity.
(From the twenty-seventh chapter.)
Jambū, kharjūra, dāḍima, nārikela, and pūgaka; jalavimbā, trapuṣa, urvāru, and pīnaka;
as well as badarī, lavalī, dhātrī, panasa, āmra, and harītakī.
The lotus-root (śālūka), clusters of lotuses, kaśeru, karamardaka, nāgaraṅga, madhuka, sweet tendukā fruits,
ānāḍa, pumpkin (kuṣmāṇḍa), and the fruit of the vāsantī— all these are sweet.
Tilakānna, peas, mung beans, and kidney beans;
rice, barley grain, and wild rice (nīvāra), as well as saffron;
cumin, cloves, coriander, and nutmeg.
Elaka, camphor, sandalwood, agallochum, mustaka, sarala, devadāru, black bhallātaka, ginger,
pungent substances, black pepper, salt, and pippalī.

The fruit of the *śivā* tree, the fruit of the *svakṣāmrā*, and that of the *panasa*; the black pod (*kṛṣṇakoṣa*), the *granthiparṇa*, sprouts from heaven, and grapes; the *vakula*, the *kacvī* fruit, and cut pieces of sugarcane.
These are for rinsing the mouth, fragrant, and also digestive;
likewise,
those from the mountains, those that are round, and those produced by deception.

One should avoid the *lakṣmī*, the *lakucha*, the *tilaka*, the small *tillaka*, the *hintāla*, the *panasa*, the *āmra*, the *pīvara*, the *baddhajīraka*, the large *śoṭā*, the *badarī*, and the mountain-grown varieties.
One should avoid the small cucumber (*urvāruka*), the small *jīvantī*,
*madhuka*, *madhurī*, grapes, and peas that are not round;
likewise, one should avoid white and black mung beans (*mudga*) and its fruit.
The coconut fruit, the golden-hued orange,
the golden-hued coconut, as well as milk-grain, Soma-grain, wild rice (nīvāra), kalamba, and sixty-day rice (ṣaṣṭika).

Large grains, small grains, bark-grown grains, and upāsuka— these, headed by *vrīhi*, are indeed fit for consumption as sacrificial offerings (*haviṣya*). Pearl-like rice and red vegetables are declared to be the best among these excellent varieties.
O Goddess, one should avoid sugarcane, white trapusa, as well as mṛgaphala fruits,
the sprouting of a jar of liquor, food grown on the riverbank,
and likewise śrāvaṇika grain when consuming sacrificial oblations (haviṣya).
O Goddess, during religious observances (*vrata*), betel leaf (*tāmbūla*) with its lime powder (*parṇacūrṇaka*) is considered meat (*āmiṣa*);
likewise, for one who is ill, even meat is considered non-meat (*nirāmiṣa*). The *lakuc* fruit is meat; furthermore, the round fruit (*vartula*) and that which is crushed by hand are not to be eaten.
O Goddess, one should avoid eggplant, white or red varieties, and even white *pūtika* during a vow; now hear the rule for a diet of fruits.
A diet of fruits accompanied by prostrations (*namaskāra*) is distinguished as superior, or else that which includes cow products (*sagavya*).
Having filled three parts [of the stomach], one should abandon water as food in the Kali age;
O Maheśānī! fruit is the food for householders in the Kali Yuga.
O Maheśvarī! regarding food consisting of sesame seeds, one may take a hundred [grains] or half of that.
If one subsists on milk, the fruit [of the fast] is equal to that of eating chickpeas; if one subsists on the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), the fruit is equal to that of eating fruit.
If one subsists on clarified butter, it is equal to one *tola* of sacrificial food (*haviṣya*). Now hear the rule for sacrificial food:
it may be cooked rice prepared by oneself, or by one's wife, or by a brother.
Having eaten for his mother, father, or teacher, or having cooked [for them],
he should eat a light meal, having conquered anger, while observing the vow of *haviṣya* food. Likewise:
The sprout of the cane (vetrāṅkura), as well as mustā, rock salt (saindhava) produced from the Indus region,
and likewise substances such as sacrificial offerings originating from the mountains, have been proclaimed. Also, the leaves of the bilva, āmalaka, sesame, and the vadhara tree.
When it is time for the consumption of sacrificial food (haviṣya), they prescribe sacrificial grain (haviṣyānna).
For the meal during the haviṣya vow, one may use a beautiful vessel, a leaf, a leaf of the Palāśa tree,
or the bark or leaf of the Kadalī plant.

In the Saura vow, one should avoid pungent substances; in the Śaiva, food; in the Vaiṣṇava, *koradūṣa* grain; and in the Śākta, one should avoid *śāli* rice. In all vows, one must renounce betel nut, as well as fermented gruel (*āranālaka*).
One should not eat what has been cut with iron, nor should one eat what is broken by hand; likewise, one should not eat food that has remained on a *kālikā* or on a jackfruit leaf.
In this world was born a righteous soul named Dayārām Viśvās, renowned for his own fame; his son was the one endowed with all virtues, named Rāmaharī.
Two sons were born to him: Śrī Sukṛtiyuta Jagannāth Mohan and Prāṇakṛṣṇa; the elder was Śrī Prāṇakṛṣṇa.
The full moon to the row of night-blooming lilies that are the assembly of the virtuous.
Instructed by him, Rāmatoṣaṇa composed the Śrī-Prāṇatoṣiṇī-vallī, which brings satisfaction to the minds of the learned and the refined.
Out of consideration for the capacity of the intended audience and out of fear of burdening the treatise with excessive length, I have not explained every detail of its composition.
O wise ones! With palms joined in reverence, I entreat you that you yourselves should investigate the entire work.
Thus ends the third section, the Arthakāṇḍāṅga, of the Śrī-Prāṇatoṣiṇī, composed by Paṇḍita Rāmatoṣaṇa Vidyālaṅkāra Bhaṭṭācārya, with the approval of Śrī Prāṇakṛṣṇa Viśvāsa.
